32644.e: The USA promised to exchange dollars held by foreign central banks for gold at this price. The other currencies had fixed exchange rates to the dollar.
32644.m: In the Bretton Woods system, an ounce of gold cost 35 dollars.

32645.q: Which two organisations were agreed on at the Bretton Woods conference?
a: International Monetary Fund and World Bank
32645.e: The International Monetary Fund was to help with balance of payments problems, and the World Bank was to finance reconstruction. Both have their headquarters in Washington.
32645.m: The IMF and the World Bank were created at Bretton Woods.

32646.q: Which British economist represented his country at Bretton Woods and proposed a world currency called the bancor?
32646.e: Keynes wanted to create an international unit of account. However, it was largely the plan of the American Harry Dexter White, with the dollar at the centre, that won.
32646.m: At Bretton Woods, Keynes proposed the bancor as a world currency.

32647.q: Which US president ended the duty to exchange dollars for gold in 1971?
32647.e: On 15 August 1971, Nixon closed the “gold window”. This “Nixon shock” began the end of the Bretton Woods system.
32647.m: The Nixon shock of 1971 ended the dollar's link to gold.

32648.q: What built-in weakness did the Bretton Woods system have?
a: The more dollars the world needed, the less the gold reserves covered them
It had no fixed exchange rates at all
Only European currencies were tied to gold
The USA was not allowed to send dollars abroad
32648.e: In 1960, the economist Robert Triffin showed that the USA had to run deficits to supply the world with dollars. The more dollars were in circulation, the less they were covered by gold.
32648.m: The Triffin dilemma describes the built-in weakness of Bretton Woods.

32649.q: When did Switzerland join the International Monetary Fund?
32649.e: Voters approved joining the IMF and the World Bank in a popular vote in May 1992. Before that, Switzerland had only taken part in the Bretton Woods system indirectly.
32649.m: Switzerland has been a member of the IMF since 1992.

32650.q: Which war triggered the first oil crisis in October 1973?
32650.e: Egypt and Syria attacked Israel. Arab oil states then cut production and imposed an embargo on countries supporting Israel.
32650.m: The oil crisis of 1973 followed the Yom Kippur War.

32651.q: How many car-free Sundays did the Federal Council order at the end of 1973 because of the oil crisis?
32651.e: In November and December 1973, the roads were closed to cars on three Sundays. Many people used them for walking, cycling or roller skating.
32651.m: Switzerland had three car-free Sundays in 1973.

32652.q: In 1973/74 the oil price rose from about 3 to about 12 dollars per barrel. By what percentage did it rise?
32652.e: The increase is 12 minus 3, which is 9 dollars. 9 divided by 3 is 3, so 300 per cent; the price therefore quadrupled.
32652.m: Quadrupling is the same as an increase of 300 per cent.

32653.q: Which organisation of oil-producing states was founded in Baghdad in 1960?
32653.e: The Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries was meant to coordinate its members' oil policies. Its headquarters are now in Vienna.
32653.m: OPEC was founded in Baghdad in 1960.

32654.q: What is the combination of stagnation and high inflation that hit many industrialised countries after 1973 called?
32654.e: Expensive energy pushed prices up while production and employment fell. The usual recipes of economic policy hardly worked.
32654.m: Stagflation combines a stagnant economy with rising prices.

32655.q: How many litres does a barrel, the usual unit of measurement for crude oil, hold?
32655.e: An American oil barrel holds 42 gallons, which is about 159 litres. Oil prices are still given in dollars per barrel today.
32655.m: A barrel of crude oil holds about 159 litres.

32656.q: Which organisation did the industrialised countries found in 1974 in response to the oil crisis?
32656.e: The IEA was meant to secure its members' energy supply, for example through shared emergency stocks. Switzerland is one of the founding members.
32656.m: The IEA was founded in 1974 as a response to the oil crisis.

32657.q: From when to when was Margaret Thatcher British Prime Minister?
32657.e: Thatcher was the first woman in this office. Her policy of privatisation and deregulation became known as Thatcherism.
32657.m: Margaret Thatcher governed Great Britain from 1979 to 1990.

32658.q: What is the economic policy of US President Ronald Reagan called?
32658.e: Reagan relied on tax cuts, deregulation and a tight monetary policy. At the same time, defence spending and the budget deficit rose.
32658.m: Reagan's economic policy is called Reaganomics.

32659.q: Where was the Mont Pelerin Society, an important network of neoliberal thinkers, founded in 1947?
32659.e: Friedrich August von Hayek invited economists and philosophers to a hotel on Mont Pèlerin above Vevey. The society still exists today.
32659.m: The Mont Pelerin Society was founded in Switzerland in 1947.

32660.q: Which book did Friedrich August von Hayek publish in 1944?
32660.e: In it, Hayek warned that a state-planned economy leads to a loss of freedom. The book became a key text of neoliberalism.
32660.m: In “The Road to Serfdom”, Hayek warned against the planned economy.

32661.q: Which university is the economist Milton Friedman and his monetarist school closely linked to?
32661.e: Friedman taught in Chicago for decades and received the Nobel Prize in Economics in 1976. The Chicago School stressed free markets and controlling the money supply.
32661.m: Milton Friedman shaped the Chicago School.

32662.q: Which state-owned company did the Thatcher government privatise in 1984 with a large share sale?
32662.e: The sale of the telephone company was the largest stock market flotation in the world at the time. Many private individuals bought shares for the first time.
32662.m: The privatisation of British Telecom in 1984 became a symbol of Thatcherism.

32663.q: What is the deregulation of the London financial centre on 27 October 1986 called?
32663.e: Fixed commissions were scrapped and electronic trading replaced the trading floor. As a result, London became one of the most important financial centres in the world.
32663.m: The Big Bang of 1986 deregulated the London financial centre.

32664.q: What was the bundle of neoliberal reform recommendations for developing countries drawn up in 1989 called?
32664.e: In it, the economist John Williamson summed up the demands of the IMF, the World Bank and the US government. They included budget discipline, privatisation and trade liberalisation.
32664.m: The Washington Consensus summed up neoliberal reforms.

32665.q: During which period did the witch hunts in Central Europe reach their peak?
32665.e: The great waves of persecution did not fall in the Middle Ages but in the early modern period. Mass trials took place especially between about 1560 and 1630.
32665.m: The witch hunts were above all a phenomenon of the early modern period.

32666.q: What is the name of Heinrich Kramer's work, published in 1486, that gave a theoretical justification for the witch hunts?
32666.e: The “Malleus Maleficarum”, in English “Hammer of Witches”, described supposed witchcraft and how to act against it. Thanks to printing, it spread widely.
32666.m: The Hammer of Witches of 1486 provided instructions for persecuting witches.

32667.q: Who is considered the last person in Europe to be executed as a “witch”?
32667.e: Anna Göldi was executed in Glarus in 1782, officially for poisoning, but in fact as a witch. In 2008 she was cleared by the Glarus cantonal parliament.
32667.m: Anna Göldi from Glarus is considered Europe's last executed witch.

32668.q: Which test was meant to show whether someone was a witch by throwing the tied-up person into water?
32668.e: Anyone who floated on the surface was considered guilty, because the pure water supposedly rejected a pact with the Devil. The test was disputed even among lawyers of the time.
32668.m: The swimming test was a cruel trial by ordeal in the witch hunts.

32669.q: Which criminal code issued by Emperor Charles V in 1532 formed the legal basis for many witch trials in the Empire?
32669.e: The “Carolina” regulated criminal procedure and also the use of torture. It threatened harmful sorcery with death by burning.
32669.m: The Carolina of 1532 was the criminal code of the Holy Roman Empire.

32670.q: According to today's estimates, what share of the people executed as witches were women?
32670.e: About 75 to 80 per cent of the victims were women. In some regions, however, many men were also convicted.
32670.m: Most victims of the witch hunts were women.

32671.q: In which region of today's Switzerland did some of the earliest witch trials in Europe take place around 1428?
32671.e: In Valais, persecutions began around 1428, in which the idea of a sect of witches appeared for the first time. Western Switzerland was one of the early centres of persecution.
32671.m: Valais was an early centre of witch trials.

32672.q: What characterises the second stage of the demographic transition model?
a: The death rate falls, the birth rate stays high
The birth rate falls, the death rate stays high
32672.e: In the early transition stage, better food and hygiene lower mortality. At first the birth rate stays high, so the population grows strongly.
32672.m: In the second stage, the gap between births and deaths opens up.

32673.q: In the demographic transition model, what is the gap between the birth rate and the death rate called?
32673.e: The difference between the two rates gives the natural population growth. In the transition stage, this gap is especially wide.
32673.m: The wider the population gap, the faster the population grows.

32674.q: Which scholar warned in 1798 that the population was growing faster than food production?
32674.e: Malthus believed that the population grows geometrically, but food only arithmetically. Famines were therefore unavoidable.
32674.m: Malthus saw population growth as a danger to the food supply.

32675.q: Roughly how high must the average number of children per woman be in industrialised countries for a population to stay stable without immigration?
32675.e: This replacement level is a little above 2 because not all children reach adulthood. Switzerland has been well below it for decades.
32675.m: The replacement level is about 2.1 children per woman.

32676.q: Which factor contributed especially to the fall in the death rate in Europe in the 19th century?
32676.e: Higher farm yields, clean water and sewers lowered mortality. Antibiotics only came into widespread use in the 20th century.
32676.m: Food and hygiene lowered mortality in the 19th century.

32677.q: What characterises the late stage of the demographic transition in today's industrialised countries?
a: High birth rate, low death rate
Low birth rate, high death rate
32677.e: At the end of the transition, both rates are low and growth is small or negative. As a result, society ages.
32677.m: At the end of the demographic transition, society ages.

32678.q: What characterises the first stage of the demographic transition model?
a: High birth rate and high death rate
Low birth rate and low death rate
High birth rate, low death rate
Low birth rate, high death rate
32678.e: In pre-industrial societies, many children were born, but hunger and epidemics led to many deaths. The population therefore grew only slowly.
32678.m: In the first stage, high births and high mortality balance each other out.

32679.q: Which island near New York served as the main immigration station of the USA from 1892?
32679.e: Around 12 million people were processed on Ellis Island until 1954. Today there is an immigration museum there.
32679.m: Ellis Island was the immigrants' gateway to America.

32680.q: Which settlement in Wisconsin was founded in 1845 by emigrants from a Swiss canton?
32680.e: Families from Glarus fled poverty and unemployment in the textile industry. New Glarus still keeps up Swiss traditions today.
32680.m: New Glarus in Wisconsin was founded by emigrants from Glarus.

32681.q: Which US law of 1862 promised settlers about 160 acres of land if they farmed it?
32681.e: Anyone who farmed the land for five years became its owner. This attracted many European emigrants to the West.
32681.m: The Homestead Act attracted settlers with free land.

32682.q: Which event triggered mass emigration from Ireland in the years 1845 to 1849?
a: The Great Famine caused by potato blight
32682.e: A fungus destroyed the potato harvest, the main food, several times. About one million people died and millions emigrated.
32682.m: Potato blight drove many Irish people to America.

32683.q: What were the political refugees who went to the USA after the failed revolution of 1848 called?
32683.e: Liberals and democrats such as Carl Schurz fled persecution. In the USA, many of them campaigned against slavery.
32683.m: The Forty-Eighters were revolutionaries of 1848 who fled to America.

32684.q: Which famine crisis after the eruption of the Tambora volcano triggered a wave of emigration from Switzerland in 1816 and 1817?
32684.e: Ash from Tambora cooled the climate in 1816 and harvests failed. There was a bitter famine in eastern Switzerland.
32684.m: After the Year Without a Summer, many Swiss people emigrated.

32685.q: Which port at the mouth of the Weser was an important emigration port in the 19th century?
32685.e: Millions of people travelled overseas from Bremerhaven. Today the German Emigration Centre there remembers them.
32685.m: Bremerhaven was a major emigration port on the Weser.

32686.q: What greatly shortened the crossing to America in the second half of the 19th century?
a: The building of the Panama Canal
The opening of the Suez Canal
32686.e: Sailing ships often took six weeks or more. Steamers covered the distance in a few days to about two weeks.
32686.m: Steamships made crossing the Atlantic faster and safer.

32687.q: What is the middle-class group that defined itself mainly through university education, such as doctors, lawyers and professors, called?
32687.e: The educated middle class (Bildungsbürgertum) drew its prestige from knowledge and culture. The business middle class, by contrast, relied on property and companies.
32687.m: The educated middle class defined itself through education rather than birth.

32688.q: What is the era between 1815 and 1848 that stands for middle-class home life and withdrawal into private life called?
32688.e: Under the Restoration, many middle-class people withdrew from politics into family life. Furniture, music-making at home and cosiness shaped the style.
32688.m: Biedermeier stands for middle-class domestic life.

32689.q: Which middle-class political movement provided all the Federal Councillors in the Swiss federal state from 1848 to 1891?
32689.e: Liberals and Radicals had won the Sonderbund War and shaped the federal state. Only in 1891 was a Catholic Conservative, Josef Zemp, elected.
32689.m: As the party of the middle class, the Liberals shaped the young federal state.

32690.q: Which role model shaped the middle-class family in the 19th century?
a: Husband at work, wife at home
Wife at work, husband at home
32690.e: The middle class separated the man's public sphere from the woman's private sphere. Working-class families usually could not afford this ideal.
32690.m: The middle-class family divided paid work and housework by gender.

32691.q: Which 1901 novel by Thomas Mann describes the decline of a merchant family from Lübeck?
32691.e: The novel shows the decline of a middle-class family over four generations. Thomas Mann received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1929.
32691.m: Buddenbrooks tells of the decline of a merchant family.

32692.q: Which musical instrument was a typical status symbol in the 19th-century middle-class drawing room?
32692.e: A piano in the living room showed wealth and education. Daughters often had piano lessons as part of their upbringing.
32692.m: The piano was a sign of middle-class education.

32693.q: Which form of organisation was particularly typical of the social and political life of the middle class in the 19th century?
32693.e: Gymnastics, choral and shooting clubs combined socialising with national and liberal ideas. In Switzerland, national festivals strengthened national feeling.
32693.m: The 19th century was the century of clubs and associations.

32694.q: What did Marx call the rule of the working class in the transition period after a revolution?
32694.e: According to Marx, the proletariat should take power to get rid of the old class order. At the end there would be a classless society.
32694.m: For Marx, the dictatorship of the proletariat was a transition stage.

32695.q: According to the Communist Manifesto, which two classes face each other in modern society?
32695.e: According to Marx and Engels, bourgeois society splits into owners of the means of production and wage workers. Their conflict drives history forward.
32695.m: In the Manifesto, the bourgeoisie and the proletariat fight each other.

32696.q: Which philosopher influenced the young Marx so strongly that Marx reinterpreted his dialectics in a materialist way?
32696.e: In Berlin, Marx belonged to the Young Hegelians. He took over Hegel's dialectics but replaced the spirit with material conditions as the driving force.
32696.m: Marx turned Hegel's dialectics upside down.

32697.q: What did Marx call the value that workers create beyond their wages and that the capitalist keeps?
32697.e: According to Marx, workers receive only the equivalent of their labour power. The entrepreneur takes the extra value they create.
32697.m: For Marx, surplus value is the source of profit.

32698.q: Which newspaper did Karl Marx run in 1842 and 1843 before it was banned by the censors?
32698.e: As editor-in-chief, Marx sharply criticised the Prussian government. After the ban he went to Paris.
32698.m: Marx began his career as a journalist at the Rheinische Zeitung.

32699.q: What is Marx's view of history called, according to which economic conditions shape society?
32699.e: According to Marx, the mode of production determines politics, law and culture. History appears as a series of class struggles.
32699.m: Historical materialism explains history through the economy.

32700.q: What does Marx call the state in which workers become estranged from the product of their work and from themselves?
32700.e: In the Paris Manuscripts of 1844, Marx described how the worker has no control over his product. Work thus becomes a mere duty instead of self-fulfilment.
32700.m: Alienation is a key concept of the young Marx.

32701.q: Who paid the contributions to the German health insurance of 1883?
32701.e: The insured paid two thirds and the employers one third of the contributions. The state did not contribute directly.
32701.m: The first health insurance was paid for jointly by workers and employers.

32702.q: Which law of 1878 was the “stick” in Bismarck's social policy?
32702.e: The Anti-Socialist Law banned social democratic associations and newspapers. With social insurance as the “carrot”, Bismarck wanted to turn the workers away from socialism.
32702.m: Bismarck combined repression and social reform.

32703.q: From what age did workers originally receive an old-age pension under the law of 1889?
32703.e: The age limit was first set at 70, which few people reached. In 1916 it was lowered to 65.
32703.m: The first German old-age pension was only paid from the age of 70.

32704.q: Who financed the accident insurance of 1884 in the German Empire?
32704.e: Business owners paid the contributions through employers' liability associations. In return, they were largely freed from liability for accidents at work.
32704.m: Accident insurance was paid for by the employers.

32705.q: Which social insurance did the German Empire under Bismarck introduce first?
32705.e: After the Imperial Message of 1881 came health insurance in 1883, accident insurance in 1884 and old-age and disability insurance in 1889. Unemployment insurance only came in 1927.
32705.m: The health insurance of 1883 was Bismarck's first social insurance.

32706.q: Which Swiss federal law of 1877 limited working hours in factories to 11 hours a day?
32706.e: The Factory Act also banned factory work for children under 14. It was considered one of the most progressive laws protecting workers in Europe.
32706.m: The Factory Act of 1877 protected Swiss factory workers.

32707.q: In which year did the AHV (old-age insurance) come into force in Switzerland?
32707.e: The people clearly approved the AHV Act in 1947, and it came into force on 1 January 1948. The constitutional article for it dated back to 1925.
32707.m: The Swiss AHV has existed since 1948.

32708.q: Which pioneers founded a consumer cooperative in England in 1844 that is seen as the model for modern cooperatives?
32708.e: The “Rochdale Society of Equitable Pioneers” sold food to its members at fair prices. Its principles still shape cooperatives today.
32708.m: The Rochdale Pioneers founded the modern consumer cooperative.

32709.q: Who founded rural loan societies in the 19th century to protect farmers from moneylenders?
32709.e: Raiffeisen was a mayor in the Westerwald and saw the hardship of the farmers. His societies were based on self-help and joint liability.
32709.m: Raiffeisen founded savings and loan societies for farmers.

32710.q: In which legal form have the Raiffeisen banks in Switzerland been organised since their beginnings around 1900?
32710.e: The first Swiss Raiffeisen bank was set up in 1900 in Bichelsee in Thurgau, following the German model. The Raiffeisen banks are still cooperatives owned by their members today.
32710.m: The Raiffeisen banks in Switzerland are cooperatives.

32711.q: Which principle applies to votes in a classic cooperative?
a: Votes according to share of capital
32711.e: Unlike in a public limited company, the capital invested does not count. Every member has an equal say.
32711.m: In a cooperative, every member has one vote.

32712.q: Who is considered the founder of the credit cooperatives for tradespeople from which the Volksbanken grew?
32712.e: Schulze-Delitzsch aimed at craftsmen and small business owners in the towns. He relied consistently on self-help without state aid.

32713.q: In which year did Gottlieb Duttweiler turn Migros into cooperatives?
32713.e: Migros was founded in 1925 as a public limited company. In 1941, Duttweiler gave it to his customers in the form of cooperatives.
32713.m: Migros has been organised as cooperatives since 1941.

32714.q: Which recognition did the idea of cooperatives receive from UNESCO in 2016?
32714.e: At Germany's request, the idea and practice of cooperatives was added to the list of intangible cultural heritage. It was the first German element to be listed there.
32714.m: The idea of cooperatives is intangible cultural heritage of humanity.

32715.q: How did John Snow prove in London in 1854 that cholera is spread through water?
a: He mapped cases around a water pump
He found the pathogen under the microscope
32715.e: Snow marked the deaths in Soho on a map, and they clustered around the pump in Broad Street. After the pump handle was removed, the epidemic died down.
32715.m: Using a map, John Snow discovered the link between cholera and drinking water.

32716.q: Which German doctor identified the cholera pathogen in 1883 and made it known?
32716.e: Robert Koch found the bacterium on an expedition to Egypt and India. The Italian Filippo Pacini had already described it in 1854, but nobody paid attention.
32716.m: Robert Koch made the cholera pathogen known.

32717.q: Why was the cholera epidemic of 1892 in Hamburg much worse than in neighbouring Altona?
a: Hamburg did not filter its drinking water
32717.e: Hamburg took unfiltered water from the Elbe, while Altona had a sand filter plant. About 8,600 people died in Hamburg.
32717.m: Clean drinking water protected Altona from cholera in 1892.

32718.q: Which measure did hygienists such as Max von Pettenkofer promote in the 19th century to contain epidemics such as cholera?
a: Sewers and a clean water supply
32718.e: In 1865, Pettenkofer was given the first chair of hygiene in Munich. He campaigned for sewers and clean drinking water, which made towns healthier.
32718.m: Sewers and clean water pushed back epidemics in the towns.

32719.q: Which event in 1858 led to the building of a modern sewer system in London?
32719.e: In the hot summer of 1858, the polluted Thames smelled unbearable. Afterwards, Joseph Bazalgette built a sewer system that also helped contain cholera.
32719.m: The Great Stink gave London a modern sewer system.

32720.e: The cholera pathogen gets into water with faeces and is then drunk. That is why in the 19th century, for example in 1867 in the canton of Zurich, cholera hit mainly districts without clean water.

32721.q: From which region did cholera spread to Europe in several pandemics from 1817?
32721.e: The first cholera pandemic began in 1817 in the Ganges delta. From 1830, the disease also reached Europe.
32721.m: In the 19th century, cholera came to Europe from India.

32722.q: Why was the flu pandemic of 1918 named the “Spanish flu”?
32722.e: Neutral Spain did not censor the reports, unlike the countries at war. That is why the disease seemed especially widespread there.
32722.m: The Spanish flu did not come from Spain.

32723.q: How many people in Switzerland died of the Spanish flu between July 1918 and June 1919?
32723.e: According to the Historical Dictionary of Switzerland, 24,449 people died, about 0.6 per cent of the population. Around 2 million people fell ill.
32723.m: The Spanish flu was Switzerland's greatest demographic disaster of the 20th century.

32724.q: Which age group was unusually badly hit by deaths from the Spanish flu?
32724.e: Normally, flu kills mainly the elderly and small children. In 1918 it hit young adults particularly hard, which made the death curve W-shaped.
32724.m: The Spanish flu killed a strikingly large number of young adults.

32725.q: Which subtype of the influenza virus caused the Spanish flu?
32725.e: Researchers reconstructed the virus from tissue samples taken from victims. It was an influenza A virus of the type H1N1.
32725.m: The Spanish flu was caused by an H1N1 virus.

32726.q: Which political event in Switzerland coincided with the second wave of flu in November 1918?
32726.e: Soldiers sent in to keep order fell ill in huge numbers, and hundreds died. The middle classes and the workers blamed each other.
32726.m: The general strike and the flu sharpened tensions in Switzerland in 1918.

32727.q: Which wave of the Spanish flu was the deadliest?
32727.e: The first wave in spring was mostly mild. In autumn 1918 the virus came back much more dangerous.
32727.m: The second wave in autumn 1918 claimed the most victims.

32728.q: Which measures did Swiss cantons take in 1918 against the spread of the flu?
32728.e: In many places schools, cinemas and churches were closed and events were banned. Vaccines and antibiotics did not exist yet.
32728.m: Against the flu of 1918, only distance and bans helped.

32729.q: What did the Federal Constitution of 1874 require for primary school?
a: It had to be compulsory and free at state schools
It was run by the Confederation instead of the cantons
It had to be held in German in all cantons
It could only be run by the Church
32729.e: The constitution demanded sufficient, compulsory and free primary education under state control. However, responsibility for schools stayed with the cantons.
32729.m: The Federal Constitution of 1874 made primary school compulsory and free.

32730.q: Which proposal did Swiss voters reject in 1882 because they feared federal supervision of schools?
32730.e: The plan was for a federal secretary for education. Conservatives fought the “Schulvogt” as an attack on cantonal and church rights.
32730.m: The Schulvogt was clearly defeated at the ballot box in 1882.

32731.q: Which survey of all schools in Switzerland did the Helvetic education minister carry out in 1799?
32731.e: Philipp Albert Stapfer had teachers asked about school buildings, pupil numbers and pay. The answers are a unique source for the history of schools.
32731.m: The Stapfer survey shows the state of schools around 1800.

32732.q: Which tests made the differences in education between the cantons publicly visible from 1875?
32732.e: When they were called up, young men were tested in reading, writing, arithmetic and civics. The cantons were then compared in league tables.
32732.m: The recruit tests compared the level of education in the cantons.

32733.q: With which decree did Frederick II introduce compulsory schooling for country children in Prussia in 1763?
32733.e: The regulations required children to attend school from the age of 5 to 13 or 14. Because there were too few teachers, it was put into practice only patchily for a long time.
32733.m: Prussia introduced compulsory schooling early, at least on paper.

32734.q: Why did the Reformation promote literacy?
a: Believers were supposed to read the Bible themselves
The Church banned pictures in books
32734.e: Luther and Zwingli stressed studying the Bible for yourself. Bible translations into the everyday language and catechisms encouraged schools.
32734.m: The Reformation made reading a matter of faith.

32735.q: Which Swiss educator shaped state schools with the motto “head, heart and hand”?
32735.e: Pestalozzi worked in places such as Stans, Burgdorf and Yverdon. He called for a well-rounded education, also for poor children.
32735.m: Pestalozzi wanted to educate head, heart and hand equally.

32736.q: In which year did Great Britain ban the slave trade in its empire?
32736.e: The Slave Trade Act of 1807 banned trading in enslaved people. Slavery itself was only abolished by the law of 1833.
32736.m: Great Britain banned the slave trade in 1807.

32737.q: Which British Member of Parliament led the fight against the slave trade for decades?
32737.e: From 1789, Wilberforce brought motions to Parliament again and again. He died in 1833, shortly after the abolition of slavery had been agreed.
32737.m: William Wilberforce was the leading figure of the British abolitionists.

32738.q: Which state was created in 1804 from a successful uprising of enslaved people?
32738.e: In the French colony of Saint-Domingue, enslaved people rose up from 1791. In 1804, Haiti was declared an independent republic.
32738.m: Haiti came out of the only successful slave revolution.

32739.q: Which escaped enslaved woman led many enslaved people to freedom via the “Underground Railroad”?
32739.e: Harriet Tubman escaped from Maryland in 1849 and went back several times to free others. The Underground Railroad was a secret network of helpers.
32739.m: Harriet Tubman became the symbol of helping people escape.

32740.q: Which country was the last in the Americas to abolish slavery, in 1888?
32740.e: Slavery in Brazil was ended with the “Golden Law” (Lei Áurea). No other country had brought in so many enslaved people from Africa.
32740.m: In 1888, Brazil was the last country in the Americas to end slavery.

32741.q: Which 1852 novel by Harriet Beecher Stowe strengthened the movement against slavery in the USA?
32741.e: The novel described the suffering of enslaved people and became a bestseller. It sharpened the conflict between the northern and southern states.
32741.m: Uncle Tom's Cabin shook up the American public.

32742.q: In which year did France finally abolish slavery in its colonies?
32742.e: The National Convention had already abolished slavery in 1794, but Napoleon brought it back in 1802. Victor Schoelcher pushed through the final abolition in 1848.

32743.q: Which measure in June 1948 is seen as the starting signal for the West German economic miracle?
a: The currency reform with the Deutsche Mark
The building of the Berlin Wall
32743.e: On 20 June 1948, the Reichsmark was replaced by the Deutsche Mark. Overnight, the shop windows filled up with goods again.
32743.m: The currency reform of 1948 started the economic miracle.

32744.q: Which economics minister is considered the father of the social market economy in West Germany?
32744.e: In 1948, Ludwig Erhard lifted many price controls and relied on competition. He was economics minister from 1949 to 1963.
32744.m: Ludwig Erhard shaped the social market economy.

32745.q: What was the US aid programme that supported the rebuilding of Western Europe from 1948 called?
32745.e: The European Recovery Program went back to a speech by Secretary of State George C. Marshall in 1947. It provided loans, raw materials and food.
32745.m: The Marshall Plan helped rebuild Western Europe.

32746.q: What are the boom years from 1945 to about 1975 called in France?
32746.e: The term comes from the economist Jean Fourastié in 1979. It describes three decades of strong growth and full employment.
32746.m: The Trente Glorieuses were France's thirty golden years.

32747.q: Which event in 1973 ended the long post-war boom in Europe?
a: The fall of the Berlin Wall
32747.e: The Arab oil-producing countries cut oil production and the oil price rose sharply. In Switzerland, a recession followed in which hundreds of thousands of jobs were lost.
32747.m: The oil crisis of 1973 ended the post-war boom.

32748.q: Which car became the symbol of the West German economic miracle?
32748.e: The Beetle was built millions of times and made the car affordable for large parts of the population. The Trabant, by contrast, was the car of East Germany.
32748.m: The VW Beetle stood for the rise of West Germany.

32749.q: Where did Migros open Switzerland's first self-service shop in 1948?
32749.e: The shop on Zurich's Seidengasse took over the idea from the USA. Customers now took the goods off the shelves themselves.
32749.m: Self-service came to Switzerland with Migros in 1948.

32750.q: Which shopping centre opened in 1970 as the first large shopping centre in Switzerland?
32750.e: Shoppi Tivoli in Aargau relied on customers coming by car and on large car parks. It took over the American model of the mall.
32750.m: The first large Swiss shopping centre was built in Spreitenbach.

a: Buying to show others your own status
32751.e: The economist Thorstein Veblen coined the term in 1899. It means consumption that mainly shows off wealth and prestige, such as expensive designer clothes or luxury cars.
32751.m: Conspicuous consumption serves mainly as a status symbol.

32752.q: Which method of production made the Model T car affordable for many people from 1913?
a: Home working in the putting-out system
32752.e: With the assembly line, Henry Ford drastically cut production time and costs. The term Fordism stands for mass production and mass consumption.
32752.m: The assembly line made mass consumption possible.

32753.q: Where was the first stretch of motorway in Switzerland opened in 1955?
32753.e: The short stretch ran from Lucerne to Ennethorw. Mass car ownership became a feature of the consumer society.
32753.m: The first Swiss motorway was built near Lucerne in 1955.

32754.q: What did Vance Packard criticise in his 1957 bestseller “The Hidden Persuaders”?
a: The power of the trade unions
32754.e: Packard described how advertising experts use psychology to appeal to unconscious desires. The book became an international bestseller.
32754.m: Vance Packard drew attention to manipulation through advertising.

32755.q: What did the economist John Kenneth Galbraith criticise in his 1958 book “The Affluent Society”?
a: That private wealth exists alongside public poverty
That workers' wages are too high
That the state builds too many schools
32755.e: Galbraith described the affluent society and criticised the fact that private wealth existed alongside public poverty.
32755.m: Galbraith criticised the contrast between private wealth and public poverty.

32756.q: Whose death in Berlin on 2 June 1967 radicalised the student movement?
32756.e: Benno Ohnesorg was shot by a police officer at a demonstration against the Shah of Persia. His death set off protests across West Germany.
32756.m: The death of Benno Ohnesorg became a beacon for the 68ers.

32757.q: What is the Zurich street battle of June 1968, in which young people demanded an autonomous youth centre, called?
32757.e: The young people demanded the empty temporary Globus building as a youth centre. On 29 June 1968, there were violent clashes with the police.
32757.m: The Globus riot of 1968 was the high point of Zurich's 68ers.

32758.q: Which French president came under pressure from student protests and a general strike in May 1968?
32758.e: The protests began at the universities, then millions of workers went on strike. De Gaulle dissolved parliament and won the new elections, but resigned in 1969.
32758.m: In May 1968, President de Gaulle came under pressure.

32759.q: Which spokesman of the West German student movement was seriously injured in an assassination attempt in April 1968?
32759.e: On 11 April 1968, a young labourer shot at Dutschke in Berlin. Afterwards there were blockades against the Springer publishing house.
32759.m: The attack on Rudi Dutschke intensified the protests of 1968.

32760.q: Which war was a main reason for the worldwide student protests of the late 1960s?
32760.e: Television pictures of the war outraged many young people. Protests against the way the USA waged the war linked movements on several continents.
32760.m: The Vietnam War mobilised young people worldwide.

32761.q: What was the political opposition outside the Bundestag during the Grand Coalition in West Germany called?
32761.e: The Extra-Parliamentary Opposition arose because there was hardly any opposition left in the Bundestag. Among other things, it fought against the emergency laws of 1968.
32761.m: The APO moved protest onto the streets.

32762.q: Which philosopher of the Frankfurt School became a leading thinker of the student movement with “One-Dimensional Man”?
32762.e: In 1964, Marcuse argued that consumer society suppresses critical thinking. His writings were read by many students.
32762.m: Herbert Marcuse supplied the 68 movement with theoretical ideas.

32763.q: What was the shared flat founded in West Berlin in 1967 that attacked middle-class ways of life with provocative actions called?
32763.e: Kommune I rejected the nuclear family and private property and sought provocation in the media. It became the symbol of the alternative lifestyles of the 68ers.
32763.m: Kommune I questioned the middle-class nuclear family.

32764.q: According to Caesar, which Helvetian nobleman planned the Helvetii’s move to Gaul?
32764.e: Orgetorix persuaded the Helvetii to leave and wanted to gain power for himself in the process. He died before they set off, but the plan was carried out anyway.
32764.m: Orgetorix planned the departure of the Helvetii.

32765.q: Who, as the aged leader of the Helvetii, negotiated with Caesar in 58 BC, having defeated a Roman army decades earlier?
32765.e: In 107 BC Divico led a Helvetian force to victory over a Roman consular army. In 58 BC he appeared before Caesar as an envoy.
32765.m: Divico embodied the old military glory of the Helvetii against Rome.

32766.q: Why could the Helvetii not cross the Rhône at Geneva into the Roman province in 58 BC?
a: Caesar had the Rhône bridge torn down and blocked the way
A flood had swept away all the bridges
32766.e: Caesar hurried to Geneva, had the bridge destroyed and fortified the riverbank. The Helvetii therefore had to take a detour over the Jura.
32766.m: In 58 BC Caesar blocked the Helvetii’s way at Geneva.

32767.q: According to Caesar, in which script were the population lists found in the Helvetii’s camp written?
32767.e: The Celts often used the Greek alphabet for lists and inscriptions. Caesar reports that the lists were written in Greek letters.
32767.m: The Helvetii wrote their lists in Greek letters.

32768.q: What did the Helvetii have to do after their defeat at Bibracte?
a: Return to their homeland and rebuild their settlements
32768.e: Caesar did not want the land of the Helvetii to stay empty so that Germanic tribes could move in. He therefore sent them back and had them rebuild their settlements.
32768.m: After Bibracte the Helvetii had to return home.

32769.q: According to Caesar, what did the Helvetii do before setting off in 58 BC so that nobody would want to turn back?
a: They burned their towns and villages
They destroyed all the bridges over the Rhine
They sacrificed their weapons to the gods
32769.e: According to Caesar, the Helvetii set fire to about 12 towns and 400 villages. They took only enough flour for three months, so there was no going back.
32769.m: Before leaving, the Helvetii burned down their settlements.

32770.q: From which source do we know most about the Battle of Bibracte?
a: From Caesar’s account of the Gallic War
32770.e: Caesar described the campaign himself in “De bello Gallico”. Because he was both the commander and the author, his account must be read critically.
32770.m: Our main source on Bibracte is Caesar himself.

32771.q: Which Roman province was created after the Alpine campaign in the area of today’s Grisons, Tyrol and southern Bavaria?
32771.e: After the conquest in 15 BC the area became the province of Raetia. Its name lives on in the word Romansh (in German Rätoromanisch).
32771.m: The province of Raetia came out of the Alpine campaign.

32772.q: On which body of water was there a naval battle fought by the Romans under Tiberius during the Alpine campaign of 15 BC?
32772.e: Tiberius advanced from the west and defeated the Vindelici, among other places in a battle on Lake Constance, as Strabo reports.
32772.m: In 15 BC Tiberius even fought with ships on Lake Constance.

32773.q: Which victory monument at La Turbie above Monaco celebrates the conquest of the Alpine peoples under Augustus?
32773.e: The Tropaeum Alpium was built around 7/6 BC. Its inscription lists 46 defeated Alpine peoples.
32773.m: The Tropaeum Alpium at La Turbie names the defeated Alpine peoples.

32774.q: What strategic consequence did the Alpine campaign of 15 BC have for Rome?
a: The Alpine passes and the land up to the Danube came under Roman control
Rome lost the province of Gallia Narbonensis
The Helvetii were settled in Gaul
Rome gave Valais to the Germanic tribes
32774.e: With the campaign Augustus secured the direct routes from Italy over the Alps to the north. The area up to the Danube became part of the Roman domain.
32774.m: The Alpine campaign opened the routes over the Alps to the Danube for Rome.

32775.q: Which present-day Swiss town was called Curia in Roman times and became the capital of the province of Raetia prima?
32775.e: Curia lay on the important route over the passes of the Grisons. In late antiquity the town became the capital of the province of Raetia prima and later the seat of a bishop.
32775.m: In late antiquity Chur was the capital of the province of Raetia prima.

32776.q: Which national language recalls the Roman province of Raetia in its German name?
32776.e: Romansh developed from the Latin spoken in the province of Raetia. Its German name, Rätoromanisch, refers to the Raeti, the earlier inhabitants of the area.
32776.m: Romansh carries the name of the province of Raetia in German.

32777.q: Which Roman province bordered Raetia to the east?
32777.e: East of the river Inn began the province of Noricum, roughly in the area of today’s Austria. In the west Raetia bordered Germania superior.
32777.m: Raetia bordered the province of Noricum at the Inn.

32778.q: Which border fortification protected the province of Raetia in the north from the 2nd century?
32778.e: The Raetian Limes was about 166 km long and joined the Upper Germanic Limes. In the late 2nd century parts of it were rebuilt as a stone wall.
32778.m: The Raetian Limes secured Raetia’s northern border.

32779.q: Which abbreviation for Switzerland goes back to the name of the Helvetii?
32779.e: The Latin name of the state, Confoederatio Helvetica, recalls the Celtic Helvetii. This is where the abbreviation CH and the name Helvetia on coins come from.
32779.m: The abbreviation CH stands for Confoederatio Helvetica.

32780.q: What legal status did the Helvetii get in relation to Rome after 58 BC?
32780.e: Caesar concluded a treaty of alliance (foedus) with the Helvetii. They kept self-government but were under Roman supremacy.
32780.m: After Bibracte the Helvetii were foederati allied with Rome.

32781.q: Which Roman historian reports on the fate of the Helvetii in AD 69?
32781.e: In his “Histories”, Tacitus describes the Year of the Four Emperors, 69. In it he tells how the Helvetii were caught between the sides and harshly punished.
32781.m: Tacitus reports on the Helvetii in the Year of the Four Emperors.

32782.q: What happened to the Helvetii in the civil war year of AD 69?
a: They were harshly punished by troops of Vitellius under Caecina
They founded an empire of their own
They were given the province of Raetia
32782.e: The Helvetii sided with Galba and clashed with troops of Vitellius. Caecina then had their territory laid waste, and many Helvetii were killed or enslaved.
32782.m: In the Year of the Four Emperors, AD 69, the Helvetii suffered from Caecina’s punitive campaign.

32783.q: Which Roman town was the capital of the Helvetii?
32783.e: Aventicum, today’s Avenches in the canton of Vaud, was the capital of the Civitas Helvetiorum. Remains of the amphitheatre and the town wall can still be seen today.
32783.m: Aventicum, today Avenches, was the capital of the Helvetii.

32784.q: Under which Roman emperor was Aventicum raised to the status of a colony?
32784.e: Vespasian had personal ties to the Helvetii; his father had lived among them. Around AD 71 he made Aventicum a colony, after which the town flourished.

32785.q: Which present-day place in the canton of Vaud stands on the site of the Roman town of Aventicum?
32785.e: Aventicum was the capital of the Helvetii. The Romans called Nyon Noviodunum, Yverdon Eburodunum and Martigny Octodurus.

32786.q: What was the importance of Aventicum in Roman times?
a: It was the capital of the Helvetii
It was the largest legionary camp on the Rhine
It was the capital of the province of Raetia
It was the most important town of the Allobroges
32786.e: Aventicum was the capital of the civitas of the Helvetii and became a colony under Emperor Vespasian around AD 70. The large legionary camp was at Vindonissa.
32786.m: Aventicum was the capital of the Helvetii.

32787.q: Which famous find from Aventicum shows a Roman emperor?
a: A gold bust of Marcus Aurelius
A bronze equestrian statue of Augustus
32787.e: The gold bust was found in 1939 in a drain near the Cigognier temple. A copy stands in the Roman Museum in Avenches, the original in the museum in Lausanne.
32787.m: The gold bust of Emperor Marcus Aurelius was found in Aventicum.

32788.q: Which Roman building in Avenches is used for operas and concerts today?
32788.e: Gladiator fights used to take place in the well-preserved amphitheatre. Today it hosts the Avenches Opera Festival and rock concerts.
32788.m: The amphitheatre of Avenches is used as an open-air stage today.

32789.q: Where does the Cigognier temple in Avenches get its name from?
a: From storks that nested on its last column
32789.e: Cigogne is the French word for stork. For a long time storks nested on the only column still standing.
32789.m: The Cigognier is named after the storks on its column.

32790.q: Where did Bishop Marius move his seat from Aventicum to in the late 6th century?
32790.e: Marius of Avenches moved the bishop’s seat to Lausanne. With that, Aventicum finally lost its role as a capital.
32790.m: Under Marius of Avenches the bishop’s seat moved to Lausanne.

32791.q: How was Aventicum connected to the waterway to the Aare and the Rhine?
a: Through harbours on Lake Murten and a canal
Through a canal directly to Lake Geneva
Via the Rhône and the Great St Bernard
32791.e: Aventicum had a harbour on the southern shore of Lake Murten and one at the end of a canal. Via Lake Neuchâtel and Lake Biel it was connected to the Aare and the Rhine.
32791.m: Via Lake Murten and the Jura lakes, Aventicum was connected to the Rhine.

32792.q: At the confluence of which rivers did the legionary camp of Vindonissa lie?
32792.e: Vindonissa lay in today’s Windisch in Aargau, on a plateau near the Wasserschloss, where the Reuss and the Limmat flow into the Aare.
32792.m: Vindonissa watched over the confluence of the Aare, Reuss and Limmat.

a: The only Roman legionary camp in what is now Switzerland
The Roman capital of the Helvetii
A Celtic sanctuary on Lake Geneva
A Roman pass station on the Great St Bernard
32793.e: From about AD 14, legions with thousands of soldiers were stationed at Vindonissa. The capital of the Helvetii, on the other hand, was Aventicum.
32793.m: Vindonissa was the only legionary camp on Swiss soil.

32794.q: In which present-day place was the legionary camp of Vindonissa?
32794.e: The name Windisch goes back to Vindonissa. Augst, Avenches and Nyon were also Roman places, but not legionary camps.
32794.m: Vindonissa was in today’s Windisch in Aargau.

32795.q: Where was the late antique bishop’s seat of Vindonissa moved to around 600?
32795.e: In the 6th century a bishop of Windisch called Bubulcus is recorded. Around 600 the seat was moved to Konstanz on Lake Constance.
32795.m: The diocese of Windisch lived on in the diocese of Konstanz.

32796.q: What makes the so-called rubbish mound by the north gate of Vindonissa so valuable for research?
a: It contains hundreds of wooden writing tablets
It holds the grave of an emperor
It is the oldest theatre in Switzerland
It contains the legion’s war chest
32796.e: In the damp rubbish mound, organic materials were preserved, including about 600 wooden writing tablets. They give an insight into the everyday life of the soldiers.
32796.m: In the rubbish mound of Vindonissa, wooden tablets with soldiers’ letters survived.

32797.q: How did people write on the wooden writing tablets from Vindonissa?
a: With a stylus in a layer of wax
32797.e: The tablets were coated with wax, into which people scratched with a stylus. Where the stylus went through into the wood, the writing can still be read today.
32797.m: Roman soldiers wrote with a stylus on wax tablets.

32798.q: Which fortification was built on the site of Vindonissa around AD 300?
32798.e: The late antique fort Castrum Vindonissense was built as part of the Danube-Iller-Rhine Limes. It was abandoned after 406.
32798.m: In late antiquity the Castrum Vindonissense protected the Rhine frontier.

32799.q: Which present-day Swiss region did the Roman road over the Great St Bernard connect with Italy?
32799.e: After Rome had conquered the Aosta Valley in 25 BC, the pass road led from Aosta to Martigny in Valais. From there it continued to Lake Geneva and into Gaul.
32799.m: The Great St Bernard connects Valais with the Aosta Valley.

32800.q: Which two Roman places did the road over the Great St Bernard connect?
32800.e: The pass road led from Valais at Martigny over into the Aosta Valley. It was the shortest route from Italy to Lake Geneva and Gaul.
32800.m: The Great St Bernard route went from Martigny to Aosta.

32801.q: In which war did Rome send a legion into Valais in 57 BC to open the way over the pass?
32801.e: Caesar sent his legate Galba to Octodurus (Martigny). After fierce attacks by the tribes of Valais, however, he withdrew.
32801.m: As early as the Gallic War, Rome wanted to secure the pass.

32802.q: Which structure has run under the Great St Bernard since 1964?
32802.e: The Great St Bernard Tunnel was opened in 1964. It was the first road tunnel through the Alps and can be used all year round.
32802.m: Since 1964 a road tunnel has run under the Great St Bernard.

32803.q: Which famous dog breed is linked to the hospice on the Great St Bernard Pass?
32803.e: Since the 17th century, the canons of the hospice kept large dogs that helped search for lost travellers. This led to the St Bernard breed.
32803.m: The St Bernard comes from the hospice on the Great St Bernard Pass.

32804.q: Who founded the hospice on the Great St Bernard around the middle of the 11th century?
32804.e: Bernard of Aosta founded the hospice for travellers. The pass and the hospice still bear his name today.
32804.m: The hospice and the pass are named after Bernard of Aosta.

32805.q: Which military commander crossed the Great St Bernard with an army in May 1800?
32805.e: Napoleon led about 40,000 soldiers over the pass into Italy. Shortly afterwards he won the Battle of Marengo.
32805.m: In 1800 Napoleon marched his army over the Great St Bernard.

32806.q: Which present-day region’s name goes back to Sapaudia, where the Burgundians were settled in 443?
32806.e: The name Savoy developed from the late antique name Sapaudia. At that time it covered the area around Lake Geneva.
32806.m: The name Savoy comes from the late antique Sapaudia.

32807.q: Which Frankish king was baptised around 500, influenced by his Burgundian wife?
32807.e: Clovis married the Catholic Burgundian Clotilde. His baptism made the Franks Catholic Christians, which later became important for the whole of Western Europe.
32807.m: Clovis was baptised under the influence of his Burgundian wife.

32808.q: Which present-day language border in Switzerland is linked to the territory of the Burgundians and that of the Alemanni?
a: The border between French and German
The border between German and Romansh
The border between French and Italian
The border between German and Italian
32808.e: The Burgundians in the west adopted the language of the Romance-speaking population, which became French. In the east, German prevailed with the Alemanni.
32808.m: The Burgundians and the Alemanni shaped the German-French language border.

32809.q: Which people conquered the kingdom of the Burgundians in 534?
32809.e: The Burgundians were able to defeat the Franks once more in 524. Ten years later, however, the sons of Clovis finally conquered the Burgundian kingdom.
32809.m: In 534 the Burgundian kingdom fell to the Franks.

32810.q: Which faith did the Burgundian king Sigismund adopt, linking him with the Romance-speaking population?
32810.e: Many Burgundians were at first Arian Christians, whereas the local Romance-speaking people were Catholic. Sigismund converted to the Catholic faith and founded the Abbey of Saint-Maurice in 515.
32810.m: Sigismund converted to the Catholic faith of the Romance-speaking people.

32811.q: Which collection of laws applied to the Romance-speaking population in the Burgundian kingdom?
32811.e: In the Burgundian kingdom, law depended on the person: Burgundians lived by their own law, Romance-speaking people by the Lex Romana Burgundionum, a selection of Roman law.
32811.m: The Lex Romana Burgundionum applied to the Romance-speaking people in the Burgundian kingdom.

32812.q: Which defeat by the Huns in 436 became part of the legend of the Nibelungs?
a: The destruction of the Burgundian kingdom on the Rhine around Worms
The Battle of the Catalaunian Plains
32812.e: In 436 Hunnic auxiliaries of Rome crushed the Burgundian kingdom on the middle Rhine. King Gundahar corresponds to Gunther in the Nibelungenlied.
32812.m: The fall of the Burgundians on the Rhine lives on in the Nibelungenlied.

32813.q: How is the name “Alemanni” often interpreted?
a: All men, meaning an alliance of many groups
32813.e: The name is usually explained as “all men” or “people as a whole”. It refers to an alliance of different Germanic groups.
32813.m: The name Alemanni probably means “all men”.

32814.q: Which Roman frontier did the Romans give up around 260, so that the Alemanni could push into the area of today’s Switzerland?
a: The barrier on the Great St Bernard
32814.e: Around 260 the Romans gave up the Limes between the Rhine and the Danube. After that the Rhine was the frontier again, and the Alemanni repeatedly raided the Central Plateau.
32814.m: After the fall of the Limes around 260, the Alemanni pushed into the Central Plateau.

32815.q: Which group of dialects does Swiss German belong to?
32815.e: The Alemanni settled the Central Plateau from the 5th century. Their language lives on in the Alemannic dialects, which also include Swabian and Alsatian.
32815.m: Swiss German is an Alemannic dialect.

32816.q: Which law code of the Alemanni was written down in the early 8th century?
32816.e: The Lex Alamannorum was written down under Duke Lantfrid. Among other things it regulated fines and church rights.
32816.m: The law of the Alemanni was recorded in the Lex Alamannorum.

32817.q: Which people defeated the Alemanni around 500 and brought them under their rule?
32817.e: The Frankish king Clovis defeated the Alemanni around 496 and 506. By 537 the whole of Alemannia had come under Frankish rule.
32817.m: Around 500 the Franks conquered the Alemanni.

32818.q: How can you still recognise the old border between the Alemanni and the Burgundians in Switzerland today?
a: Roughly by the language border between German and French
By the cantonal border between Uri and Ticino
By the border between Catholic and Protestant areas
By the line of the Jura
32818.e: The Alemanni spoke a Germanic language, while the Burgundians adopted the Latin of the Romans. This roughly gave rise to today’s language border, which more or less follows the river Saane (Sarine).
32818.m: The German-French language border goes back to the Alemanni and the Burgundians.

32819.q: Which place-name endings are typical of Alemannic settlements in German-speaking Switzerland?
32819.e: Names such as Ossingen or Rüschlikon go back to Alemannic settlers. The ending -ikon developed from -inghofen, which roughly means “at the farms of the people of ...”. Endings such as -dunum and -acum are Celtic-Roman.
32819.m: Place names ending in -ingen and -ikon are of Alemannic origin.

32820.q: What special rank does the Abbey of Saint-Maurice have among the monasteries of Europe?
a: It is considered the oldest continuously existing monastery in the Western world
It is the largest monastery in the Alps
It was the first Cistercian monastery
It is the highest monastery in Europe
32820.e: Since its founding in the early 6th century, a religious community has lived at Saint-Maurice without interruption. In 2015 the abbey celebrated 1,500 years.
32820.m: Saint-Maurice is considered the oldest continuously existing monastery in the Western world.

32821.q: Which people ruled Valais when King Sigismund founded the Abbey of Saint-Maurice in 515?
32821.e: Sigismund was king of the Burgundians, whose kingdom then also included Valais and western Switzerland. In 515 he founded the monastery at Agaunum.
32821.m: The Abbey of Saint-Maurice was founded in 515 by the Burgundian king Sigismund.

32822.q: Which school do the canons of the Abbey of Saint-Maurice run?
32822.e: The abbey has long run a college with a secondary school. It is one of the best-known secondary schools in Valais.
32822.m: The canons of Saint-Maurice run a secondary school.

32823.q: Why was Agaunum, today’s Saint-Maurice, already important in Roman times?
a: It lay at a narrow point of the Rhône valley on the way to the Great St Bernard
It was the capital of the Helvetii
The largest salt mine in the Alps was there
It lay right on the shore of Lake Geneva
32823.e: At Saint-Maurice the Rhône valley becomes very narrow. Anyone going from Lake Geneva over the Great St Bernard to Italy had to pass through here; the Romans collected customs duties at this spot.
32823.m: Saint-Maurice lies at a narrow point of the Rhône valley.

32824.q: Which legend lies behind the name Saint-Maurice?
a: Maurice and the Theban Legion are said to have died here as martyrs
Saint Maurice is said to have defeated a dragon here
Maurice is said to have been the first pilgrim to cross the Alps here
Maurice is said to have founded the world’s first monastery here
32824.e: According to the legend, the officer Maurice and his Christian soldiers from Egypt refused to act against Christians. They were executed at Agaunum around 300.
32824.m: Saint-Maurice is named after the martyr Maurice.

32825.q: What is the Abbey of Saint-Maurice especially known for among experts today?
32825.e: The treasure contains important goldsmiths’ work such as the Teuderic reliquary and a sardonyx vase. It is one of the richest church treasures in Europe.
32825.m: The church treasure of Saint-Maurice is one of the most valuable in Europe.

32826.q: Which religious order has looked after the Abbey of Saint-Maurice since the 12th century?
32826.e: Augustinian canons have lived at Saint-Maurice since 1128.
32826.m: Augustinian canons have worked at Saint-Maurice since 1128.

32827.q: Which country did the wandering monk and founder of monasteries Columbanus come from?
32827.e: Columbanus came from the Irish monastery of Bangor. He represents the Irish mission on the Continent.
32827.m: Columbanus was an Irish wandering monk.

32828.q: Which famous monastery did Columbanus found in the Vosges before moving to Lake Constance?
32828.e: Around 590 Columbanus founded Annegray, Luxeuil and Fontaine in the Frankish kingdom. Because of a conflict with the royal court, he had to leave around 610.
32828.m: Luxeuil in the Vosges was Columbanus’s most important monastery.

32829.q: Which companion of Columbanus stayed behind at Lake Constance around 612 and gave his name to a Swiss town?
32829.e: Gall stayed behind ill when Columbanus went on to Italy. He lived as a hermit by the river Steinach, where the monastery and the town of St Gallen later grew up.
32829.m: Gall, a follower of Columbanus, gave St Gallen its name.

32830.q: Why did Gall part from Columbanus in 612 and stay at Lake Constance?
a: He was ill and could not travel on
He was banished by the king
He wanted to return to Ireland
32830.e: According to the Life of Gall, he had a fever and stayed behind when Columbanus went on to Italy. He withdrew as a hermit into the Arbon forest.
32830.m: Because of an illness, Gall stayed behind at Lake Constance.

32831.q: How do we mainly know today how Saint Gall lived?
a: From accounts of his life written by monks after his death
32831.e: The Lives of Gall were written long after his death; Walahfrid Strabo of Reichenau revised an older version around 833. They mix facts and legends.
32831.m: Our picture of Gall comes mainly from medieval accounts of his life.

32832.q: According to tradition, which country did the wandering monk Gall come from?
32832.e: According to tradition, Gall came from Ireland to the Continent with Columbanus. At that time Irish monks were spreading Christianity in Central Europe.
32832.m: Gall came to Lake Constance as an Irish wandering monk.

32833.q: According to the account of his life, which office is Gall said to have turned down?
a: The office of Bishop of Konstanz
The office of Duke of Alemannia
The office of chancellor at the Frankish court
32833.e: According to the Life, Gall refused election as Bishop of Konstanz and recommended his pupil John instead.
32833.m: Gall preferred to remain a hermit rather than become Bishop of Konstanz.

32834.q: Which monk of St Gallen, nicknamed “the Stammerer”, became famous for his sequences?
32834.e: Notker (around 840 to 912) wrote sequences for the Mass and the “Gesta Karoli Magni”. He is one of the most important scholars of St Gallen.
32834.m: Notker the Stammerer made St Gallen famous with his sequences.

32835.q: Which anchoress was killed in St Gallen during the Hungarian raid of 926 and later became the first woman to be canonised by a pope?
32835.e: Wiborada had warned of the Hungarian raid, so the monks and books could be brought to safety. She was canonised in 1047.
32835.m: Wiborada warned St Gallen about the Hungarians and died as a martyr.

32836.q: Which famous medieval heroic epic survives in an important manuscript in the Abbey Library of St Gallen?
32836.e: Codex Sangallensis 857 contains one of the most important manuscripts of the Nibelungenlied, from the 13th century. It is considered an especially reliable version.
32836.m: An important manuscript of the Nibelungenlied is kept in St Gallen.

32837.q: From which century did the abbots of St Gallen hold the rank of Princes of the Empire?
32837.e: Abbot Ulrich von Sax was raised to the rank of Prince of the Empire in 1206/1207. Since then people have spoken of the Prince-Abbey of St Gallen.
32837.m: From the early 13th century the abbots of St Gallen were Princes of the Empire.

32838.q: What is special about the Plan of St Gall?
a: It is the oldest surviving architectural plan of the Middle Ages
It is the oldest printed book in Switzerland
It shows the first map of the Confederation
It is a Roman town plan
32838.e: The plan was made in the early 9th century and shows an ideal monastery with a church, workshops and gardens. It is kept in the Abbey Library of St Gallen.
32838.m: The Plan of St Gall is the oldest surviving architectural plan of the Middle Ages.

32839.q: From which period does the Plan of St Gall date?
32839.e: The plan was drawn around 820 in the monastery of Reichenau and sent to the abbot of St Gallen. At that time Charlemagne’s successors were ruling.
32839.m: The Plan of St Gall dates from the Carolingian period.

32840.q: Which famous abbey in a 20th-century novel closely resembles the Plan of St Gall?
a: The abbey in “The Name of the Rose”
32840.e: The Benedictine abbey in Umberto Eco’s novel “The Name of the Rose” (1980) corresponds in principle to the Carolingian monastery plan.
32840.m: Umberto Eco’s fictional abbey is modelled on the Plan of St Gall.

32841.q: What is happening at Campus Galli near Messkirch?
a: A monastery based on the Plan of St Gall is being built using medieval methods
The original plan is on display in a museum
32841.e: Since 2013 craftspeople there have been building the monastery from the Plan of St Gall. They use only tools and techniques from the Middle Ages, so the building will take decades.
32841.m: At Campus Galli the Plan of St Gall is becoming reality.

32842.q: Which cantons, among others, belong to the diocese of Chur?
a: The Grisons, Ticino and St Gallen
32842.e: Today the diocese of Chur includes the Grisons, Schwyz, Uri, Glarus, Obwalden, Nidwalden and Zurich. It is one of the oldest dioceses in Switzerland.
32842.m: The canton of Zurich also belongs to the diocese of Chur.

32843.q: To which church province did Chur belong until the division of the Frankish Empire in 843?
32843.e: Chur was at first a suffragan diocese of Milan and therefore looked south. After 843 it came under the church province of Mainz.
32843.m: Until 843 the diocese of Chur belonged to the church province of Milan.

32844.q: To whom is the diocese of Chur directly subject today?
32844.e: Since 1803 Chur has not belonged to any church province. Like all Swiss dioceses, it is directly subject to the Holy See.
32844.m: The diocese of Chur is directly subject to the Pope.

32845.q: Why was the Bishop of Chur so powerful in the Middle Ages?
a: He was also a secular lord and controlled important Alpine passes
He was also Emperor of the Empire
He owned all the salt mines in the Alps
He led the Swiss Federal Diet
32845.e: The bishop owned land, castles and customs posts on the passes of the Grisons. This made him both a religious and a secular ruler.
32845.m: The Bishop of Chur ruled important passes as both a religious and a secular lord.

32846.q: Which reform by Charlemagne around 806 weakened the power of the bishops of Chur?
a: The separation of the diocese from the county
32846.e: With the so-called Divisio, secular administration was handed to a Frankish count. In the process the bishop lost much of his property.
32846.m: In Raetia, Charlemagne separated the county from the diocese.

32847.q: Which saint is the patron of the diocese of Chur and, according to legend, the first to bring the faith to Raetia?
32847.e: Saint Lucius is said to have brought Christianity to Raetia. The legend even made him a British king.
32847.m: Saint Lucius is the patron saint of the diocese of Chur.

32848.q: Which monastery in the diocese of Chur is a UNESCO World Heritage Site because of its wall paintings from the time of Charlemagne?
32848.e: The Convent of St John in Müstair was founded around 775. Its early medieval frescoes are unique, and it has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1983.
32848.m: Müstair Abbey is World Heritage because of its Carolingian frescoes.

32849.q: Which empire broke apart before the Kingdom of Upper Burgundy was founded in 888?
32849.e: After the Carolingian Empire broke apart, Rudolph I had himself proclaimed king at Saint-Maurice in 888.
32849.m: Upper Burgundy arose in 888 from the collapsing Carolingian Empire.

32850.q: Which part of present-day Switzerland mainly belonged to the Kingdom of Upper Burgundy?
32850.e: Upper Burgundy covered western Switzerland and parts of present-day France. Its expansion eastwards was stopped near Winterthur in 919.
32850.m: Upper Burgundy lay mainly in present-day western Switzerland.

32851.q: What came into being when King Rudolph II united Upper and Lower Burgundy around 930?
32851.e: Hugh of Provence gave up Lower Burgundy, and in return Rudolph II gave up his claims in Italy. This created a united Kingdom of Burgundy.
32851.m: Around 930 the united Kingdom of Burgundy came into being.

32852.q: Which famous empress came from the royal house of Upper Burgundy?
32852.e: Adelaide was the daughter of King Rudolph II of Burgundy. She became empress through her marriage to Otto the Great.
32852.m: Empress Adelaide came from Upper Burgundy.

32853.q: Whom did Adelaide of Burgundy marry in 951?
32853.e: After the death of her first husband, Lothair of Italy, Adelaide was held prisoner. Otto I freed her and married her in 951.
32853.m: Adelaide of Burgundy became the wife of Otto the Great.

32854.q: Under whose protection was the Kingdom of Burgundy in the 10th century?
a: Under the protection of the Ottonian kings
Under the protection of the Byzantine emperor
Under the protection of the Caliph of Córdoba
Under the protection of the kings of England
32854.e: King Conrad of Burgundy grew up at the Saxon court and was protected by Otto I. His long reign from 937 to 993 is regarded as peaceful.
32854.m: In the 10th century Burgundy was under the protection of the Ottonians.

32855.q: What happened to the Kingdom of Burgundy in 1033?
a: It passed to the Holy Roman Empire
It became part of the Swiss Confederacy
It broke up into separate cantons
32855.e: After the death of Rudolph III, Emperor Conrad II had himself crowned King of Burgundy at Payerne in 1033. Burgundy thus passed to the Empire.
32855.m: From 1033 Burgundy belonged to the Holy Roman Empire.

32856.q: Which town castle did Duke Berthold V of Zähringen have built around 1190 at the eastern end of the Aare loop in Bern?
32856.e: Nydegg Castle protected the Aare crossing of the new town. The people of Bern demolished it around 1268/70; today the Nydegg Church stands in its place.
32856.m: Nydegg Castle guarded the Aare crossing in early Bern.

32857.q: Which family inherited a large part of the Zähringers’ possessions in Switzerland after the Zähringer line died out?
32857.e: The Kyburgs were related to the Zähringers by marriage and received Burgdorf, Thun and Fribourg, among other places.
32857.m: The Zähringer inheritance in Switzerland went mostly to the Kyburgs.

32858.q: Which Bern town charter is dated 1218 but was probably written later?
a: The Golden Bull of Bern (Goldene Handfeste)
32858.e: The Goldene Handfeste names Emperor Frederick II as its issuer. Historians consider it a later Bernese forgery meant to secure the town’s freedoms.
32858.m: The Goldene Handfeste secured Bern’s freedoms as an imperial city.

32859.q: Which town on the High Rhine in today’s Aargau was one of the Zähringer towns?
32859.e: Around 1090 the Zähringers inherited the estates of the Counts of Rheinfelden and developed the place into a town.
32859.m: Rheinfelden on the High Rhine is a Zähringer town.

32860.q: Which town in the Black Forest did the Zähringers found in 1120, which became the model for later foundations?
32860.e: Conrad and Berthold III of Zähringen founded Freiburg im Breisgau as a market town in 1120. Its town law influenced other Zähringer towns.
32860.m: Freiburg im Breisgau was the first large Zähringer town.

32861.q: Which feature is typical of the layout of the Zähringer towns?
a: A wide main street serving as a market place
A round ring around a castle
A grid based on a Roman camp plan
32861.e: In Bern or Fribourg a wide street forms the market axis, along which the houses stand on regular plots.
32861.m: Zähringer towns often have a wide market street as their axis.

32862.q: Which castle is the Zähringer family named after?
a: Zähringen Castle near Freiburg im Breisgau
A castle in Alsace near Strasbourg
32862.e: The ancestral castle of Zähringen lies north of Freiburg im Breisgau. The dukes named themselves after it from the late 11th century.
32862.m: The Zähringers bear the name of their castle near Freiburg im Breisgau.

32863.q: Which valley community of the Forest Cantons was the first to receive a royal charter of freedom in 1231?
32863.e: King Henry (VII) issued the Uri charter of freedom in 1231. Schwyz followed in 1240, Unterwalden only later.
32863.m: In 1231 Uri was the first Forest Canton to receive a charter of freedom.

32864.q: What legal status did Uri gain through the charter of freedom of 1231?
32864.e: Uri was now directly subject to the king, with no territorial lord in between. This did not make it independent of the Empire.
32864.m: Imperial immediacy means a territory is directly subject to the king.

32865.q: How did the charter of freedom of 1240 justify the special status of the people of Schwyz?
a: They had placed themselves under the Empire voluntarily
They had lent the emperor money
They had built an imperial castle
They had taken the Pope prisoner
32865.e: The emperor praised the people of Schwyz for placing themselves under the protection of the Empire of their own free will. In return he took them under his special protection.
32865.m: In 1240 the people of Schwyz voluntarily placed themselves under the protection of the Empire.

32866.q: Why was the imperial freedom of Schwyz legally uncertain after 1240?
a: The Habsburgs did not recognise the charter
32866.e: The Habsburgs continued to claim rights of rule in Schwyz. They therefore did not accept the charter.
32866.m: The Habsburgs did not recognise the Schwyz charter of freedom.

32867.q: What did it mean for the Forest Cantons that King Henry VII appointed an imperial bailiff over them in 1309?
a: They were directly subject to an official of the king, not to Habsburg
They became a duchy of their own
They had to pay taxes to Habsburg
They lost their charters of freedom
32867.e: Count Werner of Homberg administered the king’s rights in the Forest Cantons as imperial bailiff. This placed them directly under the Empire and not under Habsburg.
32867.m: In 1309 the king placed the Forest Cantons under their own imperial bailiff.

32868.q: Why did King Louis the Bavarian confirm the freedoms of the Forest Cantons in 1316?
a: They supported him in the dispute over the throne against the Habsburg Frederick
They paid him a large sum of gold
They had given him the Gotthard
32868.e: In the dispute over the throne, Louis stood against the Habsburg Frederick the Fair. The Forest Cantons supported Louis, shortly after their victory at Morgarten, and in return had their rights confirmed.
32868.m: In the dispute over the throne, Louis the Bavarian strengthened the Forest Cantons against Habsburg in 1316.

32869.q: What strategic interest lay behind the Hohenstaufen charters of freedom for the Forest Cantons?
32869.e: Once the route through the Reuss gorge was opened, a short way to Italy led across the Alps. No territorial lord was to control its northern approach.
32869.m: The Hohenstaufen wanted to keep the northern approach to the Gotthard under imperial control.

32870.q: Which gorge had to be made passable in the Middle Ages so that the route over the Gotthard could be used?
32870.e: Only with footbridges and the Devil’s Bridge in the Schöllenen in the 13th century was the way into the Urseren valley opened. The Gotthard then became the shortest route to Italy.
32870.m: Opening up the Schöllenen opened the Gotthard route.

32871.q: With which canton did the Urseren valley conclude a Landrecht (treaty of protection) in 1410?
32871.e: Through the Landrecht of 1410, Urseren bound itself closely to its northern neighbour. That neighbour then controlled the entire northern ramp of the pass.
32871.m: In 1410 Urseren joined Uri through a Landrecht.

32872.q: What were the warehouses on the Gotthard route called, where goods were reloaded and passed on?
32872.e: In the Susten, muleteers stored the goods until the next muleteers’ cooperative took them over. Fees were charged for this.
32872.m: Susten were warehouses for the transport of goods over the Alpine passes.

32873.q: What were the chapel and hospice at the top of the Gotthard Pass for?
a: They gave travellers shelter and lodging
They were an imperial customs post
They were the residence of a bishop
They were a border fortress against Milan
32873.e: A chapel was consecrated at the top of the pass as early as 1230, and a hospice was added later. Muleteers, traders and pilgrims found help there.
32873.m: The Gotthard Hospice gave travellers shelter.

32874.q: What were the men called who carried goods over the Gotthard with pack animals in the Middle Ages?
32874.e: Muleteers led mules and horses with loads over the pass. They were organised in cooperatives and handed over the goods in the Susten.
32874.m: Muleteers transported goods over the passes with pack animals.

32875.q: Which structure replaced the Twärren Bridge from 1708 and is regarded as Switzerland’s first traffic tunnel?
32875.e: The passage, originally 64 metres long, was blasted through the rock in 1707 and 1708. After that, people no longer had to get round the rock face on a hanging footbridge.
32875.m: The Urnerloch of 1708 is regarded as Switzerland’s first traffic tunnel.

32876.q: For which Alpine route was the Schöllenen Gorge the most difficult obstacle?
a: For the route over the Gotthard
For the route over the Simplon
For the route over the Great St Bernard
For the route over the Julier
32876.e: The Schöllenen lies between Göschenen and Andermatt in the Reuss valley. Only once it was passable did the Gotthard become an important north-south link.
32876.m: The Schöllenen opened the way over the Gotthard.

32877.q: Who probably made the Schöllenen passable with a mule track around 1200?
a: Walser people from the Urseren valley
32877.e: It is assumed that Walser settlers from the Urseren valley built the track with bridges over the Reuss. This is not proven for certain, and the exact date of construction is disputed.
32877.m: The Walser probably made the Schöllenen passable around 1200.

32878.q: What happened in 1888 to the stone Devil’s Bridge of 1595?
a: It was moved to a museum
32878.e: After a new bridge was opened next to it in 1830, the old one was no longer maintained. It collapsed on 2 August 1888.
32878.m: The old Devil’s Bridge collapsed in 1888.
