32879.q: When was today’s third Devil’s Bridge opened to motor traffic?
32879.e: A wider road bridge was built next to the 19th-century bridge. The older one is now used by pedestrians and cyclists.
32879.m: The third Devil’s Bridge for cars was opened in 1958.

32880.q: What does the White Book of Sarnen contain?
a: The oldest written version of the liberation story with Tell
The original version of the Federal Charter of 1291
Today’s laws of the canton of Obwalden
A list of all the Alpine pastures in Obwalden
32880.e: Besides copies of documents, the book tells of bailiffs, the Rütli and William Tell. It is the oldest known version of this story.
32880.m: The White Book of Sarnen is the first source to tell the Tell story.

32881.q: Where does the White Book of Sarnen get its name from?
32881.e: The name refers to the white pigskin binding, which dates from the 17th century. It has nothing to do with the contents.
32881.m: The White Book is named after the colour of its binding.

32882.q: Roughly when was the White Book of Sarnen written?
32882.e: The book was written between 1470 and 1472, about 180 years after the Federal Charter. It is therefore not a contemporary source.
32882.m: The White Book was not written until around 1470.

32883.q: Which meeting place of the conspirators is mentioned for the first time in the White Book of Sarnen?
32883.e: The chronicle tells how Stauffacher, Fürst and the young Melchtaler met there at night. Older sources do not yet know this place.
32883.m: The Rütli first appears in the White Book of Sarnen.

32884.q: How do historians judge William Tell today?
a: As a legendary figure whose existence is not proven
As a well-documented Landammann of Uri
As an invented figure from the 20th century
As a historical king of the Confederates
32884.e: Tell does not appear in documents from around 1300. The story was written down only about 170 years later and has models in other legends.
32884.m: William Tell is a legendary figure.

32885.q: Which writer made the Tell story world-famous with a play in 1804?
32885.e: Schiller’s “William Tell” was first performed in Weimar in 1804. Goethe had recommended the subject to him after a journey to Central Switzerland.
32885.m: Schiller’s play made Tell famous worldwide.

32886.q: Which Nordic tale also contains an apple shot and is considered a possible model for the Tell story?
32886.e: Around 1200 Saxo Grammaticus told of the archer Toko, who had to shoot an apple from his son’s head. Many researchers see this as a model for the Tell story.
32886.m: The legend of Toko tells of an apple shot even before Tell.

32887.q: According to the White Book, what wrong does the bailiff Landenberg do to the farmer in the Melchtal?
32887.e: Landenberg has the farmer’s team of oxen taken away. The story explains why the young Melchtaler joins the conspirators.
32887.m: In the White Book, Landenberg takes the Melchtal farmer’s oxen.

32888.q: According to the White Book, how is Sarnen Castle taken?
a: By a tunnel under the wall
32888.e: Subjects bring the bailiff gifts and leave the gate open as they do so. At a horn signal the allies storm in.
32888.m: According to the White Book, Sarnen Castle fell through a trick.

32889.q: Where did the chronicler Aegidius Tschudi come from?
32889.e: Tschudi was born there in 1505 and came from a family of Landammänner. He was a politician, bailiff and historian.
32889.m: Aegidius Tschudi was a chronicler from Glarus.

32890.q: What is the name of Tschudi’s main work on Swiss history?
32890.e: The work covers the period from 1001 to 1470. It was not printed until 1734 to 1736 in Basel.
32890.m: Tschudi’s main work is the Chronicon Helveticum.

32891.q: To which year did Tschudi date the Rütli oath?
32891.e: Tschudi set the oath on 8 November of that year. Only in the 19th century did a different founding year prevail because of the Federal Charter.
32891.m: Tschudi dated the Rütli oath to 1307.

32892.q: Which writer relied heavily on Tschudi’s chronicle for his 1804 play “William Tell”?
32892.e: The writer took characters and the course of the liberation from the chronicle. In this way Tschudi shaped the image of the founding to this day.
32892.m: Schiller’s “William Tell” is based mainly on Tschudi’s chronicle.

32893.q: Which office did Tschudi hold in a condominium (common lordship)?
32893.e: Tschudi was bailiff in Sargans and twice in the County of Baden. There he had access to many old documents.
32893.m: Tschudi served as bailiff in Sargans and Baden.

32894.q: Which religious side did Tschudi firmly join in the second half of his life?
32894.e: Tschudi became the spokesman of the Catholic side in Glarus. The Tschudi War from 1560, named after him, shows how bitter the religious dispute was.
32894.m: Tschudi fought for the Catholic cause in Glarus.

32895.q: Why do historians have to use Tschudi’s chronicle carefully today?
a: He embellished events and partly invented exact dates
It was only discovered in the 20th century
It is written in an unknown secret script
It only reports on the canton of Glarus
32895.e: Tschudi wanted to tell a complete history. Where sources were missing, he added dates and details, for example for the Rütli oath. Some of his statements are therefore unreliable.
32895.m: Tschudi’s chronicle also contains invented dates and embellishments.

32896.q: How is Aegidius Tschudi regarded in Swiss historiography?
a: As the first Federal Councillor of Switzerland
As the creator of the first national map
32896.e: Tschudi collected documents and wrote down the history of the Confederacy in more detail than anyone before him. He was a Catholic, not a reformer.
32896.m: Aegidius Tschudi is regarded as the father of Swiss history.

32897.q: What special feature did the Lucerne alliance of 1332 contain with regard to Habsburg?
32897.e: The lordly rights of the town’s ruler were expressly reserved in the alliance. In practice, however, the alliance still weakened his position in Lucerne.
32897.m: The Lucerne alliance formally reserved Habsburg’s rights.

32898.q: Which battle of 1386 finally freed Lucerne from Habsburg rule?
32898.e: The Confederates defeated Duke Leopold III of Austria, who fell in the fighting. Afterwards Lucerne was able to expand its territory greatly.
32898.m: After the victory of 1386, Lucerne broke away from Habsburg.

32899.q: What problem did the alliance of 1332 cause within the town of Lucerne?
a: Tensions with groups loyal to Habsburg
The loss of its market rights
32899.e: Part of the nobility and the citizens remained loyal to Austrian rule. Lucerne was therefore torn between two camps for decades.
32899.m: The alliance of 1332 split Lucerne into pro-Habsburg and pro-Confederate groups.

32900.q: Which Habsburg castle with a toll station did the people of Lucerne destroy in 1385, helping to trigger the Sempach War?
32900.e: The people of Lucerne resented the Habsburg tolls north of the town. Destroying the castle was an open challenge.
32900.m: By destroying Rothenburg in 1385, the people of Lucerne challenged Habsburg.

32901.q: Which hero of the Battle of Sempach in 1386 is regarded today as a legendary figure whose existence is disputed?
32901.e: Winkelried is said to have seized the knights’ spears and so torn a gap in their ranks. The story appears in sources only long after the battle.
32901.m: Winkelried is the legendary hero of Sempach.

32902.q: When did Zurich join the alliance with the Forest Cantons and Lucerne?
32902.e: On 1 May of that year Zurich allied itself with Uri, Schwyz, Unterwalden and Lucerne. The reason was the town’s conflict with Habsburg.

32903.q: How did Rudolf Brun come to power in Zurich in 1336?
a: Through an overthrow of the council
32903.e: On 7 June 1336 a crowd led by Brun stormed the town hall, and the councillors fled. A popular assembly then gave him power for life.
32903.m: Rudolf Brun came to power in 1336 through an overthrow.

32904.q: In Brun’s constitution, what was the association of nobles and wealthy merchants alongside the guilds called?
32904.e: The Constaffel provided some of the councillors, the guilds the others. It lasted until the end of the old order.
32904.m: In Zurich the Constaffel represented nobles and merchants.

32905.q: Who gained a share in the government of Zurich for the first time through Brun’s guild constitution of 1336?
32905.e: Before that, nobles and rich merchants controlled the council. After 1336 the guilds provided some of the councillors.
32905.m: With the guild constitution, craftsmen entered the Zurich council.

32906.q: What happened in the Zurich Night of Murder in 1350?
a: Banished opponents attempted a surprise attack
A fire destroyed the old town
32906.e: On the night of 23 to 24 February 1350, banished opponents tried to overthrow and murder Brun. He had been warned, and the attack failed.
32906.m: In the Zurich Night of Murder, an attack on Rudolf Brun failed.

32907.q: Against which power did Zurich seek protection with the alliance of 1351?
32907.e: After the overthrow of 1336 and the Night of Murder, Zurich was in conflict with Habsburg. The alliance with the Forest Cantons and Lucerne was meant to protect the town.
32907.m: In 1351 Zurich allied itself with the Confederates against Habsburg.

32908.q: How did Rudolf Brun behave towards Habsburg towards the end of his life?
32908.e: In 1356 Zurich allied itself with Austria, and in 1359 Brun entered Austrian service for money. He died in 1360.
32908.m: At the end of his life Rudolf Brun moved closer to Habsburg.

32909.q: According to the Priests’ Charter, in which cases could clergy still go before a church court?
a: In cases of murder and manslaughter
32909.e: The Church remained responsible for these areas. In all other cases the court of the locality applied.
32909.m: According to the Priests’ Charter, only marriage and spiritual matters stayed with church courts.

32910.q: What did the Priests’ Charter demand of Austrian retainers living in the territory of the cantons?
a: To move out of the territory
32910.e: These people had to swear allegiance to the Confederates. In a conflict, this oath took precedence over all other ties.
32910.m: According to the Priests’ Charter, Austrian retainers had to swear an oath to the Confederates.

32911.q: What was the consequence of the attack of 1370 for the Zurich provost Bruno Brun?
32911.e: Brun had imprisoned a Lucerne official and refused to accept a secular court. Zurich banished him, whereupon he asked Austria for help.
32911.m: Bruno Brun was banished from Zurich after his attack.

32912.q: According to historians, what change in legal thinking does the Priests’ Charter show?
a: From personal law to territorial law
From customary law to Roman law
From town law to imperial law
From church law to family law
32912.e: It was no longer a person’s status but the territory in which they lived that determined the court. The cantons thus asserted their rule over their territory.
32912.m: With the Priests’ Charter, law applied more by territory than by person.

32913.q: How did the cantons refer to their network of alliances jointly for the first time in the Priests’ Charter?
32913.e: With this phrase the cantons spoke of themselves as a territorial unit for the first time. It shows a growing sense of community.
32913.m: In the Priests’ Charter the cantons first call themselves “unser Eydgnoschaft”.

32914.q: Which form of private violence did the Priests’ Charter forbid?
32914.e: Disputes were to be settled in court rather than by private military raids. This strengthened the authority of the cantons.
32914.m: The Priests’ Charter forbade the feud.

32915.q: According to the Sempach Charter, who was allowed to ask the other cantons for military help?
a: The council or Landsgemeinde of a canton
Only the captains in the field
32915.e: Requests for help had to be justified and come from the authorities. This was meant to prevent unauthorised military campaigns.
32915.m: According to the Sempach Charter, only a canton’s authorities could request help.

32916.q: What is the significance of the Sempach Charter of 1393?
a: It was the first common military code of the Confederate cantons
It was the first Federal Charter of the original cantons
It regulated the election of the first Landammann
32916.e: After the experiences of the Battle of Sempach, the cantons agreed on common rules for war. The charter is considered an important basis for the cohesion of the Confederacy.
32916.m: The Sempach Charter was the first common military code of the Confederates.

32917.q: According to the Sempach Charter, which rule was meant to stop the army breaking up in the middle of a battle?
a: Plundering was only allowed after victory
Every warrior had to bring a horse
Fighting took place only on Sundays
Each canton fought under a foreign banner
32917.e: Anyone plundering during the battle was missing from the fight. So the booty could only be collected after victory and then shared out fairly.
32917.m: According to the Sempach Charter, plundering was only allowed after victory.

32918.q: According to the Sempach Charter, whom or what did warriors expressly have to spare?
a: Women as well as churches and monasteries
32918.e: The Sempach Charter forbade violence against women and the plundering of churches and monasteries. Exceptions applied only if enemies entrenched themselves there.
32918.m: The Sempach Charter protected women, churches and monasteries.

32919.q: According to the Sempach Charter, what awaited warriors who fled from battle?
32919.e: Deserters endangered the whole army. The charter therefore provided punishments for flight and disobedience.
32919.m: According to the Sempach Charter, deserters were punished.

32920.q: According to the Sempach Charter, what applied among warriors from different cantons in a joint army?
a: Each canton fought on its own
32920.e: Violence among Confederates was forbidden, even in the camp. This was meant to keep the army together.
32920.m: In the joint army, the Sempach Charter required peace among Confederates.

32921.q: Which church event was the background to the conquest of the Aargau?
32921.e: The assembly was meant to end the split in the Church with several popes. A Habsburg duke disrupted it by helping one of the popes.
32921.m: The conquest of the Aargau was linked to the Council of Constance.

32922.q: What was the most important aim of the Council of Constance from 1414?
a: To end the split in the Church with several popes
32922.e: At that time there were three popes at once. The council deposed them and elected Martin V in 1417. Because Duke Frederick IV helped a pope to flee, he lost the Aargau.
32922.m: The Council of Constance ended the split in the Church.

32923.q: What nickname did Duke Frederick IV of Austria have?
32923.e: The mocking name refers to his lack of money after losing many territories. He ruled mainly in Tyrol.
32923.m: Frederick IV of Austria was called “of the Empty Pockets”.

32924.q: Which punishment did King Sigismund impose on Duke Frederick IV in 1415?
32924.e: Sigismund declared Frederick an outlaw and called on the imperial estates to occupy his territories. The Confederates followed this call.
32924.m: In 1415 King Sigismund placed Frederick IV under the imperial ban.

32925.q: Which canton secured the largest part of the Aargau in 1415?
32925.e: This canton conquered Aarau, Zofingen, Lenzburg and Brugg, among others. The so-called Lower Aargau remained its subject territory until 1798.
32925.m: Bern won the largest part of the Aargau in 1415.

32926.q: How did the Confederates administer the conquered County of Baden after 1415?
a: As a condominium ruled by several cantons
As a separate canton with equal rights
32926.e: Several cantons governed Baden together and sent a bailiff in turn. Such common lordships also held the Confederates together.
32926.m: In 1415 the County of Baden became a condominium (common lordship).

32927.q: Which canton at first did not take part in the conquest in 1415 because of a peace with Austria?
32927.e: This canton referred to the peace it had concluded with Austria in 1412. Only in 1443 did it join in ruling the County of Baden.
32927.m: Uri held back in 1415 because of its peace with Austria.

32928.q: Why was the loss of the Aargau in 1415 particularly bitter for the Habsburgs?
a: Their ancestral castle, the Habsburg, was there
Their most important silver mines were there
Their only access to the sea was there
32928.e: Habsburg Castle near Brugg gave the family its name. In 1415 it fell to Bern when the Confederates conquered the Aargau.
32928.m: With the Aargau, the Habsburgs lost their ancestral castle in 1415.

32929.q: Who administered a condominium on behalf of the ruling cantons?
a: A mayor chosen by the subjects
An imperial bailiff of the emperor
32929.e: The ruling cantons sent a bailiff in turn. Each year he had to account for income and expenditure at the annual audit.

32930.q: How did the Confederates acquire their condominiums?
a: Through the marriages of their Landammänner
32930.e: The Confederates conquered the Aargau in 1415, and seven cantons bought the County of Sargans in 1483. This created subject territories ruled jointly by several cantons.
32930.m: Condominiums came about through conquest or purchase.

32931.q: Why was Bellinzona so important to the cantons of Central Switzerland?
a: It controlled the routes south from the Alpine passes
It was the capital of Savoy
It had the largest salt mine in the Alps
It was the seat of the Pope
32931.e: Uri, Schwyz and Nidwalden ruled Bellinzona until 1798. Its castles blocked the valley through which the routes from the Gotthard, Lukmanier and San Bernardino passed.
32931.m: Bellinzona was the key to the passes in the south.

32932.q: What were the “ennetbirgische Vogteien” of the Old Swiss Confederacy?
a: Subject territories south of the Alps
32932.e: “Ennetbirgisch” means beyond the mountains. Lugano, Locarno, Mendrisio and the Maggia valley were governed jointly by twelve cantons.
32932.m: The ennetbirgische Vogteien lay in today’s Ticino.

32933.q: Which side won the Second War of Villmergen in 1712?
a: The Protestant cantons of Zurich and Bern
The Catholic cantons of Central Switzerland
32933.e: The victorious Protestant cantons pushed the Catholic ones out of the rule over the County of Baden. This shifted the balance in the Confederacy towards the Protestants.
32933.m: In 1712 the Protestant cantons won the Second War of Villmergen.

32935.q: Where does the name “Tagsatzung” (Federal Diet) come from?
a: From “einen Tag setzen” (to set a day)
From the morning prayer at the start
From the length of one day
32935.e: People agreed on, that is “set”, a day for a joint meeting. The name came from this.
32935.m: The name Tagsatzung comes from “einen Tag setzen”, to set a day.

32936.q: Which town was the permanent meeting place of the Federal Diet from 1742 to 1797?
32936.e: After the Second War of Villmergen, the previous main meeting place lost importance. From 1742 the Diet met only in this Thurgau town.
32936.m: In the 18th century the Federal Diet met in Frauenfeld.

32937.q: What was the canton called that led the Federal Diet and handled the Confederacy’s correspondence?
32937.e: The Vorort invited people to the meetings and held the chair. In the Old Swiss Confederacy this was usually Zurich.
32937.m: The Vorort led the Federal Diet.

32938.q: Which chamber of the Federal Assembly is regarded as the successor of the Federal Diet?
32938.e: As in the past, the cantons are represented in this chamber. Unlike in the Diet, however, its members vote without instructions.
32938.m: The Council of States is the successor of the Federal Diet.

32939.q: Which area on upper Lake Zurich passed to Schwyz as a result of the Old Zurich War?
32939.e: Pfäffikon, Wollerau and Hurden passed to Schwyz. They still belong to this canton today.
32939.m: Die Höfe on Lake Zurich passed to Schwyz in the Old Zurich War.

32940.q: What were Zurich and Schwyz arguing about at the start of the Old Zurich War?
a: The inheritance of the last Count of Toggenburg
32940.e: Count Frederick VII of Toggenburg died in 1436 without heirs. Zurich and Schwyz both claimed his territory, and this led to war.
32940.m: The Old Zurich War began with the dispute over the Toggenburg inheritance.

32941.q: With which power did Zurich ally itself against the other Confederates in the Old Zurich War?
32941.e: In 1442 Zurich concluded an alliance with King Frederick III of the House of Habsburg. The other Confederates saw this as a betrayal of the alliance.
32941.m: In the Old Zurich War, Zurich allied itself with Habsburg.

32942.q: Which battle of 1444 outside the gates of Basel belongs to the Old Zurich War?
a: Battle of St. Jakob an der Birs
32942.e: Habsburg had called in French mercenaries, the Armagnacs, to help. A small Confederate force fought at St. Jakob an der Birs almost to the last man.
32942.m: In 1444 Confederates fought the Armagnacs at St. Jakob an der Birs.

32943.q: What made the Old Zurich War special in the history of the Confederacy?
a: Confederate cantons waged war on each other
The Confederates fought France for the first time
It lasted over a hundred years
It was the first war of religion
32943.e: From 1440 to 1450 Zurich fought against Schwyz and the other cantons. The alliance threatened to break apart but was renewed in 1450.
32943.m: In the Old Zurich War, Confederates fought Confederates.

32944.q: How did the Old Zurich War end in 1450?
a: Zurich stayed in the alliance but had to give up its alliance with Habsburg
Zurich was expelled from the Confederacy
Schwyz had to hand Die Höfe to Zurich
Habsburg conquered the town of Zurich
32944.e: An arbitration ruling forced Zurich to dissolve its alliance with Habsburg. In 1450 the alliance was sworn anew in Einsiedeln.
32944.m: In 1450 Zurich returned to the alliance without its Habsburg alliance.

32945.q: Roughly how large was the Confederate army at St. Jakob an der Birs?
32945.e: This small band faced an enemy many times stronger, of about 20,000 men. Only a few survived.
32945.m: About 1,500 Confederates fought at St. Jakob an der Birs.

32946.q: What consequence did the defeat at St. Jakob an der Birs in 1444 nevertheless have for the Confederates?
a: Their reputation as feared warriors grew greatly
They lost the town of Basel
They had to pay taxes to France
32946.e: The small band fought to the death against an enemy many times stronger. The enemy was impressed, withdrew and soon made peace with the Confederates.
32946.m: The defeat at St. Jakob strengthened the Confederates’ reputation.

32947.q: What was the red wine called that was grown near the battlefield of St. Jakob until the 19th century?
32947.e: The name referred to the blood of the fallen Confederates. In this way the memory of the battle stayed alive in everyday life.
32947.m: The wine of St. Jakob was called Schweizerblut in memory of the battle.

32948.q: In which war did the Battle of St. Jakob an der Birs take place in 1444?
32948.e: In the Old Zurich War, Zurich, allied with Habsburg, fought against the other Confederates. Habsburg brought French mercenaries into the country for this.
32948.m: The Battle of St. Jakob belongs to the Old Zurich War.

32949.q: What were the French mercenaries called whom the Confederates fought at St. Jakob in 1444?
32949.e: The Armagnacs were feared bands of mercenaries who had been left without work after the Hundred Years’ War. The Dauphin led them to the Upper Rhine.
32949.m: At St. Jakob the Confederates fought the Armagnacs.

32950.q: Which French heir to the throne led the enemy army at St. Jakob an der Birs in 1444?
a: The Dauphin Louis, later Louis XI
32950.e: At the request of Frederick III, King Charles VII sent his son with a large mercenary army to the Upper Rhine. After the battle the Dauphin quickly made peace with the Confederates.
32950.m: In 1444 the Dauphin Louis led the army at St. Jakob.

32951.q: Which ruler asked the French king for troops against the Confederates in 1444?
32951.e: Frederick III supported Zurich in the Old Zurich War. He asked Charles VII for help, and the Dauphin came with a large mercenary army.
32951.m: In 1444 Habsburg brought in French mercenaries against the Confederates.

a: An unauthorised military raid from the rural cantons
A campaign by Bern against Burgundy
32952.e: About 2,000 men marched against Geneva without permission from their authorities in order to collect money. The towns saw this as a danger to order.
32952.m: The Saubannerzug of 1477 sharpened the dispute between towns and rural cantons.

32953.q: Which dispute did the Covenant of Stans of 1481 settle?
a: The dispute between the town cantons and the rural cantons
The dispute between Catholics and Protestants
The dispute between Switzerland and France
The dispute between farmers and nobles in Thurgau
32953.e: After the Burgundian Wars, the towns and rural cantons quarrelled over booty and new allies. In Stans they reached an agreement in 1481.
32953.m: The Covenant of Stans settled the dispute between towns and rural cantons.

32954.q: According to tradition, what role did Niklaus von Flüe play in the Covenant of Stans?
a: His advice helped the quarrelling cantons to agree
He wrote the treaty as town clerk
32954.e: The hermit from the Ranft had a message delivered to the Federal Diet in Stans. Afterwards the agreement was reached.
32954.m: Niklaus von Flüe contributed to the agreement of Stans.

32955.q: What did the Covenant of Stans forbid in order to prevent unrest?
32955.e: No gatherings could take place without the permission of the authorities. Stirring up other cantons’ subjects was also forbidden.
32955.m: The Covenant of Stans forbade unauthorised gatherings.

32956.q: Which two towns were admitted to the alliance in 1481 thanks to the Covenant of Stans?
32956.e: The rural cantons had long refused to admit more towns. With the agreement in Stans, Fribourg and Solothurn became Confederate cantons.
32956.m: In 1481 Fribourg and Solothurn joined the Confederacy.

32957.q: What significance does Niklaus von Flüe have for Switzerland today?
a: He is regarded as the patron saint of Switzerland
He is regarded as the first President of the Confederation
He is regarded as the inventor of neutrality by law
He is regarded as the founder of the Red Cross
32957.e: Brother Klaus was canonised in 1947 and is venerated as the country’s patron saint. His advice “Don’t make the fence too wide” is often linked with Swiss restraint.
32957.m: Brother Klaus is the patron saint of Switzerland.

32958.q: In which war did Niklaus von Flüe serve as a soldier before his life as a hermit?
32958.e: As a young man Niklaus went to war against Zurich with the men of Obwalden. Later he became a councillor and judge.
32958.m: Niklaus von Flüe fought in the Old Zurich War.

32959.q: Where is Niklaus von Flüe buried?
32959.e: His remains lie in the parish church of this village in Obwalden. It is an important place of pilgrimage.
32959.m: Brother Klaus is buried in Sachseln.

32960.q: On which day does the Catholic Church in Switzerland celebrate the feast of Brother Klaus?
32960.e: The day of his death, 21 March, is already dedicated to St Benedict. That is why he is celebrated in autumn.
32960.m: The feast of Brother Klaus is on 25 September.

32961.q: How does the well-known prayer attributed to Brother Klaus begin?
32961.e: The prayer asks God to take away everything that separates us from him and to give everything that leads to him. It is still often prayed today.
32961.m: The prayer of Brother Klaus begins with “My Lord and my God”.

32962.q: At which Diet is advice from Brother Klaus said to have prevented the break-up of the Confederacy in 1481?
32962.e: The cantons were arguing about admitting Fribourg and Solothurn and about the Burgundian booty. After a message from Brother Klaus, they agreed on the Covenant of Stans.
32962.m: Brother Klaus helped with the Covenant of Stans in 1481.

32963.q: Which decisions of the Diet of Worms of 1495 did the Confederates reject, thereby sharpening the conflict with the Empire?
a: The Imperial Chamber Court and the Common Penny
The Golden Bull and the public peace ban
The imperial ban and the imperial army levy
The election of the prince-electors and the imperial circles
32963.e: The imperial reform of 1495 created a supreme imperial court and a general imperial tax. The Confederates refused to recognise either, which increased tensions with Maximilian I.
32963.m: The Confederates would submit neither to the Imperial Chamber Court nor to the Common Penny.

32964.q: Which dispute in Rhaetia is regarded as the immediate trigger of the Swabian War?
a: The conflict between the League of God’s House and Tyrol over the Val Müstair
The dispute between Uri and Milan over the Leventina
The feud between Zurich and Schwyz over the Toggenburg
The quarrel between Bern and Savoy over Vaud
32964.e: Habsburg Tyrol and the League of God’s House argued over rights in the Val Müstair and the Vinschgau. Because the Grisons leagues had recently allied with the Confederates, the conflict spread in early 1499.
32964.m: The Swabian War began with a dispute over the Val Müstair in the Grisons.

32965.q: Which battle in July 1499 decided the Swabian War in favour of the Confederates?
32965.e: At Dornach the Confederates took the imperial army by surprise on 22 July 1499. The defeat made Maximilian I ready for the Peace of Basel.
32965.m: The Battle of Dornach decided the Swabian War in 1499.

32966.q: Which Grisons leader, according to tradition, became a hero at the Battle of Calven by urging his men on as he was dying?
32966.e: Benedikt Fontana, mortally wounded at the Calven, is said to have kept spurring on his comrades. In the Grisons he became a symbol of resistance to Habsburg.
32966.m: Benedikt Fontana is regarded as the Grisons hero of the Battle of Calven.

32967.q: What consequence did the Peace of Basel in 1499 have for the Confederacy?
a: It effectively broke away from the Holy Roman Empire
It had to pay Habsburg taxes every year
32967.e: After the Swabian War the Confederates no longer had to recognise the imperial reform. The Confederacy only formally left the Empire in 1648.
32967.m: From 1499 the Confederacy was effectively independent of the Empire.

32968.q: Which area on Lake Constance had the Confederates conquered in 1460 and held on to in the Swabian War?
32968.e: Thurgau had been a Confederate condominium since 1460. After 1499 they also took over the regional court there from the town of Constance.
32968.m: Thurgau remained Confederate after the Swabian War.

32969.q: What is the Swabian War of 1499 called from the German and Austrian point of view?
32969.e: Each side named the war after its enemy. The Confederates spoke of the Swabian War; in the Empire it was called the Swiss War.
32969.m: In the Empire the Swabian War was called the Swiss War.

32970.q: Which alliance of southern German princes, towns and knights stood on King Maximilian’s side in the Swabian War?
32970.e: The Swabian League had been founded in 1488 as an alliance to keep the public peace and fought against the Confederates in 1499. This is also where the Swiss name of the war comes from.
32970.m: In the Swabian War the Confederates fought the Swabian League and Habsburg.

32971.q: Which event of 1500 is known as the “Betrayal of Novara”?
a: Swiss mercenaries let Ludovico Sforza fall into French captivity
French troops broke a ceasefire with Bern
Venice handed Novara to the emperor without a fight
The Pope dismissed the Swiss troops without pay
32971.e: Swiss mercenaries in Sforza’s service refused to fight their countrymen in the French army, and Ludovico Sforza was captured. Hans Turmann from Uri was later executed as a traitor.
32971.m: In the Betrayal of Novara, Duke Ludovico Sforza fell into French hands.

32972.q: Which territory did the Confederates keep permanently from the Milanese Wars?
32972.e: The areas around Lugano, Locarno and Mendrisio became Confederate condominiums. The Val d’Ossola and Milan were lost again after 1515.
32972.m: Ticino is a lasting result of the Milanese Wars.

32973.q: Which French city did the Confederates besiege in 1513, forcing a treaty there that King Louis XII never recognised?
32973.e: After their victory at Novara, the Confederates advanced into Burgundy and besieged Dijon. The treaty negotiated there, with large payments, was not ratified by the king.
32973.m: The Treaty of Dijon of 1513 was never confirmed by the French king.

32974.q: What consequence did the defeat at Marignano in 1515 have for the Confederates?
a: They gave up their great-power policy in Italy
They lost all their territories in Ticino
They became part of the Kingdom of France
32974.e: After Marignano the Confederates concluded the Perpetual Peace with France in 1516. After that they no longer attempted conquests of their own in Italy.
32974.m: After Marignano the Confederates gave up great-power politics.

32975.q: Against which French king did the Confederates fight at Marignano in 1515?
32975.e: The young King Francis I wanted to reconquer the Duchy of Milan. In the two-day battle his army defeated the Confederates.
32975.m: At Marignano King Francis I defeated the Confederates.

32976.q: In which battle of 1522 did Swiss mercenaries in French service suffer heavy losses from Spanish arquebusiers behind a ditch?
32976.e: At La Bicocca north of Milan, the impatient Swiss attacked a fortified position. The fire of the handguns showed that the pike square was vulnerable to modern firepower.
32976.m: The Battle of Bicocca showed the limits of the Swiss pike squares.

32977.q: What happened to King Francis I at the Battle of Pavia in 1525, in which Swiss mercenaries also fought for him?
32977.e: The imperial troops of Charles V defeated the French army, and Francis I was captured. The Swiss in the French army also suffered heavy losses.
32977.m: At Pavia King Francis I was taken prisoner by the imperial forces.

32978.q: Which valley south of the Simplon did the Confederates hold from 1512 to 1515 but lose again after Marignano?
32978.e: The Val d’Ossola with Domodossola was occupied in 1512. After the defeat of 1515 it fell back to France and Milan.
32978.m: The Val d’Ossola with Domodossola was only briefly Confederate.

32979.q: What was the densely packed battle formation of the Confederate foot soldiers with long pikes called?
32979.e: The Gewalthaufen was a large block of pikemen with halberdiers fighting inside it. In the 15th century it was very successful against armies of knights.
32979.m: The Gewalthaufen was the typical battle formation of the Confederates.

32980.q: Roughly how long was a long pike of the Confederate foot soldiers around 1500?
32980.e: The pikes were about five metres long. This let the front ranks keep horsemen at a distance while the rear ranks pushed forward.
32980.m: The mercenaries’ long pike was about five metres long.

32981.q: With which weapon did especially strong mercenaries in the front rank break up the enemy’s rows of pikes?
32981.e: The two-handed sword was a very long sword wielded with both hands. Anyone using it in the dangerous front rank received double pay as a Doppelsöldner.
32981.m: Doppelsöldner often fought with the two-handed sword in the front rank.

32982.q: Which southern German mercenaries were trained on the Swiss model and were regarded as the greatest rivals of the Swiss mercenaries?
32982.e: Maximilian I promoted the Landsknechts, who adopted the tactics and weapons of the Confederates. There was bitter hostility between the two groups of mercenaries.
32982.m: The Landsknechts were the greatest competitors of the Swiss mercenaries.

32983.q: Which French saying refers to the fact that Swiss mercenaries fought only for pay?
32983.e: The saying means “No money, no Swiss”. It became known partly through Racine’s comedy “Les Plaideurs” and reflects experiences with strikes over pay.
32983.m: “Point d’argent, point de Suisses” means there were no Swiss mercenaries without money.

32984.q: What were the contracts called in which a canton officially provided troops to a foreign power on fixed terms?
32984.e: A military capitulation set out the number of soldiers, pay, jurisdiction and conditions of service. In this way mercenary service was organised by the state from the 16th century.
32984.m: Military capitulations regulated the official mercenary service of Swiss troops.

32985.q: What was the bodyguard of Swiss mercenaries called that served at the French royal court from the end of the 15th century?
32985.e: The Hundred Swiss, in French “Cent-Suisses”, guarded the king personally. They show how closely mercenary service was linked to the French court.
32985.m: The Hundred Swiss were the Swiss bodyguard of the French kings.

32986.q: Which exception to the ban on foreign military service for Swiss people still applies today?
a: Service in the Pontifical Swiss Guard
Service in the French Foreign Legion
32986.e: Since the 19th century, Swiss citizens have in principle been forbidden to join foreign forces. The Pope’s guard remained an exception because it counts as a police and protection force.
32986.m: Foreign military service is forbidden, except in the Pontifical Swiss Guard.

32987.q: What distinguishes a private pension (Partikularpension) from a public pension in the Old Swiss Confederacy?
a: It went to individual people instead of to the canton
It was paid only in goods
It was levied from the subjects
It applied only to war invalids
32987.e: Public pensions went into the cantons’ treasuries, private pensions to influential individuals. The private payments in particular were seen as bribery and were especially controversial.
32987.m: Private pensions were payments by foreign powers to individual politicians.

32988.q: With which decision did the Federal Diet try in 1503 to ban private pensions and unauthorised mercenary service?
32988.e: The Pension Charter of 1503 banned accepting private money from foreign lords. However, it could not be enforced and was lifted again a few years later.
32988.m: The Pension Charter of 1503 was meant to ban private pensions but had no effect.

32989.q: What did ordinary people call politicians who let themselves be paid by foreign princes?
32989.e: The crown was a French gold coin in which many pensions were paid. The mocking name “Kronenfresser” expressed people’s anger at the corrupt lords.
32989.m: Corrupt pension lords were insulted as Kronenfresser, crown-eaters.

32990.q: What is the 1513 uprising of the Bernese rural population against the pension lords in the town called?
32990.e: After the campaign to Dijon, farmers marched from Köniz to Bern in 1513 and demanded that those receiving pensions be punished. There was similar unrest in Lucerne and Solothurn.
32990.m: In the Köniz uprising of 1513, Bernese farmers protested against the pension lords.

32991.q: Which canton was the only one not to join the mercenary alliance with France in 1521?
32991.e: Under Zwingli’s influence, Zurich rejected the French alliance. In 1522 Zurich banned pensions and mercenary service completely.
32991.m: Zurich stayed out of the French mercenary alliance of 1521.

32992.q: In which 1522 writing did Zwingli warn the people of Schwyz against foreign military service and pensions?
a: “Divine Admonition to the Confederates of Schwyz”
32992.e: After the defeat at Bicocca, Zwingli warned the people of Schwyz against mercenary service, which he said corrupted morals. The other writings are by Luther, Calvin and Erasmus.
32992.m: In the “Divine Admonition”, Zwingli fought against mercenary service.

32993.q: Why did pensions strengthen the power of the urban and rural ruling classes in the long term?
a: Because they concentrated money and offices in the hands of a few families
Because they were distributed directly to all citizens
Because they went only to monasteries
Because they replaced the subjects’ taxes
32993.e: Families who received pensions and commanded mercenary regiments became rich and politically influential. This encouraged the rise of patrician and magistrate families.
32993.m: The pension system encouraged the rise of a few rich families.

32994.q: After which defeat did the Confederates conclude the Perpetual Peace with France in 1516?
32994.e: At Marignano France defeated the Confederates in 1515. About a year later the Perpetual Peace was concluded, and it lasted almost three centuries.
32994.m: After Marignano the Confederates made peace with France in 1516.

32995.q: In the Perpetual Peace, what choice did France give the Confederates regarding the areas around Lugano and Locarno?
a: To keep them or give them up for money
To hand them over to the Pope
To administer them as a duchy
32995.e: France offered an extra sum of money if the Confederates gave up the bailiwicks south of the Alps. The Confederates decided to keep the territory.
32995.m: In 1516 the Confederates chose to keep the Ticino bailiwicks rather than take extra money.

32996.q: Which territories were the Three Leagues allowed to keep after the Perpetual Peace?
32996.e: The Grisons leagues had occupied these areas in 1512. France recognised their possession, which remained subject territory of the Three Leagues until 1797.
32996.m: Valtellina, Chiavenna and Bormio stayed with the Three Leagues after 1516.

32997.q: In which French trading city did Confederate merchants gain important customs advantages thanks to the Perpetual Peace?
32997.e: Lyon was an important trade fair city for cloth and financial business. The trading privileges there were very valuable for towns such as St Gallen, Basel and Zurich.
32997.m: The Perpetual Peace brought Swiss merchants advantages in Lyon.

32998.q: Which French king solemnly swore to renew the alliance with the Confederates in Notre-Dame Cathedral in 1663?
32998.e: A large Confederate delegation travelled to Paris in 1663. The oath sworn by Louis XIV is recorded on famous tapestries and paintings.
32998.m: In 1663 Louis XIV renewed the alliance with the Confederates in Paris.

32999.q: What long-term foreign policy consequence did the Perpetual Peace have for the Confederacy?
a: A close tie to France as its most important partner
A permanent alliance with Habsburg against France
32999.e: With the peace and the mercenary alliances that followed, France became the most important partner and the largest employer of Swiss mercenaries. This tie shaped foreign policy until the end of the Ancien Régime.
32999.m: After 1516 France became the Confederates’ most important partner.

33000.q: What did the Perpetual Peace provide for future disputes between France and the Confederates?
33000.e: Conflicts were no longer to be settled with weapons but by arbitrators from both sides. Such arbitration had long been common in the Confederacy.
33000.m: The Perpetual Peace relied on an arbitration court in disputes.

33001.q: Which battle of 1515 meant the failure of Schiner’s policy against France?
33001.e: Schiner had led the Confederates against France in the struggle for Milan. With the defeat at Marignano he lost much of his influence.
33001.m: Schiner’s anti-French policy failed at Marignano.

33002.q: By which pope was Matthäus Schiner made a cardinal in 1511?
33002.e: Julius II rewarded Schiner for his efforts in winning the Confederates for the Holy League against France. The same pope also founded the Swiss Guard.
33002.m: Pope Julius II made Schiner a cardinal in 1511.

33003.q: What did Cardinal Schiner mainly use his power in the Confederacy for?
a: He recruited Confederate mercenaries for the Pope
He spread the Reformation in Valais
He made peace between all the cantons
He founded the University of Basel
33003.e: Schiner was an ally of Pope Julius II. With speeches and money he won the Confederates over to campaigns against France in Italy.
33003.m: Schiner brought Confederate mercenaries into the Pope’s service.

33004.q: Which alliance against France did Schiner lead the Confederates into in 1512?
33004.e: The Holy League under Pope Julius II wanted to drive France out of Italy. Schiner recruited the Confederates, who then undertook the Pavia campaign.
33004.m: Schiner brought the Confederates into the Holy League against France.

33005.q: Whose election as King of the Romans did Schiner support in 1519?
33005.e: Schiner was a determined opponent of France and therefore backed the Habsburg Charles. Charles V was elected in 1519 against Francis I.
33005.m: In 1519 Schiner supported the election of the Habsburg Charles V.

33006.q: Where and of what did Matthäus Schiner die in 1522?
a: In Sion of a battle wound
33006.e: Schiner was staying in Rome after the death of Pope Leo X and died there of the plague in 1522. At times he was even talked about as a possible pope.
33006.m: Cardinal Schiner died of the plague in Rome in 1522.

33007.q: Which Valais district (Zenden) did Matthäus Schiner come from?
33007.e: Schiner was born around 1465 in Mühlebach near Ernen in Goms. He came from a humble background and rose through the Church.

33008.q: What secular position did the Bishop of Sion hold in Schiner’s time alongside his spiritual office?
a: He was Count and Prefect of Valais
He was imperial vicar in Italy
33008.e: The bishops of Sion traced their secular rule back to the supposed gift of Charlemagne, the “Carolina”. As rulers, however, they constantly struggled with the Zenden for power.
33008.m: The Bishop of Sion was also the secular ruler of Valais.

33009.q: What were the associated territories (Zugewandte Orte) of the Old Swiss Confederacy?
a: Allies without the full rights of the thirteen cantons
33009.e: Associated territories such as Biel, St Gallen or Geneva were allied with one or more cantons. They were independent but had less say than the full cantons.
33009.m: Associated territories were allies with fewer rights.

33010.q: Which imperial city in Alsace was allied with the Confederates from 1515 and joined France in 1798?
33010.e: As an island surrounded by Habsburg and later French territory, Mulhouse depended on the Confederates. In 1798, under economic pressure, the city united with France.
33010.m: Mulhouse in Alsace was allied with the Confederates until 1798.

33011.q: Which former associated territory became a Swiss canton in 1815?
33011.e: Geneva had been allied with Bern and Fribourg since the 16th century. In 1815 it was admitted as a canton together with Valais and Neuchâtel.
33011.m: Geneva became a Swiss canton in 1815.

33012.q: Which associated principality passed to the King of Prussia in 1707?
33012.e: After the House of Orléans-Longueville died out, the estates of Neuchâtel chose the King of Prussia as their prince. Neuchâtel nevertheless remained allied with the Confederates.
33012.m: From 1707 the King of Prussia was Prince of Neuchâtel.

33013.q: With which cantons did Geneva conclude a co-citizenship treaty in 1526 to protect itself against Savoy?
33013.e: The co-citizenship treaty of 1526 strengthened the citizens of Geneva against the Duke of Savoy and the bishop. With it Geneva became an associated territory.
33013.m: In 1526 Geneva allied itself with Bern and Fribourg.

33014.q: With which cantons did the Prince-Bishop of Basel ally himself in 1579?
a: Only with the town of Basel
33014.e: Prince-Bishop Jakob Christoph Blarer von Wartensee sought support for Catholic reform. His alliance with the Catholic cantons made the prince-bishopric an associated territory.
33014.m: In 1579 the Prince-Bishopric of Basel allied itself with the Catholic cantons.

33015.q: Which two larger mountain republics were linked with the Confederates as associated territories in the early modern period?
33015.e: Valais and the Three Leagues in the Grisons were independent states with alliances with individual cantons. They only became full cantons in 1815 and 1803 respectively.
33015.m: Valais and the Grisons were long only associated territories of the Confederacy.

33016.q: Which rights did the associated territories usually not have compared with the thirteen cantons?
a: They had no share in the condominiums
They could not pass their own laws
They had to pay taxes to the Federal Diet
33016.e: The associated territories were independent but did not help rule the common subject territories such as Thurgau or the Ticino bailiwicks. At the Federal Diet, too, they usually had only a limited say.
33016.m: Associated territories did not help rule the condominiums.

33017.q: Which of the Three Leagues was most closely linked to the Bishopric of Chur?
a: The League of the Ten Jurisdictions
33017.e: The League of God’s House was formed in 1367 from the subjects of the Bishop of Chur, the “House of God”. It wanted to limit the bishop’s power.
33017.m: The League of God’s House united the valleys of the Bishopric of Chur.

33018.q: According to tradition, under which tree was the Grey League sworn in Trun in 1424?
33018.e: The maple of Trun is an important symbol of the Grisons. A piece of the old trunk is kept in Trun, and a new tree has been planted beside it.
33018.m: According to legend, the Grey League was sworn under the maple of Trun.

33019.q: After the death of which nobleman did the court communities in the Prättigau and around Davos join together in 1436 to form the League of the Ten Jurisdictions?
33019.e: With the death of the last Toggenburg in 1436, his lordship threatened to fall apart. The ten jurisdictions therefore allied for mutual protection.
33019.m: The League of the Ten Jurisdictions was founded in 1436 after the death of the last Toggenburg.

33020.q: What is the document of 1524 called by which the three leagues joined together to form a common free state?
a: The Federal Charter of the Three Leagues
33020.e: The Federal Charter of 1524 permanently united the League of God’s House, the Grey League and the League of the Ten Jurisdictions. It was the basis of the Free State of the Three Leagues.
33020.m: The Federal Charter of 1524 founded the Free State of the Three Leagues.

33021.q: What did the Articles of Ilanz of 1524 and 1526 mainly regulate?
a: Limiting the secular power of the Bishop of Chur
Dividing the Valtellina among the leagues
Introducing Romansh as an official language
33021.e: With the Articles of Ilanz, the communities restricted the rights of the bishop and the monasteries. At the same time the communities were allowed to choose their own faith.
33021.m: The Articles of Ilanz cut back the power of the Bishop of Chur.

33022.q: What is the 1620 massacre of Protestants in the Valtellina called?
33022.e: In July 1620 Catholic inhabitants of the Valtellina, with Spanish support, killed many Protestants. The event was a high point of the Grisons troubles.
33022.m: The Valtellina Massacre of 1620 sharpened the Grisons troubles.

33023.q: Which pastor and later military leader shaped the Grisons troubles and was murdered in Chur in 1639?
33023.e: Jenatsch first fought on the Protestant side, later changed his faith and worked with Spain to win back the Valtellina. He was struck dead at a celebration in Chur in 1639.
33023.m: Jürg Jenatsch is the best-known figure of the Grisons troubles.

33024.q: In which three places did the assembly of the Three Leagues meet in turn?
33024.e: Each league had its main town: Chur for the League of God’s House, Ilanz for the Grey League and Davos for the League of the Ten Jurisdictions. The assembly moved between these places.
33024.m: The assembly of the Three Leagues met in turn in Chur, Ilanz and Davos.

33025.q: What were the Zenden in old Valais?
a: The seven districts of Upper Valais that governed the land
The taxes the farmers paid to the bishop
The passes over the Valais Alps
The mercenary troops of the Bishop of Sion
33025.e: The seven Zenden stretched from Goms to Sion. They formed a kind of league of communities and later also ruled Lower Valais.
33025.m: The Zenden were the seven ruling districts of Upper Valais.

33026.q: From whom did the people of Upper Valais take Lower Valais in 1475 during the Burgundian War?
33026.e: With Bern’s help, the people of Valais defeated the Savoyards near Sion. After that, Lower Valais was subject territory of the Zenden until 1798.
33026.m: In 1475 the people of Upper Valais conquered Savoyard Lower Valais.

33027.q: What was the protest symbol called with which Valais farmers rallied support in uprisings against powerful lords?
33027.e: The Mazze was a wooden club with a carved face, into which supporters hammered a nail. It was placed in front of the accused person’s house and counted as a threat.
33027.m: With the Mazze, the people of Valais called for uprisings against the powerful.

33028.q: What was the highest secular official elected by the council of the Zenden called?
33028.e: The Landeshauptmann led the council and represented the land alongside the bishop. Over time he gained more and more power compared with the bishop.
33028.m: In old Valais the Landeshauptmann stood at the head of the Zenden.

33029.q: Who was the ruler of Valais in the Middle Ages?
33029.e: The Bishop of Sion also had secular power. Over time the Zenden pushed him back, and in the 17th century he lost his rule over the land.
33029.m: In medieval Valais the Bishop of Sion ruled.

33030.q: Which word is the term “Zenden” probably derived from?
a: From the Latin word for ten
33030.e: It is thought to come from Latin “decem” or “decenus”, meaning ten or tenth. In French the Zenden are called “dizains”.
33030.m: The name Zenden is probably linked to the number ten.

33031.q: Since when has Lower Valais no longer been subject to the Upper Valais Zenden?
33031.e: Lower Valais was freed in 1798 with the Helvetic Revolution. However, equal status remained a point of dispute until the 19th century.
33031.m: In 1798 the rule of the Zenden over Lower Valais ended.

33032.q: Which valley south of the Gotthard did Uri rule alone from the 15th century?
33032.e: Uri secured the Leventina as access to the Gotthard route. It remained a subject territory of Uri until 1798.
33032.m: The Leventina was a subject territory of Uri.

33033.q: In which battle of 1478 did Confederates and people of the Leventina defeat a Milanese army?
33033.e: At Giornico in the Leventina, a small Confederate force defeated the much larger army of Milan. This secured Uri’s rule south of the Gotthard.
33033.m: The victory at Giornico in 1478 strengthened Uri’s rule in the Leventina.

33034.q: Which areas were administered jointly by twelve cantons as transalpine bailiwicks from 1512?
a: Lugano, Locarno, Mendrisio and the Maggia valley
33034.e: The Confederates conquered these areas in 1512 during the Milanese Wars. Bellinzona, Riviera and Blenio, on the other hand, belonged only to Uri, Schwyz and Nidwalden.
33034.m: Lugano, Locarno, Mendrisio and the Maggia valley were condominiums of the twelve cantons.

33035.q: Which of the thirteen cantons had no share in the twelve-canton bailiwicks in Ticino?
33035.e: Appenzell only became a full canton in 1513, after the areas had been conquered. That is why it received no share in the rule south of the Alps.
33035.m: Appenzell had no part in the Ticino bailiwicks.

33036.q: Since when has Ticino been a separate canton with equal rights?
33036.e: Until 1798 the Ticino valleys were subject territories of the Confederates. With Napoleon’s Act of Mediation, Ticino became a canton in 1803.
33036.m: Ticino has been a canton since 1803.

33037.q: Where did most of the Protestants expelled from Locarno flee to in 1555?
33037.e: The Catholic cantons enforced the expulsion of the Protestants of Locarno. In Zurich, families such as Orelli and Muralt later became important.
33037.m: Many Protestants expelled from Locarno found a new home in Zurich.

33038.q: Against which ruler did the Leventina rise up unsuccessfully in 1755?
33038.e: The people of the Leventina resisted interference with their rights. Uri crushed the uprising with the help of other cantons and had the leaders executed.
33038.m: The Leventina uprising of 1755 was directed against Uri.

33039.q: How long did a bailiff’s term of office in the Ticino bailiwicks usually last?
33039.e: The ruling cantons provided the bailiff in turn, usually for two years. Many bailiffs used this short time to recover what they had spent on getting the office.
33039.m: A Ticino bailiff usually ruled for only two years.

33040.q: Who ruled Vaud before Bern conquered it in 1536?
33040.e: Vaud belonged to Savoy for a long time. In 1536 Bern used a campaign to help Geneva as an opportunity to conquer the territory.

33041.q: Which ally under pressure did Bern officially want to help in 1536?
33041.e: Geneva was besieged by the Duke of Savoy and called on Bern for help. Bern used the campaign to occupy Savoyard Vaud at the same time.
33041.m: The campaign to free Geneva led to Bern’s conquest of Vaud.

33042.q: Which canton also secured Savoyard territories in 1536, for example around Romont and Estavayer?
33042.e: Fribourg took advantage of Savoy’s weakness and occupied several lordships near its territory. That is why these places belong to the canton of Fribourg today.
33042.m: Fribourg also gained territory from Savoy in 1536.

33043.q: Which event in October 1536 prepared the way for the introduction of the Reformation in Vaud?
33043.e: In Lausanne, Farel, Viret and Calvin debated with Catholic clergy. Afterwards Bern introduced the Reformation in Vaud by edict.
33043.m: After the Disputation of Lausanne, Vaud became Protestant.

33044.q: Which castle on Lake Geneva did Bern capture in 1536, freeing the prisoner François Bonivard?
33044.e: As an opponent of Savoy, Bonivard had been imprisoned in Chillon for years. Lord Byron later made him famous with the poem “The Prisoner of Chillon”.
33044.m: When Chillon was captured in 1536, François Bonivard was freed.

33045.q: Until when did Vaud remain under Bernese rule after the conquest of 1536?
33045.e: Vaud was Bernese subject territory for over 260 years. In 1798 it declared itself independent with French support, and in 1803 it became a canton.

33046.q: Which college did Bern found in Lausanne in 1537 to train Protestant pastors?
33046.e: The Academy of Lausanne is regarded as the oldest Protestant college in the French-speaking world. The University of Lausanne later grew out of it.
33046.m: The Academy of Lausanne was founded in 1537 for Protestant pastors.

33047.q: Which princely house tried to conquer Geneva with the Escalade in 1602?
33047.e: The Duke of Savoy wanted to win back Geneva, the former bishop’s city. However, the surprise attack on the night of 11 to 12 December 1602 failed.
33047.m: Savoy attacked Geneva in 1602 in the Escalade.

33048.q: Why does Geneva celebrate the Escalade around 12 December, even though by today’s calendar the attack took place around 21 December?
a: Because Geneva used the Julian calendar at the time
Because the festival was moved because of Christmas
Because the date was only fixed in 1815
Because the attack lasted two weeks
33048.e: Protestant Geneva still used the Julian calendar, according to which the attack took place on 11 and 12 December. Today the festival is celebrated on the weekend around 12 December.
33048.m: The date of the Escalade follows the old Julian calendar.

33049.q: How did the Savoyards try to get into the city of Geneva in 1602?
a: With ladders over the city wall
With cannons through the main gate
33049.e: The name Escalade comes from the French “escalader”, to climb. The attackers climbed the walls with ladders at night but were discovered.
33049.m: Escalade means climbing the city wall.

33050.q: Why do people in Geneva smash a chocolate pot at the Escalade?
a: It recalls the soup a Genevan woman poured on the attackers
It stands for the destroyed city gate
It recalls the hunger after a siege
33050.e: According to legend, the Mère Royaume poured hot vegetable soup on an attacker and hit him with the pot. The chocolate marmite recalls this.
33050.m: The chocolate marmite recalls the soup of the Mère Royaume.

33051.q: Which reformer, Calvin’s successor, had Psalm 124 sung after the attack was beaten off?
33051.e: The very elderly Theodore Beza led the thanksgiving service. Psalm 124 begins roughly with the thought that God stood by his people.
33051.m: After the Escalade, Theodore Beza had Psalm 124 sung in thanks.

33052.q: What is the Cortège de l’Escalade in Geneva?
a: A boat race on Lake Geneva
A shooting festival outside the city
A church service in the cathedral
33052.e: Hundreds of people in clothes and armour from around 1600 march through the old town. They recall the defeat of the Savoyard surprise attack of 1602.
33052.m: In the Cortège, Genevans in costume march through the old town.

33053.q: What happened to the Savoyard soldiers who were captured alive during the Escalade?
a: They were released for a ransom
They had to serve Geneva as mercenaries
They were handed over to Bern
33053.e: Because no war had been declared, Geneva treated the attackers not as prisoners of war but as criminals. They were executed the next day.
33053.m: Captured attackers of the Escalade were executed in Geneva.

33054.q: Why is the Escalade regarded as an important event for Genevan identity?
a: It secured the independence of the Protestant city republic
It led to Geneva joining as a canton
It ended the Reformation in Geneva
It made Geneva the capital of Savoy
33054.e: By beating off the attack, Geneva remained independent and Protestant. A year later Savoy gave up its claims by treaty.
33054.m: The Escalade stands for the freedom Geneva defended.

33055.q: On which day did the first Swiss Guards arrive in Rome, which is regarded as the founding date?
33055.e: About 150 Swiss entered Rome under Captain Kaspar von Silenen. Pope Julius II had recruited them as his bodyguard.
33055.m: The Pontifical Swiss Guard has existed since 22 January 1506.

33056.q: Which event does the swearing-in of new Swiss Guards every year on 6 May commemorate?
a: The founding of the Guard in 1506
33056.e: On 6 May 1527, when imperial mercenaries attacked Rome, most of the guards died defending the Pope. Since then new guards have been sworn in on this day.
33056.m: On 6 May the Guard remembers its action during the Sack of Rome in 1527.

33057.q: Where was Pope Clement VII able to flee in 1527 thanks to the sacrifice of the Swiss Guard?
33057.e: While most of the guards fell, the rest brought the Pope to safety along the raised passage of the Passetto di Borgo. The fortress on the Tiber held out against the attackers.
33057.m: In 1527 Clement VII escaped to Castel Sant’Angelo.

33058.q: In which language do new guards speak their oath at the swearing-in?
33058.e: Each recruit swears in his national language, that is German, French, Italian or Romansh. As he does so, he raises his right hand with three fingers outstretched.
33058.m: Guards swear their oath in their own mother tongue.

33059.q: What special position has the Swiss Guard had in the Vatican since 1970?
a: It is the only remaining guard of the Pope
It is under the command of the Swiss Army
It is a guard of honour with no weapons at all
It only guards the summer residence now
33059.e: In 1970 Pope Paul VI disbanded the other military units of the Holy See. Only the Swiss Guard remained as an armed guard.
33059.m: Since 1970 the Swiss Guard has been the Pope’s only guard.

33060.q: Which requirement must applicants for the Pontifical Swiss Guard meet?
a: Swiss citizenship and the Catholic faith
33060.e: Guards must be Swiss, Catholic and unmarried and must have completed basic military training. When they join they may be no older than 30.
33060.m: Swiss Guards are Catholic Swiss citizens.

33061.q: What is the plumed helmet called that Swiss Guards wear with their full dress uniform?
33061.e: The morion is a helmet with an upturned brim and a crest, as was common in the 16th century. On ceremonial occasions the Guard wears it with a coloured plume.
33061.m: With their full dress uniform, guards wear the morion.

33062.q: Which pope founded the Pontifical Swiss Guard in 1506?
33062.e: In 1506 Julius II brought Swiss mercenaries to Rome as his bodyguard. On 22 January 1506 the first 150 guards entered the Vatican.
33062.m: Pope Julius II founded the Swiss Guard in 1506.

33063.q: Which cantons were the main opponents of Protestant Zurich in the First War of Kappel in 1529?
33063.e: Lucerne, Uri, Schwyz, Unterwalden and Zug held on to the old faith. Zurich, on the other hand, had introduced the Reformation under Zwingli.
33063.m: In the First War of Kappel, Zurich faced the five inner cantons.

33064.q: With which economic means did the Protestant towns put pressure on Central Switzerland in 1531?
a: With a ban on cheese exports
With a devaluation of the currency
33064.e: Zurich and Bern blocked the supply of grain and salt to the inner cantons. These responded in October 1531 with a declaration of war.
33064.m: The food blockade of 1531 led directly to the Second War of Kappel.

33065.q: Which faith was favoured in the condominiums by the Second Peace of Kappel?
33065.e: Catholic minorities were protected and communities were allowed to return to the old faith. Protestant communities did not receive equal protection.
33065.m: The Second Peace strengthened the Catholics in the condominiums.

33066.q: Which alliance did the five inner cantons conclude with Austria in 1529?
33066.e: The Catholic cantons sought support from the Habsburg Archduke Ferdinand. The alliance was a response to the alliance of the Protestant towns.
33066.m: In 1529 the Christian Union linked the inner cantons with Austria.

33067.q: What was the alliance of Zurich with Protestant towns such as Constance, Bern and Basel called?
33067.e: From 1527 Zurich built up a network of co-citizenship treaties with Protestant towns. It was directed against Habsburg and the Catholic cantons.
33067.m: In the Christian Civic Union the Protestant towns joined together.

33068.q: Which well-known story is told about the First War of Kappel in 1529?
a: Soldiers of both sides ate a milk soup together
The armies settled things with a wrestling match
Zwingli converted the Catholic soldiers with a sermon
33068.e: According to tradition, men from Central Switzerland placed a pot of milk on the border and men from Zurich added bread. The “Kappel milk soup” is seen as a symbol of the Swiss willingness to compromise.
33068.m: The Kappel milk soup stands for reconciliation among Confederates.

33069.q: Whose successor did Heinrich Bullinger become as head of the Zurich church in 1531?
33069.e: Zwingli fell at the Battle of Kappel in 1531. Bullinger took over his office and led the Zurich church until 1575.

33070.q: Which theological dispute did the Consensus Tigurinus of 1549 concern?
33070.e: Zurich and Geneva understood the Lord’s Supper differently and found a common formula. In doing so they also set themselves apart from Lutheran teaching.
33070.m: The Consensus Tigurinus settled the question of the Lord’s Supper between Zurich and Geneva.

33071.q: Where did the young Bullinger teach from 1523?
a: At Kappel Abbey on the Albis
33071.e: At the age of 19, Bullinger became a teacher at the school of the Cistercian abbey of Kappel. There he promoted the ideas of the Reformation.
33071.m: Bullinger began his career as a teacher at Kappel Abbey.

33072.q: Which confession of faith did Bullinger write in 1536 together with Oswald Myconius and Leo Jud?
33072.e: The confession summarised the teaching of the Protestant Swiss towns. It was an early attempt to present the Swiss Reformation as a united whole.
33072.m: The First Helvetic Confession was written in Basel in 1536.

33073.q: In which country were Bullinger’s writings especially widely read in the 16th century?
33073.e: Bullinger’s collection of sermons, the Decades, was translated and widely used in the English church. He also corresponded with many English people.
33073.m: Bullinger strongly influenced the Reformation in England.

33074.q: Which reformer worked in Geneva at the same time as Bullinger?
33074.e: Calvin shaped the Reformation in Geneva. In 1549 Bullinger and Calvin agreed on the Lord’s Supper in the Consensus Tigurinus.
33074.m: Bullinger in Zurich and Calvin in Geneva worked closely together.

33075.q: Which office did Charles Borromeo hold from 1564?
33075.e: From 1564 Borromeo was Archbishop of Milan and strictly reformed his diocese. It also included areas in today’s Ticino.
33075.m: Charles Borromeo worked as Archbishop of Milan.

33076.q: Which institution did Borromeo found in Milan in 1579 for priests from Switzerland?
33076.e: In the Collegium Helveticum young Swiss men were to become well-trained Catholic priests. It was a key tool of Catholic reform in the Confederacy.
33076.m: The Collegium Helveticum trained Swiss priests in Milan.

33077.q: At which council, which launched the Catholic Reform, did Borromeo play a major part in the final phase?
33077.e: In 1562/63 Borromeo promoted the last session and directed the editing of the Roman Catechism. Afterwards he consistently put its decisions into practice.
33077.m: Borromeo put the decisions of the Council of Trent into practice.

33078.q: Which movement was the Catholic Reform promoted by Charles Borromeo a response to?
33078.e: After the Protestants split away, the Catholic Church wanted to remedy abuses and strengthen its faith. Borromeo carried out this renewal particularly consistently.
33078.m: Borromeo was a leading figure of the Catholic Reform.

33079.q: In which Grisons valley did Borromeo have people accused of witchcraft in 1583?
33079.e: Of 108 accused, eleven were burned; the rest returned to the Catholic Church under torture. The trials show the harsh side of the Counter-Reformation.
33079.m: The Mesolcina witch trials of 1583 are a dark chapter of the Counter-Reformation.

33080.q: Which order promoted by Borromeo founded its first friary in German-speaking Switzerland in Altdorf in 1581?
33080.e: The Capuchins, close to ordinary people, preached in the Catholic cantons and strengthened the faith of the common people. Soon more friaries followed, for example in Lucerne and Stans.
33080.m: The Capuchins were important bearers of the Catholic Reform in Switzerland.

33081.q: Why did Charles Borromeo travel through the Catholic cantons of Central Switzerland in 1570?
a: To examine abuses in the Church and clergy
To make peace with the Protestants
To found a diocese of Lucerne
33081.e: Borromeo visited monasteries and parishes and saw many abuses, such as poorly trained priests. Afterwards he promoted the training of priests and orders such as the Capuchins.
33081.m: Borromeo visited Central Switzerland in 1570 to renew the Church.

33082.q: What is the “San Carlone” in Arona on Lake Maggiore?
a: A huge copper statue of the saint
A pilgrimage church with his tomb
33082.e: The statue, about 23 metres high, was made in the 17th century in his home town of Arona. Visitors can climb up inside it into the head.
33082.m: The San Carlone in Arona commemorates Charles Borromeo.

33083.q: What did Borromeo do during the plague of 1576 to 1578 in Milan?
a: He arranged for the clergy to flee to the countryside
33083.e: He stayed in the city and personally looked after the sick and the poor. This harmed his health but increased the veneration for him.
33083.m: During the plague Borromeo himself helped the sick in Milan.

33084.q: In which period was the Golden League of the Catholic cantons founded?
a: In the period of the Catholic Reform
In the period of the Enlightenment
In the period of the Helvetic Republic
In the period of the Burgundian Wars
33084.e: The league was sworn in 1586. It fell in the period of the Catholic Reform after the Council of Trent.
33084.m: The Golden League was founded during the Catholic Reform.

33085.q: Who joined together in the Golden League?
a: The guilds of the large towns
33085.e: The five cantons of Central Switzerland as well as Fribourg and Solothurn took part. They wanted to help each other protect the Catholic faith.
33085.m: In the Golden League the Catholic cantons joined together.

33086.q: Which town cantons belonged to the Golden League?
33086.e: Besides the rural cantons, three towns that had remained Catholic took part. Zurich, Bern, Basel and Schaffhausen were Protestant.
33086.m: Lucerne, Fribourg and Solothurn were the Catholic town cantons in the Golden League.

33087.q: Where does the name “Golden League” come from?
a: From the golden initial letters of the document
From the gold of mercenary pensions
33087.e: The initials of the treaty text were decorated with gold. So the name has nothing to do with payments of money.
33087.m: The Golden League owes its name to the gilded initials.

33088.q: Which town was the leading Catholic canton of the Confederacy in the 16th century?
33088.e: Lucerne was the leading canton of the Catholic cantons. The Lucerne Schultheiss Ludwig Pfyffer pushed the Golden League forward.
33088.m: In the 16th century Lucerne led the Catholic cantons.

33089.q: Why did the Golden League strain the unity of the Confederacy?
a: It put loyalty to the faith above the old alliance duties
It created its own Catholic currency
33089.e: The partners committed themselves to help each other preserve the Catholic faith, if necessary even against fellow Confederate cantons. This deepened the religious division.
33089.m: The Golden League made religion more important than the old alliances.

33090.q: With which great power did the Catholic cantons, except Solothurn, ally themselves in 1587?
33090.e: On 12 May 1587 they concluded an alliance with Spain, which then ruled the Duchy of Milan. Spain received rights of passage for troops, and the cantons received grain and pensions.
33090.m: After 1586 the Catholic cantons drew closer to Spain.

33091.q: Which church council gave the decisive push to the Catholic Reform in the 16th century?
33091.e: The council met from 1545 to 1563 and renewed the Catholic Church. The Golden League of 1586 was also part of this renewal.
33091.m: The Council of Trent launched the Catholic Reform.

33092.q: Which decree of Louis XIV triggered the great wave of Huguenot refugees in 1685?
33092.e: With this decree the king banned the Protestant faith in France. Tens of thousands of Huguenots fled abroad despite a ban on leaving the country.
33092.m: In 1685 the Edict of Fontainebleau drove the Huguenots into exile.

33093.q: At least how many Huguenots are estimated to have passed through Switzerland?
33093.e: Most of the refugees travelled on to German states, the Netherlands or England.
33093.m: Switzerland was an important transit country for Huguenots.

33094.q: Roughly how many Huguenots stayed in Switzerland permanently?
33094.e: Many towns could not provide for all the refugees and supported their onward journey. Some, however, settled permanently.
33094.m: Only some of the Huguenots settled permanently in Switzerland.

33095.q: In which areas did Huguenots give the Swiss economy important impulses?
33095.e: Many refugees were well-trained merchants, craftsmen and entrepreneurs. They brought capital, expertise and trade connections with them.
33095.m: Huguenots revived trade and finance in Switzerland.

33096.q: What did Huguenots found in towns such as Basel, Bern or St Gallen?
33096.e: The refugees held church services in their mother tongue. Some of these Églises françaises still exist today.
33096.m: In many Swiss towns the Huguenots founded French church congregations.

33097.q: How many Huguenots did Zurich take in between 1683 and 1688, although it had only about 10,000 inhabitants?
33097.e: Most of the refugees stayed only temporarily and moved on. Even so, providing for them was a huge task for the town.
33097.m: Zurich took in more Huguenots than it had inhabitants itself.

33098.q: Which town paid thousands of Huguenots travel money for their onward journey?
33098.e: The town in Bernese Vaud supported thousands of fellow believers with travel money for the way north. Many refugees moved on to German states.
33098.m: Lausanne helped many Huguenots with money for their onward journey.

33099.q: In which year did the flow of Huguenots through Switzerland reach its peak?
33099.e: Two years after the Protestant faith was banned in France, especially large numbers of people fled. The Swiss towns were heavily overburdened at the time.
33099.m: In 1687 the most Huguenots passed through Switzerland.

33100.q: In which two periods did particularly large numbers of Huguenots come to Switzerland?
33100.e: The first wave came during the French Wars of Religion. The second followed the persecutions under Louis XIV.
33100.m: The Huguenots came to Switzerland in two large waves.

33101.q: What did Johann Rudolf Wettstein from Basel achieve at the Westphalian peace congress?
a: The separation of the Confederacy from the Holy Roman Empire
The founding of the canton of Basel-Landschaft
An alliance of the Confederates with Sweden
33101.e: In the Peace of Westphalia of 1648, the Confederacy was freed from the jurisdiction of the Empire. It was thus also legally an independent state.
33101.m: In 1648 Wettstein achieved the Confederacy’s independence from the Empire.

33102.q: Against whom did the farmers rise in the Swiss Peasants’ War of 1653, which Wettstein also fought against in Basel?
33102.e: After the Thirty Years’ War prices fell and the towns devalued their coins. The farmers in Lucerne, Bern, Solothurn and Basel resisted the levies and arbitrary rule of the town lords.
33102.m: In the Peasants’ War of 1653, the farmers resisted the towns.

33103.q: Which office did Wettstein hold in Basel when he travelled to the peace congress in Westphalia?
33103.e: Wettstein had been Mayor of Basel since 1645. As envoy, he also represented the other cantons at the peace negotiations.

33104.q: In which place near Basel is the Wettstein House, which today houses a toy museum?
33104.e: Wettstein used to live there. Since 1972 the house has held a toy museum, a village museum and a wine-growing museum.
33104.m: The Wettstein House in Riehen commemorates the Basel statesman.

33105.q: Which war was ended by the Peace of Westphalia in 1648?
a: The War of the Spanish Succession
33105.e: The Thirty Years’ War lasted from 1618 to 1648 and devastated large parts of Germany. The Confederacy was largely spared.
33105.m: The Peace of Westphalia ended the Thirty Years’ War in 1648.

33106.q: Which powers agreed to the article on the Confederacy in the Peace of Westphalia?
33106.e: After long talks, Wettstein obtained the agreement of the emperor’s representatives and of the two victorious powers. France supported the request in particular.
33106.m: In 1648 the emperor, France and Sweden recognised the special status of the Confederates.

33107.q: Which measure taken by Bern in December 1652 hit the rural population particularly hard?
a: Devaluing the batzen coins by half
33107.e: The copper batzen lost half their value and could only be exchanged for three days. Many farmers lost about half their savings in this way.
33107.m: The devaluation of 1652 was one trigger of the Peasants’ War.

33108.q: Which farmers’ leader from the Emmental was executed after the Peasants’ War of 1653?
33108.e: Niklaus Leuenberger was head of the farmers’ league. After the defeat he was captured and executed in Bern in September 1653.
33108.m: Niklaus Leuenberger led the farmers in 1653 and was executed.

33109.q: Which longer-term consequence is attributed to the Peasants’ War of 1653?
