a: The authorities held back from raising taxes
33109.e: Although the towns won militarily, they depended on their subjects. Historians see the uprising as one reason why absolutism like that in France never took hold in Switzerland.
33109.m: The Peasants’ War slowed the growth of the authorities’ power.

33110.q: How did the Peasants’ War of 1653 end militarily?
a: With a victory for the town authorities
With a victory for the farmers
In a draw without a peace treaty
33110.e: The towns’ troops, supported by the Federal Diet, were better armed. After battles at Wohlenschwil and Herzogenbuchsee, the farmers had to give up.
33110.m: In the Peasants’ War of 1653 the towns won.

33111.q: In which region did the farmers’ uprising of 1653 begin?
a: In the Entlebuch in the canton of Lucerne
33111.e: The farmers of the Entlebuch rebelled against the Lucerne authorities in early 1653. The uprising quickly spread to Bern, Solothurn and Basel.
33111.m: The Peasants’ War began in the Entlebuch in 1653.

33112.q: Which figure from the founding story of the Confederacy did the farmers particularly refer to?
33112.e: The farmers saw themselves in the tradition of resistance against unjust bailiffs. Their charter of alliance was modelled on the old alliances.
33112.m: The farmers of 1653 saw themselves as William Tell’s successors.

33113.q: Subjects of which town cantons mainly formed an alliance in Sumiswald in April 1653?
33113.e: On 23 April 1653 farmers from several town cantons joined together across canton and religious borders. Subjects of Solothurn were only marginally involved.
33113.m: In Sumiswald farmers from several town cantons formed an alliance.

33114.q: Which town did the men of Zurich besiege unsuccessfully in the First War of Villmergen?
33114.e: The Zurich troops could not take the town on upper Lake Zurich. This failure also contributed to the Protestant defeat.
33114.m: The siege of Rapperswil in 1656 failed.

33115.q: Which territories did the Catholic cantons lose to the victors in 1712?
a: The County of Baden and the lower Freie Ämter
The Leventina and the Blenio valley
33115.e: Rule over these strategically important areas in the Aargau passed to Zurich, Bern and Glarus. The cantons of Central Switzerland thus lost their land bridge between the Catholic cantons.
33115.m: After 1712 the Protestant cantons ruled the County of Baden.

33116.q: What was the significance of the outcome of the Second War of Villmergen?
a: It ended the political dominance of the Catholic cantons
It led to the founding of the federal state
33116.e: Since 1531 the Catholic cantons had dominated the Federal Diet and the condominiums. After 1712 Zurich and above all Bern took the lead.
33116.m: From 1712 the Protestant cantons set the tone in the Confederacy.

33117.q: Which side won the Second War of Villmergen in 1712?
a: The Protestant cantons of Zurich and Bern
The Catholic cantons of Central Switzerland
Neither, the war ended in a draw
33117.e: After the Catholic victory of 1656, the balance of power turned in 1712. Zurich and Bern won the second battle of Villmergen.
33117.m: In 1712 the Protestant cantons won at Villmergen.

33118.q: Why did the 1655 project to renew the Confederate alliances fail?
a: Because of resistance from the Catholic cantons
Because of resistance from the farmers
33118.e: The Protestants wanted to combine the many alliances into one common treaty. The Catholic cantons feared for their leading position.
33118.m: The failure of the alliance project in 1655 sharpened the religious conflict.

33119.q: Which conflict lay behind the two Wars of Villmergen?
a: The conflict between Catholic and Protestant cantons
The conflict between towns and farmers
The conflict between German- and French-speaking Switzerland
The conflict between Habsburg and France
33119.e: Since the Reformation, the Catholic and Protestant cantons had faced each other. This led to wars at Villmergen in the Aargau in 1656 and 1712.
33119.m: The Wars of Villmergen were wars of religion.

33120.q: Why did France and Habsburg not intervene in the Confederate conflict in 1712?
a: They were tied up in the War of the Spanish Succession
They had recognised the Confederacy as neutral
They both supported the Protestant cantons
33120.e: Since 1701 both powers had been at war with each other over the Spanish inheritance. Bern and Zurich took advantage of this favourable situation.
33120.m: In 1712 the War of the Spanish Succession kept the great powers busy.

33121.q: Which town cantons are regarded as typical patrician cantons of the Ancien Régime?
33121.e: In these towns a small circle of long-established families ruled. The guilds had hardly any political influence there.
33121.m: In Bern, Lucerne, Fribourg and Solothurn the patricians ruled.

33122.q: What are town cantons called in which the craftsmen’s guilds determined the government?
33122.e: In these towns the councils were elected through the guilds. But even there, over time, an upper class of a few families developed.
33122.m: In guild cantons the guilds decided who sat on the councils.

33123.q: What did “regimentsfähig” mean in the Ancien Régime?
a: Obliged to serve in a regiment
33123.e: Only members of certain citizen families could be elected to the councils. Other inhabitants remained excluded from power.
33123.m: Only families entitled to govern (regimentsfähig) could rule the town.

33124.q: What were the ruling patricians in the town cantons often called?
33124.e: The title expressed the councils’ position of authority over their subjects. It was common throughout the Old Swiss Confederacy.
33124.m: The authorities of the Ancien Régime were called the Gracious Lords.

33125.q: What was the “Äusserer Stand” (Outer Estate) in Bern?
a: An association of young patricians who practised governing
The subject territory outside the town
The farmers’ representation on the council
33125.e: Young sons of patricians formed a kind of shadow government with its own offices. In this way they prepared for their later duties in the state.
33125.m: In the Äusserer Stand young Bernese patricians practised governing.

33126.q: What caused the circle of ruling families to shrink in the 17th and 18th centuries?
33126.e: New families were hardly ever admitted as citizens entitled to govern. Families that died out were not replaced, and power became even more concentrated.
33126.m: Closed citizenship turned the patriciate into a small elite.

33127.q: Besides state offices, what was an important source of income for many patrician families?
33127.e: As officers, patricians raised regiments for France, Spain or the Netherlands. There were also pensions from foreign powers.
33127.m: Mercenary service brought many patrician families money and prestige.

33128.q: What was Bern’s Grand Council also called, after the number of its members?
33128.e: The Grand Council was the supreme body of the Republic of Bern. Its members came exclusively from citizen families entitled to govern.
33128.m: Bern’s Grand Council was also called the Council of Two Hundred.

33129.q: Who administered the rural subject territories in the name of the town of Bern?
33129.e: The bailiffs were patricians who took on an office in the countryside for a few years. The bailiwicks often brought them considerable income.
33129.m: Bernese patricians governed the countryside as bailiffs.

33130.q: Which title was used for the head of government in Bern and Lucerne?
33130.e: In the patrician towns a Schultheiss stood at the top, whereas in Zurich and Basel it was a mayor. Landammänner led the rural cantons.
33130.m: Bern and Lucerne were led by a Schultheiss.

33131.q: Roughly how many soldiers did Davel set off with in 1723?
33131.e: The militia soldiers had actually been called together for an inspection. At first they did not know what their commander was planning.
33131.m: Davel led only a few hundred militia soldiers.

33132.q: How did Davel justify his action during his interrogations?
a: God had given him the task
He had acted out of revenge
Geneva had put him up to it
33132.e: Even under torture he named no fellow conspirators and insisted on a divine mission. This later made him a symbolic figure.
33132.m: Davel saw himself as the instrument of a divine mission.

33133.q: What aim did Major Davel pursue when he marched to Lausanne with soldiers in 1723?
a: To free Vaud from Bernese rule
To bring back the Bishop of Lausanne
To conquer the city of Geneva
33133.e: Vaud had been a subject territory of Bern since 1536. Davel wanted it to become a free canton of the Confederacy in its own right.
33133.m: Davel wanted to free Vaud from Bern.

33134.q: How did the authorities of Lausanne react to Davel’s appeal in 1723?
a: They had him arrested and handed him over to Bern
They fled the town to escape him
33134.e: The Lausanne councillors pretended to consider the plan and secretly informed Bern. Davel was arrested, interrogated and executed.
33134.m: Lausanne handed Davel over to Bern.

33135.q: Which military rank did Davel receive after 1712, by which he is still known today?
33135.e: After serving in foreign armies he was promoted for his services in the Toggenburg War. In 1717 he took command of the militia in the Lavaux.
33135.m: The people of Vaud remember him as Major Davel.

33136.q: In which year did Vaud, for whose freedom Davel had died, actually become independent of Bern?
33136.e: With the French invasion and the Helvetic Revolution, Bernese rule ended in 1798. In 1803 Vaud became a canton in its own right.
33136.m: Vaud broke away from Bern in 1798.

33137.q: How is Major Davel seen in the canton of Vaud today?
a: As a champion of Vaud’s freedom
As a traitor to the Confederacy
As the founder of the city of Lausanne
As the first Federal Councillor from Vaud
33137.e: After 1798 Davel became a symbol of the people of Vaud’s will to be free. Monuments, for example in front of the Château Saint-Maire in Lausanne, commemorate him.
33137.m: Davel is regarded as a freedom hero of Vaud.

33138.q: Under which famous generals did Davel serve in foreign service?
33138.e: From 1692 he fought for Prince Eugene of Savoy and later for the Duke of Marlborough. This experience shaped his military career.
33138.m: Davel gained war experience under Prince Eugene and Marlborough.

33139.q: Against whom was the Henzi conspiracy of 1749 in Bern directed?
a: Against the rule of the patrician families
Against the bailiffs in the Aargau
33139.e: Dissatisfied citizens, craftsmen and officers wanted to break the power of the few ruling families. The conspiracy was also called the “Burgerlärm” (citizens’ uproar).
33139.m: The Henzi conspiracy was directed against the Bernese patriciate.

33140.q: Why did the Henzi conspiracy of 1749 fail?
a: It was betrayed before it could strike
The conspirators were defeated in open battle
33140.e: In early July 1749 a theology student informed a councillor. The government acted immediately and had the leaders arrested.
33140.m: The Henzi conspiracy was exposed through betrayal.

33141.q: What happened to Samuel Henzi and two fellow conspirators on 17 July 1749?
33141.e: Henzi, Samuel Niklaus Wernier and Emanuel Fueter were executed in front of the Upper Gate. Other participants were placed under house arrest or banished.
33141.m: The leaders of the Henzi conspiracy were executed.

33142.q: Which German writer wrote a fragment of a play about Samuel Henzi?
33142.e: The fragment “Samuel Henzi” was written in 1749 and published in 1753. It is regarded as an early middle-class drama about a current political case.
33142.m: Lessing turned the Henzi case into a play.

33143.q: What, among other things, did Henzi’s reform paper demand?
a: Access for all citizens to public offices
A return to the Catholic faith
33143.e: The memorial also called for a guild constitution, popular election of officials and public state accounts. It aimed at giving the citizens more say.
33143.m: Henzi demanded that offices be open to all citizens.

33144.q: Why had Henzi already been punished and banished in 1744?
a: He had criticised the way the Grand Council was elected
He had smuggled books from Paris
33144.e: Citizens had criticised the elections to the Grand Council in written petitions. The government responded with fines and banishments.
33144.m: Henzi clashed with the authorities over political criticism as early as 1744.

33145.q: Who took part in the Henzi conspiracy?
a: Dissatisfied citizens such as craftsmen, merchants and officers
33145.e: The conspirators met secretly in a dye works in the Sulgenbach. They were citizens of Bern who were excluded from public offices.
33145.m: In the Henzi conspiracy, citizens resisted the patriciate.

33146.q: For whom did Anna Göldi work as a maid?
a: For the doctor Johann Jakob Tschudi
For the Abbot of St Gallen
33146.e: Tschudi was a doctor, councillor and judge in Glarus. He probably wanted to use the accusation to cover up an affair.
33146.m: Anna Göldi served in the house of the Glarus doctor Tschudi.

33147.q: How was Anna Göldi described in the verdict in order to avoid the word “witch”?
33147.e: In the age of the Enlightenment the court did not want to speak openly of witchcraft. In substance, however, the case was about sorcery with the devil’s powers.
33147.m: The verdict against Anna Göldi deliberately avoided the word witch.

33148.q: Why is Anna Göldi often called “the last witch”?
a: In 1782 she was one of the last women in Europe executed for witchcraft
She was the last woman to win a witch trial
She wrote the last book about witchcraft
She was the last herbalist in the canton of Glarus
33148.e: Anna Göldi was beheaded in Glarus in 1782. Critics in Germany called the verdict a “judicial murder” even at the time.
33148.m: Anna Göldi is regarded as one of the last people executed in a witch trial in Europe.

33149.q: Which Swiss author published the novel “Anna Göldin. Letzte Hexe” (Anna Göldin, the last witch) in 1982?
33149.e: The novel made the case known to a wide public.
33149.m: Eveline Hasler’s novel made Anna Göldi famous.

33150.q: What did the Glarus cantonal parliament decide about Anna Göldi in 2008?
a: It had her story removed from school books
33150.e: 226 years after the execution, the Glarus cantonal parliament declared the verdict unjust. Anna Göldi was thus officially rehabilitated.
33150.m: In 2008 Anna Göldi was rehabilitated by the canton of Glarus.

33151.q: In which century, in the middle of the Age of Enlightenment, was Anna Göldi executed?
33151.e: Anna Göldi died in 1782. At that time many educated people no longer believed in witches, so the case caused outrage throughout Europe.
33151.m: Anna Göldi was executed in 1782, in the Age of Enlightenment.

33152.q: Which body passed the death sentence on Anna Göldi on 6 June 1782?
33152.e: In Glarus, which was divided by religion, the Protestant council judged the maid. Her confession had been forced out of her under torture.
33152.m: The Protestant Council of Glarus sentenced Anna Göldi to death.

33153.q: How was Anna Göldi’s confession obtained?
a: It was forced out of her under torture
She confessed voluntarily to the pastor
A witness spoke it for her
It was determined by an ordeal in water
33153.e: In prison Anna Göldi was tortured until she admitted the accusations. Later she withdrew parts of her confession.
33153.m: Anna Göldi’s confession was forced out of her by torture.

33154.q: From the spirit of which era did the Helvetic Society arise?
33154.e: The society was founded in 1761. Enlightened men from various cantons wanted to promote education, tolerance and the common good.
33154.m: The Helvetic Society arose in the spirit of the Enlightenment.

33155.q: Who met in the Helvetic Society?
a: Mainly farmers from the mountain valleys
33155.e: At first the members met at the spa of Schinznach-Bad. They were educated men from Protestant and Catholic cantons.
33155.m: Educated men of the Enlightenment met in the Helvetic Society.

33156.q: What was the main aim of the Helvetic Society?
a: To strengthen unity across canton and religious borders
33156.e: Protestants and Catholics were to see themselves as fellow Confederates. Tolerance, education and the common good came first.
33156.m: The Helvetic Society promoted a shared Swiss identity.

33157.q: Which state did many former members of the Helvetic Society help to shape from 1798?
33157.e: Members such as Philipp Albert Stapfer took on important offices after 1798. They wanted to put Enlightenment ideas into practice in politics.
33157.m: Many Enlightenment figures from the Helvetic Society worked in the Helvetic Republic.

33158.q: Which 1758 writing by Franz Urs Balthasar of Lucerne gave an impulse to the founding?
33158.e: In it Balthasar set out ideas for a renewal of the Confederacy. The writing was very popular among enlightened patriots.
33158.m: Balthasar’s patriotic dreams inspired the Helvetic Society.

33159.q: Which famous educator was a member of the Helvetic Society?
33159.e: The members also included Philipp Albert Stapfer and Albrecht Rengger. Many of them later shaped the Helvetic Republic.
33159.m: Pestalozzi also belonged to the Helvetic Society.

33160.q: Which association has carried on the ideals of the Helvetic Society since 1914?
a: The Swiss Society for the Common Good
33160.e: Shortly before the First World War, it wanted to strengthen unity between German-speaking and French-speaking Switzerland.
33160.m: The New Helvetic Society continues the legacy of 1761.

33161.q: Why did many members of the Helvetic Society consider their aims achieved after 1848?
a: The new federal state had united Switzerland
All the cantons had become Catholic
33161.e: With the federal state of 1848, the unity of Switzerland was achieved politically. The society dissolved in 1858.
33161.m: With the federal state of 1848 the main aim was achieved.

33162.q: Why did the meetings of the Helvetic Society stop for some years from 1798?
a: Because of the French occupation and the Helvetic Republic
Because of a ban by the Pope
33162.e: No meetings took place from 1798 to 1807. After that the society resumed its activities.
33162.m: During the French period the Helvetic Society was inactive.

33163.q: Which branch of industry was Switzerland’s largest export sector around 1910, with about 18 per cent of exports?
33163.e: About 95 per cent of the embroidery, made mainly in eastern Switzerland, went abroad. The industry reached its peak shortly before the First World War.
33163.m: Around 1910 embroidery was Switzerland’s most important export sector.

33164.q: Which invention made St Gallen embroidery grow strongly in the 19th century?
33164.e: First came the hand embroidery machine, later the shuttle embroidery machine. They made it possible to produce embroidery much faster and more cheaply than by hand.
33164.m: Embroidery machines made St Gallen the world centre of embroidery.

33165.q: On which technical principle does the shuttle embroidery machine work?
a: Like a sewing machine with an upper and lower thread
Like a loom with warp and weft
Like a knitting machine with latch needles
Like hand embroidery with a double-pointed needle
33165.e: The needle carries the upper thread through the fabric, and on the back a shuttle loops it with the lower thread. This removes the time-consuming pulling through of long threads.
33165.m: The shuttle embroidery machine loops upper and lower thread like a sewing machine.

33166.q: Why did St Gallen embroidery collapse after 1914?
a: War and changing fashion made demand collapse
Switzerland banned the export of fabrics
All the embroidery machines were sold to Japan
33166.e: The First World War disrupted exports, and after the war plain clothing without much embroidery became fashionable. The Great Depression made the decline worse.
33166.m: War and fashion ended the heyday of St Gallen embroidery.

33167.q: Roughly what share of world embroidery production came from St Gallen and the surrounding area around 1910?
33167.e: Around 1910 eastern Switzerland was the leading embroidery centre in the world. About 50 per cent of world production came from the St Gallen region.
33167.m: Around 1910 about half of all the world’s embroidery came from eastern Switzerland.

33168.q: What kind of crisis hit the embroidery industry of eastern Switzerland in 1885?
a: A raw material crisis due to a lack of cotton
A banking crisis due to bad loans
33168.e: More was produced than the market could absorb. Orders fell sharply, wages dropped, and recovery only began around 1898.
33168.m: In 1885 embroidery fell into crisis because of overproduction.

33169.q: How was the embroidery pattern controlled on the automatic shuttle embroidery machine of 1898?
33169.e: In the older method, an embroiderer traced the pattern by hand with a pantograph. The automatic machine read the pattern from a punched card strip and so replaced this manual work.
33169.m: The automatic embroidery machine of 1898 was controlled by punched cards.

33170.q: Which measure taken by John Calvin promoted watchmaking in Geneva from 1541?
a: The ban on jewellery and luxury items
The founding of a state watch factory
A ban on importing French watches
33170.e: In the spirit of the Reformation, Calvin banned the wearing of jewellery. Many goldsmiths and jewellers therefore switched to making watches.
33170.m: Calvin’s ban on jewellery steered Geneva’s goldsmiths towards watchmaking.

33171.q: What was founded in Geneva in 1601 as the first institution of its kind in Switzerland?
33171.e: The Geneva watchmakers joined together in their own guild in 1601. It regulated training, quality and access to the trade.
33171.m: In 1601 the first watchmakers’ guild in Switzerland was founded in Geneva.

33172.q: In the Jura watch industry, what does “établissage” mean?
33172.e: Individual parts such as wheels, springs or cases were made in many small workshops, often in farmhouses. An entrepreneur, the établisseur, had the parts assembled into the finished watch and sold it.
33172.m: In établissage a watch was made by dividing the work among many workshops.

33173.q: According to a legend from the 1830s, who is regarded as the founder of watchmaking in the Neuchâtel Jura?
33173.e: Around 1700 the goldsmith from La Sagne set up one of the first real watchmaking workshops in the Neuchâtel Jura. Historians today consider his role as sole founder exaggerated.
33173.m: Daniel JeanRichard is regarded as the legendary founding father of Jura watchmaking.

33174.q: Why did watchmaking suit the farming families in the Jura particularly well in the 18th century?
a: It was a sideline for the long winters
It needed large amounts of water power
It used wood from the Jura forests
It was only possible on the Alpine pastures in summer
33174.e: The poor soils and long winters left a lot of time, and the farmers needed extra income. Watch parts needed little raw material but were of high value.
33174.m: In the Jura, watchmaking was an important winter income for farmers.

33175.q: Which two towns were added to the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2009 as a “watchmaking town planning” site?
33175.e: After fires, the two Neuchâtel Jura towns were rebuilt on a grid plan to suit the needs of watchmakers. The streets and houses are designed to get light to the workbenches.
33175.m: La Chaux-de-Fonds and Le Locle are UNESCO World Heritage watchmaking towns.

33176.q: What did Swiss watchmakers recognise as a threat at the 1876 World’s Fair in Philadelphia?
a: American mass production with interchangeable parts
English precision clocks for the navy
Cheap cuckoo clocks from the Black Forest
33176.e: American factories produced watches by machine in large numbers. Reports from the exhibition triggered modernisation in Switzerland and the move to factory production.
33176.m: American competition in 1876 forced the Swiss watch industry to mechanise.

33177.q: From which town did the religious refugees come who revived silk processing in Zurich in 1555?
33177.e: The Protestant families had to leave their home town because it remained Catholic. Families such as Orelli and Muralt brought capital and knowledge of the silk trade with them.
33177.m: Protestant refugees from Locarno boosted the Zurich silk industry from 1555.

33178.q: On which river did Heinrich Escher have Zurich’s first water-powered silk-twisting mill built around 1730?
33178.e: Heinrich Escher brought craftsmen from Bologna and launched Bolognese crêpe. To twist the silk threads, he used the water power of the Sihl.
33178.m: The first water-powered silk-twisting mill in Zurich stood on the Sihl.

33179.q: Which trade did Huguenots bring to Zurich after 1685?
33179.e: After the revocation of the Edict of Nantes, many French Protestants fled. In Zurich they introduced the making of knitted stockings.
33179.m: Huguenots introduced stocking knitting in Zurich.

33180.q: What role did Zurich play in the European raw silk trade in the 18th century?
a: Distribution centre for raw silk from Italy and Spain
Customs post for French silk ribbons
33180.e: Zurich merchants imported raw silk and had it made into yarn. The yarns went to Basel, France, Germany and England, among other places.
33180.m: In the 18th century Zurich was a hub for Italian and Spanish raw silk.

33181.q: Where did the Zurich silk industry increasingly obtain its raw silk after the silkworm disease around 1850?
33181.e: A disease of silkworms made production in France and Italy collapse from about 1850. Zurich traders turned to East Asia, and Japan and China became the most important suppliers.
33181.m: After the silkworm disease, Zurich’s raw silk came mainly from East Asia.

33182.q: Why was silk weaving mechanised much later than cotton spinning?
a: The fine silk thread broke easily in early machines
By law silk could only be processed by hand
Zurich lacked water power for silk
The silk weavers owned all the machine patents
33182.e: The delicate silk thread placed high demands on the technology. That is why hand weaving at home remained important until well into the 19th century.
33182.m: Because of its delicate thread, silk could only be woven by machine late on.

33183.q: What importance did the silk industry have for the canton of Zurich in the 19th century?
a: It was one of its most important industries
It was a small niche sector
It was banned and only smuggled
It only concerned the city of Zurich
33183.e: At first farming families wove at home; later many factories were built on Lake Zurich and in the surrounding area. Around 1900 Switzerland, mainly the Zurich area, produced about 47 million metres of silk fabric a year.
33183.m: In the 19th century silk was one of Zurich’s most important industries.

33184.q: In the putting-out system, who supplied home workers with raw materials and bought the finished goods from them?
33184.e: The putter-out was a merchant who advanced raw materials and marketed the products. The home workers therefore remained dependent on him and his prices.
33184.m: In the putting-out system the putter-out organised raw materials and sales.

33185.q: Which activity was the most important home work in the Zurich Oberland in the 18th century?
33185.e: In many farmhouse parlours, cotton was spun into yarn on the spinning wheel. This allowed women and children to earn extra money too.
33185.m: In the 18th century many families in the Zurich Oberland spun cotton by hand.

33186.q: What plunged hand spinning in the Zurich Oberland into a severe crisis around 1800?
a: The abolition of the putting-out system
33186.e: English spinning machines produced yarn much more cheaply and evenly. The hand spinners could no longer compete on price.
33186.m: English machine yarn pushed out hand spinning around 1800.

33187.q: Which activity did many home workers in the Zurich Oberland switch to after the decline of hand spinning?
33187.e: With the cheap machine yarn, families could weave fabrics at home. Only mechanical looms made this work unprofitable too.
33187.m: After hand spinning, hand weaving became the most important home work.

33188.q: Why were the first textile factories in the Zurich Oberland built along streams such as the Aabach?
33188.e: Switzerland had hardly any coal; water wheels and later turbines drove the machines. That is why numerous spinning mills lined the Aabach.
33188.m: The factories in the Zurich Oberland used the water power of the streams.

33189.q: What do historians call the phase of rural home industry before factory industrialisation?
33189.e: In this phase rural households produced on a large scale for markets beyond their region. It is regarded as an early stage of industrialisation proper.
33189.m: Rural home industry is known as proto-industrialisation.

33190.q: Which group of the population in the Zurich Oberland depended particularly on home work?
a: Small farmers and day labourers with little land
33190.e: Those who owned too little land could not live from farming alone. Textile home work gave these families a living and encouraged population growth.
33190.m: Above all, small farmers without enough land lived from home work.

33191.q: Which volcanic eruption is regarded as the main cause of the hunger year 1816?
33191.e: The volcano on the Indonesian island of Sumbawa erupted violently in April 1815. The ash in the atmosphere cooled the climate worldwide.
33191.m: The eruption of Tambora in 1815 caused the hunger year 1816.

33192.q: Under what name has the year 1816 gone down in climate history?
33192.e: Cold and constant rain ruined the harvests. In Switzerland it snowed down to 800 metres at least once in every month.
33192.m: 1816 is called the Year Without a Summer.

33193.q: What consequence did the hunger years 1816 and 1817 have for the population of Switzerland?
33193.e: Malnutrition weakened people, and diseases spread. The death rate rose by more than 20 per cent, and many emigrated.
33193.m: In the hunger years 1816 and 1817 markedly more people died.

33194.q: How did grain prices develop in the hunger years 1816 and 1817?
a: They rose to about three times their level
They rose by about 10 per cent
They stayed stable thanks to state reserves
33194.e: The failed harvest drove prices sharply upwards. In remote places the price even reached four times its level.
33194.m: In the hunger years grain prices multiplied.

33195.q: Why did the hunger years 1816 and 1817 hit the textile home workers of eastern Switzerland particularly hard?
a: They had to buy food while their earnings fell
They were not allowed to store supplies
They were called up for military service
They lost their land in floods
33195.e: Home workers produced hardly any food of their own and depended on the market. At the same time English competition pushed down sales and wages.
33195.m: Home workers suffered especially because they had to buy expensive bread with falling wages.

33196.q: Which volcanic eruption of 1815 is regarded as the cause of the “Year Without a Summer” in 1816?
a: The eruption of Tambora in Indonesia
The eruption of Vesuvius in Italy
The eruption of Krakatoa in Indonesia
The eruption of Hekla in Iceland
33196.e: Tambora hurled huge amounts of ash and sulphur into the atmosphere. Sunlight was weakened, and in 1816 Europe had cold, constant rain and failed harvests.
33196.m: The eruption of Tambora in 1815 led to the Year Without a Summer.

33197.q: Which population movement did the hunger crisis of 1816 and 1817 trigger in Switzerland?
a: A wave of emigration to America and Russia
A flight from the countryside into the Alpine valleys
A return of mercenaries from France
33197.e: Many impoverished families no longer saw a future at home. They looked for new land across the Atlantic or in eastern Europe.
33197.m: The hunger crisis of 1816 and 1817 led to a large wave of emigration.

33198.q: Against which machines was the Uster fire of 1832 directed?
33198.e: The factory in Oberuster had installed mechanical looms. The home weavers saw them as a danger to their earnings and set the factory on fire.
33198.m: The Uster fire was directed against mechanical looms.

33199.q: Which event of 1830 was being commemorated on the day the Uster fire took place?
33199.e: On the Ustertag in 1830, thousands had gathered and demanded a liberal constitution. The Regeneration in the canton of Zurich goes back to this assembly.
33199.m: The Uster fire took place on the anniversary of the Ustertag.

33200.q: Which era of Swiss history began around 1830 with events such as the Ustertag?
33200.e: In the Regeneration many cantons adopted liberal constitutions with popular sovereignty and equality before the law. It prepared the way for the federal state of 1848.
33200.m: From 1830 the Regeneration renewed many cantons along liberal lines.

33201.q: Who was behind the Uster fire?
33201.e: The so-called Tüchler and home workers feared for their livelihoods. They saw the weaving machines as the cause of falling wages.
33201.m: In 1832 home weavers set fire to the Uster factory out of fear for their livelihoods.

33202.q: What had the home workers demanded in the Uster Memorial before they turned to violence?
a: The introduction of the ten-hour day
33202.e: The new liberal Grand Council rejected this demand. Out of disappointment the home weavers turned to destruction.
33202.m: In the Uster Memorial the home weavers called for a ban on weaving machines.

33203.q: How were those mainly responsible for the Uster fire punished in 1833?
33203.e: A total of 75 people were arrested. The court imposed harsh prison sentences in chains on the leaders.
33203.m: Those mainly responsible for the Uster fire received long sentences in chains.

33204.q: What is the violent destruction of machines out of fear for jobs, as happened in Uster, called?
33204.e: In England, too, workers destroyed looms to protect their work. The Uster fire is the best-known Swiss example of this.
33204.m: The Uster fire is the best-known example of machine-breaking in Switzerland.

33205.q: In which decade of the 19th century did the most Swiss emigrate overseas?
33205.e: In this decade more than 90,000 people left Switzerland for overseas. The agricultural crisis and cheap ship passages encouraged emigration.
33205.m: Overseas emigration reached its peak in the 1880s.

33206.q: Which destination did almost 90 per cent of Swiss overseas emigrants choose towards the end of the 19th century?
33206.e: The USA attracted people with land and work. South America and other continents played a smaller role in terms of numbers.
33206.m: Most Swiss overseas emigrants went to North America.

33207.q: In which country did emigrants from the canton of Fribourg found the settlement of Nova Friburgo in 1819?
33207.e: After the hunger years many families looked for a new livelihood. The settlement in the highlands near Rio de Janeiro still bears the name of their homeland.
33207.m: Emigrants from Fribourg founded Nova Friburgo in Brazil in 1819.

33208.q: In which US state did emigrants from Glarus found the settlement of New Glarus in 1845?
33208.e: The Glarus government supported the emigration of poor families. New Glarus still keeps up Swiss traditions today.
33208.m: New Glarus is in the US state of Wisconsin.

33209.q: Why did some Swiss municipalities pay for poor citizens’ passage to America in the 19th century?
a: To save on future poor relief
To provide soldiers for the USA
33209.e: The home municipality had to look after its poor citizens. The passage was often tied to giving up citizenship.
33209.m: Municipalities often paid for emigration to get rid of the cost of poor relief.

33210.q: What did the federal law of 1880 regulate in connection with emigration?
a: A ban on emigration for men
The voting rights of Swiss abroad
33210.e: Agencies had often deceived and exploited emigrants. Based on the 1874 constitution, the Confederation placed them under its control.
33210.m: From 1880 the Confederation supervised emigration agencies.

33211.q: In which European country did most Swiss abroad live around 1900?
33211.e: Of about 170,000 Swiss in Europe, some 87,000 lived in the neighbouring country to the west. Many worked there in trade, hospitality and industry.
33211.m: Around 1900 most Swiss living elsewhere in Europe lived in France.

33212.q: In which year did Alfred Escher found the Schweizerische Kreditanstalt (Swiss Credit Institution)?
33212.e: The bank was founded in Zurich on the model of French investment banks. It grew into one of the largest banks in Switzerland.
33212.m: The Schweizerische Kreditanstalt was founded in 1856.

33213.q: What was Alfred Escher’s main purpose in founding the Schweizerische Kreditanstalt?
a: To raise capital for railway building
To create a national bank of issue
To finance the city’s poor relief
33213.e: Railway building swallowed enormous sums. Escher wanted to reduce dependence on foreign investors.
33213.m: Escher founded the Kreditanstalt mainly to finance the railways.

33214.q: What nickname did Alfred Escher get because of his enormous power in politics and business?
33214.e: Escher held numerous posts in parliament, government, railways and banks. Critics spoke of the “Escher system”.
33214.m: Alfred Escher was called “King Alfred” because of his great power.

33215.q: Which college in Zurich did Alfred Escher strongly campaign for?
a: The Zurich University of Teacher Education
33215.e: Escher fought for the federal technical college to come to Zurich. The Polytechnic opened in 1855; it also trained engineers for railway building.
33215.m: Alfred Escher campaigned for the Polytechnic in Zurich.

33216.q: Why did Alfred Escher resign as chairman of the board of the Gotthard Railway in 1878?
a: Because of criticism of the cost overruns
Because of his election to the Federal Council
Because of a dispute with Italy
Because of the bankruptcy of the Kreditanstalt
33216.e: The building costs rose far above the estimate, and extra financing was needed. The criticism was increasingly directed at Escher personally.
33216.m: In 1878 Escher had to resign because of the cost crisis in building the Gotthard line.

33217.q: How long was Alfred Escher a member of the National Council?
33217.e: Escher sat in the National Council from the founding of the federal state in 1848 until his death in 1882. He presided over the chamber several times.
33217.m: Alfred Escher was a National Councillor for 34 years.

33218.q: Which bank took over Credit Suisse, which had grown out of the Schweizerische Kreditanstalt, in 2023?
33218.e: Credit Suisse fell into a serious crisis of confidence in 2023. With the support of the Confederation it was taken over by the largest Swiss bank.
33218.m: The successor of Escher’s Kreditanstalt has belonged to UBS since 2023.

33219.q: Which Zurich politician and entrepreneur shaped the Swiss Northeastern Railway as its president?
33219.e: Alfred Escher drove the founding of the Northeastern Railway in 1853 and led it for a long time. He also founded the Kreditanstalt and promoted the Gotthard Railway.
33219.m: Alfred Escher shaped the Northeastern Railway.

33220.q: Which route did the Spanisch-Brötli-Bahn (Spanish Bun Railway), opened in 1847, run on?
33220.e: It was the first railway to run entirely on Swiss territory. It owes its name to a pastry from Baden that could now reach Zurich fresh.
33220.m: The Spanisch-Brötli-Bahn ran from Zurich to Baden in 1847.

33221.q: To whom did the Railway Act of 1852 leave the building of Swiss railways?
a: Private companies with a cantonal concession
33221.e: Supporters such as Alfred Escher won out against state construction. The result was a race between many private railways.
33221.m: From 1852 private companies built the railways in Switzerland.

33222.q: When did the Northeastern Railway pass into the ownership of the Swiss Federal Railways?
33222.e: In 1898 the people had voted in favour of buying back the large private railways. When it was taken over, the company’s network covered 853 kilometres.
33222.m: The Northeastern Railway was taken over by the SBB in 1902.

33223.q: Which direct link did the Bözberg Railway from Brugg to Pratteln, opened in 1875, create?
33223.e: The line was run jointly by the Northeastern Railway and the Central Railway. It saved the detour via other lines.
33223.m: Since 1875 the Bözberg Railway has linked Zurich directly with Basel.

33224.q: What happened to the Swiss National Railway, which wanted to compete with the Northeastern Railway?
a: It went bankrupt and was taken over cheaply
It became the largest railway in Switzerland
It merged with the Gotthard Railway
It was immediately nationalised by the Confederation
33224.e: The “people’s railway”, promoted from Winterthur, ran into financial difficulties. The Northeastern Railway bought the network in 1880 for a fraction of the building costs.
33224.m: The National Railway failed and passed to the Northeastern Railway in 1880.

33225.q: Which line was the first railway to reach Swiss soil, in 1844?
33225.e: The line from Alsace ended at a station in the city of Basel. However, it ran almost entirely on French territory.
33225.m: In 1844 the line from Strasbourg was the first railway to reach Switzerland.

33226.q: Which normal working day did the Federal Factory Act of 1877 lay down?
33226.e: The law was based on progressive cantonal rules. For many workers it meant a considerable reduction.
33226.m: The Factory Act of 1877 introduced the eleven-hour day.

33227.q: What did employers’ liability in the Factory Act of 1877 mean?
a: They had to answer for their workers’ accidents
They had to pay all workers a pension
They were not allowed to employ women
They had to pay taxes to the Confederation
33227.e: If a worker was injured in the factory, the employer was now liable. This rule was an important innovation throughout Switzerland.
33227.m: Since 1877 factory owners have been liable for their workers’ accidents.

33228.q: What was the result of the 1877 referendum on the Factory Act?
33228.e: The law was accepted with 51.5 per cent voting yes. It was striking that some industrial regions also voted no.
33228.m: The Factory Act was only narrowly accepted in 1877.

33229.q: Which precondition first made it possible for the Confederation to pass a factory act?
a: The total revision of the Federal Constitution in 1874
The founding of the federal state in 1848
33229.e: Before that, only the cantons could regulate factory work. The revised constitution gave the Confederation this power.
33229.m: Only the constitution of 1874 allowed a federal factory act.

33230.q: What was the task of the federal factory inspectors after 1877?
a: They checked whether firms complied with the Factory Act
33230.e: The inspectors visited factories and checked working hours, child labour and hygiene. One of the first was the Glarus doctor Fridolin Schuler.
33230.m: Factory inspectors monitored compliance with the Factory Act.

33231.q: What did the Factory Act of 1877 lay down for children?
a: Children under 14 were not allowed to work in factories
Children were only allowed to work at night
Children received the same wages as adults
There were no rules for children
33231.e: The law banned factory work for children under 14. This was meant to allow them to go to school and protect them from exploitation.
33231.m: Since 1877 factory work has been banned for children under 14.

33232.q: Which protection did the Factory Act of 1877 provide for women workers around childbirth?
a: A ban on working for 8 weeks without continued pay
A birth bonus from the Confederation
33232.e: The women were not allowed to work in the factory during this time. Since no wages were paid, this protection meant a loss of income for many families.
33232.m: The Factory Act of 1877 banned new mothers from factory work for eight weeks.

33233.q: Which canton limited the working hours of all factory workers to 12 hours by a Landsgemeinde decision in 1864?
33233.e: The law also applied to adult men and banned night work. It was one of the most progressive worker protection laws of its time.
33233.m: In 1864 Glarus led the way by limiting factory working hours to 12.

33234.q: In which region was one of the first mechanised chocolate factories in Switzerland founded in 1819?
33234.e: François-Louis Cailler founded the factory in Corsier near Vevey. The Lake Geneva region became a centre of chocolate making.
33234.m: One of the first Swiss chocolate factories was founded near Vevey in 1819.

33235.q: Who developed a milk chocolate that could be produced industrially in Vevey in 1875?
33235.e: He combined cocoa and sugar with condensed milk. The main problem was removing the water from the milk so that the chocolate would not spoil.
33235.m: Daniel Peter made milk chocolate suitable for industrial production in 1875.

33236.q: Which entrepreneur friend helped Daniel Peter with his milk powder in the experiments with milk chocolate?
33236.e: The founder of a baby food company in Vevey made milk products. His experience helped in combining milk and chocolate.
33236.m: Henri Nestlé supported Daniel Peter with his milk powder.

33237.q: Which Zurich confectioner family started making chocolate in 1845?
33237.e: The family ran a confectioner’s shop in Zurich and began making solid chocolate. Later a well-known chocolate company grew out of this.
33237.m: The Sprüngli family made chocolate in Zurich from 1845.

33238.q: Where did Philippe Suchard found his chocolate factory in 1826?
33238.e: Suchard used water power for his machines. The firm later became world-famous through a well-known milk chocolate brand.
33238.m: Philippe Suchard founded his factory in Serrières near Neuchâtel in 1826.

33239.q: Which advantage of Switzerland particularly favoured milk chocolate?
a: Plenty of milk from dairy farming
Its own cocoa plantations in Ticino
Cheap sugar from Swiss sugar cane
33239.e: In the 19th century Swiss agriculture specialised strongly in milk. Cocoa and sugar, on the other hand, had to be imported.
33239.m: Strong dairy farming was an advantage for Swiss milk chocolate.

33240.q: Into which business family did Daniel Peter marry in 1863?
33240.e: Peter married the eldest daughter of a chocolate manufacturer. That is how the trained candle-maker came to chocolate.
33240.m: Daniel Peter was the son-in-law of François-Louis Cailler.

33241.q: On which day was the Matterhorn first climbed?
33241.e: A roped party of seven climbers reached the summit. The date marks the end of the “Golden Age” of mountaineering.
33241.m: The Matterhorn was first climbed on 14 July 1865.

33242.q: Which Englishman led the first ascent of the Matterhorn?
33242.e: The illustrator and mountaineer had tried several times before without success. Just below the summit, he and his guide unroped and hurried up to be first.
33242.m: Edward Whymper was the first to stand on the Matterhorn, in 1865.

33243.q: How many of the seven members of the first ascent died on the way down?
33243.e: On the descent, Croz, Hadow, Hudson and Douglas fell down the north face. The rope to the other three broke.
33243.m: Four of the seven climbers died on the first ascent of the Matterhorn.

33244.q: Up which ridge did the roped party climb from Zermatt to the summit in 1865?
33244.e: The ridge is now the normal route from the Swiss side. It starts at the Hörnli Hut at 3,260 metres.
33244.m: The first climbers took the Hörnli Ridge.

33245.q: Who reached the summit from the Italian side three days after the first ascent?
33245.e: The mountain guide from Valtournenche climbed up the Lion Ridge. For years he had competed with Whymper to be first on the summit.
33245.m: Jean-Antoine Carrel climbed the Matterhorn from Italy in 1865.

33246.q: Where was the Swiss Alpine Club founded in 1863?
33246.e: The club was founded on the model of the English Alpine Club. It built huts and promoted the exploration of the Alps.
33246.m: The Swiss Alpine Club was founded in Olten in 1863.

33247.q: Which railway was opened in 1871 as the first mountain railway with rack-and-pinion drive in Europe?
33247.e: The line ran up the mountain from Vitznau. It made the view accessible to tourists without a hike.
33247.m: The Rigi Railway was Europe’s first rack railway, in 1871.

33248.q: Thanks to an 1864 bet by the hotelier Johannes Badrutt, which place is regarded as the birthplace of winter tourism?
33248.e: Badrutt invited English summer guests to come back in winter and promised them sunshine. The guests stayed until Easter.
33248.m: Winter tourism began in St. Moritz in 1864.

33249.q: Under what name did today’s ETH Zurich open in 1855?
33249.e: The college was usually called the Polytechnic or “Poly” for short. It was the Confederation’s first college.
33249.m: ETH began in 1855 as the Federal Polytechnic School.

33250.q: Which college became the second Federal Institute of Technology alongside Zurich in 1969?
33250.e: In 1969 the Confederation took over the technical college of the University of Lausanne. Since then there have been two federal institutes of technology: in Zurich and in Lausanne (EPFL).
33250.m: Since 1969 there has been EPF Lausanne alongside ETH Zurich.

33251.q: Which architect designed the ETH main building, completed in 1864?
33251.e: He won the architectural competition and taught at the Polytechnic himself. At first the building also housed the University of Zurich.
33251.m: Gottfried Semper designed the ETH main building.

33252.q: Which college served as the model for the Federal Polytechnic?
33252.e: The law of 7 February 1854 was based on the French engineering school. The aim was a practical technical education.
33252.m: ETH was founded on the model of the Paris École polytechnique.

33253.q: Why was the Confederation’s first college limited to technical subjects?
a: Catholic cantons opposed a full university
There were no professors for the humanities
The Federal Constitution banned all universities
Zurich did not want to teach theology
33253.e: The Catholic rural cantons feared that higher education would be dominated by Protestants and cities. As a compromise, only a technical school was created.
33253.m: Because a federal university failed, a technical college was founded in 1855.

33254.q: For a long time, what was the Zurich Polytechnic not allowed to do that universities could?
33254.e: For a long time the Polytechnic could only award diplomas. Only in 1908 did it receive the right to award doctorates, which strengthened research.
33254.m: ETH was only allowed to award doctorates from 1908.

33255.q: Which later Nobel Prize winner studied at the Polytechnic in Zurich from 1896 to 1900?
33255.e: He studied in the department for specialist teachers of mathematics and physics. From 1912 to 1914 he was also a professor there.
33255.m: Albert Einstein studied at the Zurich Polytechnic.

33256.q: With which products did the chemical industry in Basel begin in the 19th century?
33256.e: The Basel firms first made tar dyes from coal tar. Only later were medicines added.
33256.m: Basel’s chemical industry began with the production of dyes.

33257.q: From which raw material did the first Basel chemical firms make their dyes?
33257.e: Tar was produced when making lighting gas from coal. From 1859 Alexander Clavel used it in Basel to make the red dye fuchsine.
33257.m: The first Basel synthetic dyes were tar dyes from coal.

33258.q: Which local industry was an important customer for the first Basel dyes?
33258.e: Basel had been a centre for woven silk ribbons for centuries. Dye works constantly needed new, bright colours.
33258.m: Basel’s silk ribbon industry needed dyes from chemistry.

33259.q: Which legal circumstance made it easier for the Basel dye factories to rise in the 19th century?
a: The lack of patent protection for chemical processes
A ban on importing German dyes
33259.e: In Switzerland it was allowed to copy processes that were protected elsewhere. Chemical processes only became patentable in the early 20th century.
33259.m: The lack of patent protection helped the young Basel chemical industry.

33260.q: What advantages did the Rhine offer the Basel chemical firms?
a: Water for production and an outlet for waste water
33260.e: Chemical production needed large amounts of water. At that time waste water was often fed into the river untreated.
33260.m: The Rhine supplied water and took away the waste water of Basel’s chemical industry.

33261.q: Which Basel pharmaceutical group was formed in 1996 from the merger of Ciba-Geigy and Sandoz?
33261.e: The two firms, with roots in the Basel dye industry, merged in 1996 to form Novartis. Roche was never part of this merger; Syngenta was spun off from the agricultural division in 2000.
33261.m: Novartis was formed in 1996 from Ciba-Geigy and Sandoz.

33262.q: Why were the Basel dye firms able to move successfully into making medicines around 1900?
a: Their chemical knowledge of tar dyes could be used for medicines
The Rhine supplied them with medicinal plants
The Confederation required it of all chemical firms
33262.e: Many active ingredients can be made with processes similar to those for dyes. Sandoz began in 1895 with the fever remedy antipyrine, and other firms followed.
33262.m: The pharmaceutical industry grew out of Basel’s dye chemistry.

33263.q: What special double status did Neuchâtel have between 1815 and 1848?
a: A canton of the Confederacy and at the same time a Prussian principality
A French département and at the same time a Swiss canton
An associated territory and at the same time an Austrian fief
A free imperial city and at the same time a Savoyard province
33263.e: Since the Congress of Vienna, Neuchâtel had been a Swiss canton but still belonged to the King of Prussia as a principality. This double role was the root of the later conflict.
33263.m: Until 1848 Neuchâtel was both a Swiss canton and a Prussian principality.

33264.q: On which day did the Neuchâtel republicans proclaim the republic?
33264.e: The radical democratic Montagnards overthrew the royalist government and proclaimed the republic on 1 March 1848. However, the Prussian king kept up his claims.
33264.m: Neuchâtel became a republic on 1 March 1848.

33265.q: What happened in Neuchâtel on the night of 2 to 3 September 1856?
a: Federal troops dissolved the Grand Council
33265.e: Supporters of the Prussian king stormed the castle, the seat of government, in a coup. The plan had been drawn up by Count Frédéric de Pourtalès-Steiger; republicans quickly recaptured the castle.
33265.m: In September 1856 a royalist coup in Neuchâtel failed.

33266.q: Roughly how many royalists were taken prisoner after the failed coup of 1856?
33266.e: After the castle was recaptured, about 500 royalists were arrested. Their release became the core of the dispute with Prussia.
33266.m: About 500 captured royalists triggered the dispute with Prussia.

33267.q: Whom did the Federal Assembly elect as commander-in-chief on 27 December 1856 because of the danger of war with Prussia?
33267.e: After Prussia broke off diplomatic relations, parliament elected the experienced Dufour as general. Switzerland mobilised troops on the Rhine border.
33267.m: In the Neuchâtel affair Dufour was elected general once again.

33268.q: Which French ruler mediated between Switzerland and Prussia in the Neuchâtel affair?
33268.e: Napoleon III had spent part of his youth in Thurgau. His mediation led to the Paris Conference in 1857 and to a peaceful solution.
33268.m: Napoleon III helped to settle the Neuchâtel affair peacefully.

33269.q: What was the result of the treaty of 26 May 1857 for Neuchâtel?
a: The Prussian king gave up his rights to Neuchâtel
Neuchâtel was divided between Prussia and Switzerland
Prussia was allowed to keep a garrison in the castle
Neuchâtel became a neutral principality under French protection
33269.e: In the Treaty of Paris, Frederick William IV gave up his claims. He kept the title of Prince of Neuchâtel until his death in 1861, but Switzerland did not recognise it.
33269.m: Since 1857 Neuchâtel has been completely separated from Prussia.

33270.q: What right had Switzerland held in northern Savoy since the Congress of Vienna?
a: To occupy Chablais and Faucigny militarily in the event of war
To levy its own customs duties in Chablais and Faucigny
To administer the municipalities of Chablais and Faucigny
To appoint the bishops of Annecy and Geneva
33270.e: To protect its neutrality, Switzerland was allowed to occupy the neutralised provinces of Chablais and Faucigny in case of war. The area then belonged to the Kingdom of Sardinia-Piedmont.
33270.m: From 1815 northern Savoy was included in Swiss neutrality.

33271.q: In which treaty did Sardinia-Piedmont cede Savoy and Nice to France in 1860?
33271.e: On 24 March 1860 King Victor Emmanuel II ceded Savoy and Nice in the Treaty of Turin. This was the price for France’s help in the war against Austria.
33271.m: In the Treaty of Turin Savoy passed to France in 1860.

33272.q: Which area did Switzerland want to secure for itself in the Savoy affair of 1860?
a: Northern Savoy on the south shore of Lake Geneva
33272.e: Northern Savoy with Chablais and Faucigny had been included in Swiss neutrality since 1815. When Savoy passed to France in 1860, some politicians wanted to secure the area for Switzerland.
33272.m: The Savoy affair was about northern Savoy on Lake Geneva.

33273.q: On what grounds did the Federal Assembly refuse authority to march into Savoy in 1860?
a: Diplomatic means had not yet been exhausted
The army was still tied up by the Neuchâtel affair
The cantons had already rejected the invasion
Great Britain had threatened Switzerland with war
33273.e: Parliament followed the proposal of Alfred Escher and Jakob Dubs. They wanted to keep negotiating first rather than risk a war with France.
33273.m: In 1860 parliament chose diplomacy rather than force.

33274.q: What did about 150 irregular fighters from Geneva and Savoy do at the end of March 1860?
a: They seized a steamer and landed on the Savoy shore
They occupied the Federal Palace in Bern
They blew up the Rhône bridge at Geneva
They stormed the town hall of Annecy
33274.e: The irregulars wanted to secure northern Savoy for Switzerland on their own authority. Regular Swiss troops quickly brought them back.
33274.m: An irregular raid into Savoy failed miserably in 1860.

33275.q: Which formula did most men in northern Savoy choose in the referendum of April 1860?
33275.e: The people of northern Savoy were promised a free trade zone with Switzerland. They therefore voted clearly for joining France along with the zone.
33275.m: In 1860 the people of northern Savoy voted for France with a free zone.

33276.q: How did the Savoy affair of 1860 end for Switzerland?
a: All of Savoy went to France and Switzerland got nothing
Northern Savoy became a Swiss canton
33276.e: France took over Savoy and Nice completely. Switzerland received only a free trade zone, and its reputation suffered from the failure.
33276.m: In the Savoy affair of 1860 Switzerland came away empty-handed.

33277.q: Which court dealt with the dispute over the Savoy free zones until 1932?
a: The Permanent Court of International Justice in The Hague
The European Court of Justice in Luxembourg
The Swiss Federal Supreme Court in Lausanne
An arbitration court of the League of Nations in Geneva
33277.e: After France wanted to abolish the free zone in 1919, the dispute ended up before the Permanent Court of International Justice. The Savoy question thus remained open for over 70 years.
33277.m: The Savoy zones question was still before a world court in 1932.

33278.q: Which currency system did most of German-speaking Switzerland prefer before 1850?
33278.e: Eastern Switzerland traded heavily with southern Germany and therefore wanted the gulden. French-speaking Switzerland and Basel won out with the French model.
33278.m: In the choice of currency in 1850, the southern German gulden lost.

33279.q: Why was the Confederation able to introduce a single currency in 1850?
a: The Federal Constitution of 1848 gave it control of the coinage
The cantons had unanimously asked for it
France had demanded a currency union
The Federal Diet had already decided it in 1815
33279.e: Before 1848 the cantons minted their own coins, which led to chaos. With the federal state, the right to mint coins passed to the Confederation.
33279.m: Since 1848 coinage has been a matter for the Confederation.

33280.q: How was the franc divided under the Coinage Act of 1850?
33280.e: The new system was decimal: 1 franc equals 100 Rappen. This made calculating much easier compared with the old batzen and kreuzer systems.
33280.m: In 1850 the franc was divided decimally into 100 Rappen.

33281.q: Which figure is shown on the 1-franc and 2-franc coins?
33281.e: Helvetia with spear and shield has appeared almost unchanged on these coins since the 19th century. She personifies Switzerland.
33281.m: Helvetia stands on the one-franc and two-franc coins.

33282.q: Which currency union did Switzerland belong to from 1865 to 1927?
33282.e: In 1865 Switzerland formed the Latin Monetary Union with France, Belgium and Italy. The members’ silver and gold coins were valid in each other’s countries.
33282.m: Switzerland was a founding member of the Latin Monetary Union.

33283.q: Who issued banknotes in the young federal state until 1907?
33283.e: For a long time numerous banks issued their own notes, which was confusing. Only afterwards was a central bank of issue given the sole right to do so.
33283.m: Before the National Bank, many banks printed their own notes.

33284.q: Against which system of power was the Democratic Movement in the canton of Zurich directed?
33284.e: The criticism was aimed at the concentration of power in Alfred Escher and the industrialists and bankers linked to him. The movement wanted more direct say for the people instead.
33284.m: The Zurich Democrats fought against the Escher system.

33285.q: In which town did the Democratic Movement in the canton of Zurich begin in 1867?
33285.e: Winterthur was the centre of opposition to the liberal elite of the city of Zurich. The demand for a new cantonal constitution came from there.
33285.m: Winterthur was the centre of the Zurich Democrats.

33286.q: Which newspaper was an important mouthpiece of the Zurich Democrats?
33286.e: Der Landbote spread the democratic demands, as did the Bülacher Volksfreund, for example. The NZZ, on the other hand, was close to the liberal camp.
33286.m: Der Landbote spread the ideas of the Democrats.

33287.q: Which political innovation did the Zurich cantonal constitution of 1869 bring?
a: Proportional election of the cantonal parliament
33287.e: After 1869 all laws in the canton of Zurich had to be put to the people. In addition, the cantonal government was now elected directly by the people.
33287.m: In 1869 Zurich introduced the mandatory referendum on laws.

33288.q: Which group of the population mainly supported the Democratic Movement?
a: The rural and small-town middle classes
33288.e: Craftsmen, farmers, small manufacturers and workers formed its base. The leaders were often teachers, pastors, doctors and editors in the countryside.
33288.m: The Democratic Movement was a movement of the countryside.

33289.q: Which economic policy demand did the Democratic Movement make?
a: The introduction of internal customs duties
The abolition of freedom of trade
33289.e: Cantonal banks were to offer farmers and small businesses cheap loans. Other demands were progressive taxation, free schools and factory laws.
33289.m: The Democrats called for cantonal banks for farmers and small businesses.

33290.q: Besides Zurich and Thurgau, in which canton did the Democratic Movement succeed early on?
33290.e: In Basel-Landschaft the revision movement around Christoph Rolle won far-reaching popular rights in the 1860s. The Catholic-conservative cantons, on the other hand, remained untouched by it.
33290.m: Basel-Landschaft was a pioneer of direct democracy.

33291.q: How many signatures were needed in 1874 for an optional referendum at federal level?
33291.e: The Federal Constitution of 1874 set the number at 30,000 signatures of people entitled to vote. This allowed the people to vote on federal laws.
33291.m: From 1874, 30,000 signatures were enough for a referendum.

33292.q: Apart from voters, who could call for a referendum from 1874?
33292.e: The cantonal referendum gives eight cantons together the right to force a popular vote. However, it has very rarely happened.
33292.m: Eight cantons together can also call for a referendum.

33293.q: What did the optional referendum apply to under the Federal Constitution of 1874?
a: Federal laws and generally binding federal decrees
33293.e: Constitutional amendments had been subject to the mandatory referendum since 1848. From 1874 the people could also demand a vote on laws.
33293.m: The optional referendum allows federal laws to be challenged.

33294.q: What distinguishes the optional referendum from the mandatory referendum?
a: It only takes place if it is demanded with signatures
It also needs a majority of the cantons to pass
It applies only to constitutional amendments
It can only be triggered by the Federal Council
33294.e: In a mandatory referendum there is always a vote. An optional referendum needs a collection of signatures or a decision by cantons.
33294.m: An optional referendum has to be actively called for.

33295.q: In which year was the number of signatures for the optional referendum raised to 50,000?
33295.e: The increase was decided in 1977. At the same time the collection period was set at 100 days.
33295.m: Since 1977 a referendum has needed 50,000 signatures.

33297.q: Which controversial treaty gave the impulse to introduce the referendum on international treaties in 1921?
a: The Covenant of the League of Nations
33297.e: The Gotthard Treaty of 1909 with Germany and Italy caused great protest but could not be put to the people. That is why the referendum on international treaties was introduced in 1921.
33297.m: The Gotthard Treaty led to the referendum on international treaties.

33298.q: Which form of popular initiative was already possible at federal level from 1848?
a: The initiative for a total revision of the constitution
The initiative for a partial revision of the constitution
33298.e: The Federal Constitution of 1848 allowed 50,000 voters to demand a total revision. However, this form was hardly used.
33298.m: The people could already demand a total revision in 1848.

33299.q: How many signatures did the partial revision initiative require when it was introduced?
33299.e: The number was taken over from the total revision initiative. Later it was raised because the electorate had grown.
33299.m: When it was introduced, an initiative needed 50,000 signatures.

33300.q: Which popular initiative was the first to be accepted by the people and the cantons, in 1893?
a: Proportional election of the National Council
33300.e: The initiative to ban slaughtering without prior stunning was accepted on 20 August 1893. It was justified with animal welfare but was also aimed at the Jewish minority.
33300.m: The first accepted popular initiative was the ban on kosher slaughter.

33301.q: Which type of initiative still does not exist at federal level today?
a: The partial revision initiative as a worked-out draft
The initiative as a general proposal
33301.e: At federal level the people can only propose constitutional amendments, not laws. Several attempts to introduce a legislative initiative have failed.
33301.m: There is no legislative initiative at federal level.

33302.q: What is the hurdle for a federal popular initiative today (as of 2025)?
33302.e: Since 1977 an initiative has needed 100,000 valid signatures. The collection period is 18 months from publication in the Federal Gazette.
33302.m: Today an initiative needs 100,000 signatures in 18 months.

33303.q: Which dogma of the First Vatican Council of 1870 intensified the Kulturkampf in Switzerland?
a: The Assumption of Mary into heaven
33303.e: The dogma of infallibility declared the Pope’s doctrinal decisions free from error. Liberal Catholics and the state saw this as an attack on their independence.
33303.m: The infallibility dogma of 1870 provoked fierce resistance.

33304.q: Which church arose in Switzerland from the protest against the infallibility dogma?
33304.e: Catholics who rejected the dogma joined together to form a church of their own. Its church constitution was adopted at a national synod in Olten in 1876.
33304.m: The Christian Catholic Church arose during the Kulturkampf.

33306.q: Which clergyman was expelled in 1873 after Rome had appointed him Apostolic Vicar of Geneva?
33306.e: The Federal Council saw the appointment as an unlawful separation of Geneva from the Diocese of Lausanne without state approval. Mermillod had to leave the country and only became Bishop of Lausanne in 1883.
33306.m: Mermillod’s expulsion was a high point of the Kulturkampf.

33307.q: What did the Federal Council do on 12 December 1873 in the dispute with the Catholic Church?
a: It broke off relations with the Holy See
It banned all Catholic church services
It dissolved the Diocese of Chur
33307.e: The Federal Council expelled the papal nuncio. A nunciature was only set up in Switzerland again in 1920.
33307.m: At the end of 1873 Switzerland broke with the Vatican.

33308.q: Which measure did the Bern government take in the Catholic Jura in January 1874?
a: It expelled 97 priests loyal to Rome
It closed all the schools in the Jura
It took away the people of the Jura’s right to vote
33308.e: The priests had refused to recognise the state’s church laws. Under pressure from the Confederation, Bern had to reverse the expulsion in 1875.
33308.m: In the Jura the Kulturkampf hit the priests particularly hard.

33309.q: Which exceptional article from the Kulturkampf was the last to be abolished, only in 2001?
a: The ban on Catholic private schools
33309.e: The diocese article required the Confederation’s approval for new dioceses. The bans on Jesuits and monasteries had already been dropped in 1973.
33309.m: The diocese article was the last Kulturkampf article to go, in 2001.

33310.q: Which event in December 1891 is regarded as a sign of reconciliation after the Kulturkampf?
a: The election of Josef Zemp as the first Catholic Conservative to the Federal Council
The return of the papal nuncio to Bern
The lifting of the ban on Jesuits
The founding of the University of Fribourg by the Confederation
33310.e: With Josef Zemp from Lucerne, a representative of the Catholic losers of the Sonderbund War was elected to the national government for the first time. This drew the Catholic Conservatives into the federal state.
33310.m: With Josef Zemp, the Catholic Conservatives entered the Federal Council in 1891.

33311.q: Which Swiss general was the first president of the Geneva Committee?
33311.e: The highly respected Dufour gave the committee weight with his reputation. He led it until 1864.
33311.m: The committee’s first president was a Swiss general.

33312.q: Which Geneva lawyer led the ICRC from 1864 to 1910?
33312.e: Moynier shaped the organisation for almost half a century.
33312.m: Gustave Moynier led the ICRC for almost fifty years.

33313.q: Who can become a member of the ICRC’s highest body?
a: Representatives of all UN member states
One delegate from each party to a war
The presidents of the national Red Cross societies
33313.e: The ICRC is a private Swiss organisation based in Geneva. Its assembly consists only of Swiss people, which is meant to ensure its neutrality.
33313.m: The ICRC is led only by Swiss citizens.

33314.q: Which honour did Henry Dunant receive in 1901?
a: The first Nobel Prize in Medicine
33314.e: Dunant shared the first Nobel Peace Prize with the Frenchman Frédéric Passy. At that time he was living in poverty and almost forgotten.
33314.m: Dunant received the first Nobel Peace Prize in 1901.

33316.q: Legally speaking, what is the Geneva Convention of 1864?
a: The statutes of the Red Cross
A ruling of an international court
33316.e: Twelve states signed the agreement in 1864, binding themselves under international law. Many more states joined later.
33316.m: The Geneva Convention is a treaty under international law.

33317.q: Who officially convened the diplomatic conference of 1864?
33317.e: At the request of the Geneva Committee, the Federal Council invited the states to Geneva. Since then Switzerland has played a special role in international humanitarian law.
33317.m: In 1864 the Federal Council invited states to the Geneva conference.

33318.q: What was the core idea of the first Geneva Convention?
a: The wounded, field hospitals and medical staff are regarded as neutral
Prisoners of war must be released immediately
The use of poison gas is banned
33318.e: Anyone caring for the wounded may not be attacked, and the wounded of both sides are treated. The agreement had only ten articles.
33318.m: The Geneva Convention protects the wounded and those who help them.

33319.q: How is the protective emblem of a red cross on a white background usually explained?
a: As a reversal of the colours of the Swiss flag
As the coat of arms of the city of Geneva
As the sign of the Order of St John
As the flag of the Kingdom of Sardinia
33319.e: The emblem is regarded as a tribute to Switzerland, where the Convention was created. It is not a religious symbol but a neutral protective sign.
33319.m: The Red Cross reverses the colours of the Swiss flag.

33320.q: Which protective emblem did the Ottoman Empire use from 1876 instead of the red cross?
33320.e: During the Russo-Turkish War, the Ottoman Empire introduced the red crescent. Today it is recognised alongside the cross as a protective emblem.
33320.m: The red crescent arose as an alternative to the red cross.

33321.q: How many Geneva Conventions were adopted in 1949 after the Second World War?
33321.e: The four conventions protect the wounded on land, the shipwrecked, prisoners of war and civilians. They build on the Convention of 1864.
33321.m: Since 1949 there have been four Geneva Conventions.

33322.q: What was the official name of the French army that was interned in Switzerland in 1871?
a: Armée de l’Est (Army of the East)
Armée du Rhin (Army of the Rhine)
Armée du Nord (Army of the North)
Armée des Alpes (Army of the Alps)
33322.e: The Army of the East was named after its first commander, General Charles Denis Bourbaki. It had been surrounded near Pontarlier in the Franco-Prussian War.
33322.m: The Bourbaki army was the French Army of the East.

33323.q: Where can you see a huge panoramic painting of the Bourbaki army crossing into Switzerland today?
33323.e: The Bourbaki Panorama by Edouard Castres is over 100 metres long. It shows how about 87,000 French soldiers came into Switzerland at Les Verrières in 1871.
33323.m: The Bourbaki Panorama is in Lucerne.

33324.q: Roughly how many French soldiers crossed into Switzerland in February 1871?
33324.e: Between 1 and 3 February 1871, about 87,000 men and 12,000 horses crossed the border. For the young Swiss state this was an enormous task.
33324.m: In 1871 Switzerland took in about 87,000 French soldiers.

33325.q: Which canton took in no internees from the Bourbaki army?
33325.e: The soldiers were distributed among about 190 places in all the other cantons. Nobody wanted to make them cross the snowy Gotthard, since there was no tunnel yet.
33325.m: Only Ticino had no Bourbaki internees.

33326.q: How long did the internment of the Bourbaki army last?
33326.e: After the armistice the soldiers returned to France between 13 and 22 March 1871. Many had been cared for and given new clothes beforehand.
33326.m: The Bourbaki soldiers stayed in Switzerland for only a few weeks.

33327.q: Which organisation, still young at the time, helped care for the interned Bourbaki soldiers in 1871?
33327.e: The Red Cross had only been founded in Geneva in 1863. With the Bourbaki army it showed how important organised help for wounded and sick soldiers is.
33327.m: The young Red Cross helped care for the Bourbaki soldiers in 1871.

33328.q: In which city is the Bourbaki Panorama on display?
33328.e: The huge panoramic painting was made by the Genevan Édouard Castres, who had accompanied the army as a helper. It shows the border crossing at Les Verrières.
33328.m: The Bourbaki Panorama is in Lucerne.

33329.q: Which states argued their case before the Geneva arbitration tribunal of 1872?
33329.e: The USA demanded compensation for damage caused by Confederate warships that had been built in Great Britain. Both states agreed on an arbitration tribunal.
33329.m: In 1872 the USA and Great Britain argued their case in Geneva.

33330.q: What was the “Alabama”, after which the arbitration tribunal is named?
a: A commerce raider of the American Confederate states
An ironclad of the US Union states
A merchant ship of the Hudson’s Bay Company
33330.e: In the American Civil War the CSS Alabama captured more than sixty Union ships. It was sunk off Cherbourg in 1864.
33330.m: The Alabama was a Confederate raider.

33331.q: Why did the USA demand compensation from Great Britain because of the “Alabama”?
a: The ship had been built in Great Britain despite British neutrality
The crew consisted only of British soldiers
Great Britain had declared war on the USA
The Alabama had fired on American ports
33331.e: The Alabama was launched in 1862 at Birkenhead near Liverpool and then captured Union ships. Great Britain had thus broken its duty of neutrality.
33331.m: The Alabama was built in Great Britain despite its neutrality.

33332.q: What role did Switzerland play in the Alabama arbitration?
a: It provided the venue and one member of the tribunal
It brought a case against Great Britain itself
It paid the compensation to the USA
33332.e: The tribunal met in Geneva. The former Swiss Federal Councillor Jakob Stämpfli sat on it alongside representatives of the USA, Great Britain, Italy and Brazil.
33332.m: Switzerland hosted the Alabama arbitration and provided a judge.

33333.q: How did the Alabama arbitration end in 1872?
a: Great Britain had to pay compensation to the USA
The USA had to compensate Great Britain
Both states then declared war on each other
33333.e: In September 1872 the tribunal ruled in favour of the USA. In 1873 Great Britain paid 15.5 million dollars in gold.
33333.m: After the ruling, Great Britain had to pay compensation to the USA.

33334.q: Where exactly did the Alabama arbitration tribunal meet?
a: In the Federal Palace in Bern
In the Palais des Nations in Geneva
33334.e: The room in Geneva Town Hall has been called the “Salle de l’Alabama” ever since. The first Geneva Convention had also been signed there in 1864.
33334.m: The Alabama Room is in Geneva Town Hall.

33335.q: Why is the Alabama arbitration regarded as an important event in the history of international law?
a: Two great powers settled a serious dispute peacefully before an arbitration tribunal
It founded the first permanent world court
It abolished privateering on all the seas
It convicted a head of state personally for the first time
33335.e: Instead of going to war, the USA and Great Britain accepted a neutral ruling. This strengthened arbitration and Geneva’s reputation as a place of diplomacy.
33335.m: The Alabama ruling showed that arbitration can prevent wars.

33336.q: In which year was the Universal Postal Union founded in Bern?
33336.e: The treaty was signed in the Rathaus zum Äusseren Stand in Bern. It came into force on 1 July 1875.
