33336.m: The Universal Postal Union was founded in Bern in 1874.

33337.q: Who proposed the founding of the Universal Postal Union?
33337.e: The German Postmaster General Heinrich von Stephan suggested an international postal union. He is regarded as the intellectual father of the union.
33337.m: Heinrich von Stephan is the father of the Universal Postal Union.

33338.q: Under which name was the Universal Postal Union originally founded?
33338.e: Only at the second congress in Paris in 1878 did the union get the name Universal Postal Union. Many more states joined at that time.
33338.m: The Universal Postal Union was first called the General Postal Union.

33339.q: How many states founded the Universal Postal Union?
33339.e: 22 states signed the treaty in Bern, most of them from Europe, plus the USA and Egypt. 20 of them ratified it.
33339.m: 22 states founded the Universal Postal Union.

33340.q: Which basic principle did the Universal Postal Treaty create?
a: A single postal territory with equal charges for letters abroad
A common stamp for all member states
A common postal administration based in Paris
The abolition of all postage charges
33340.e: Before, letters abroad needed many bilateral treaties with different rates. Now uniform rules applied to the exchange of post between all members.
33340.m: The Universal Postal Union created a single postal territory.

33341.q: Since when has the Universal Postal Union been a specialised agency of the United Nations?
33341.e: The Universal Postal Union became a UN specialised agency in 1947. Its headquarters remained in Bern.
33341.m: The Universal Postal Union has been a UN specialised agency since 1947.

33342.q: How many member states does the Universal Postal Union have (as of 2025)?
33342.e: Since 2011 the Universal Postal Union has had 192 members. This makes it one of the largest international organisations.
33342.m: Almost every country in the world belongs to the Universal Postal Union.

33343.q: What kind of association was the Grütli Association when it was founded?
a: A patriotic educational association for craftsmen
33343.e: Journeymen craftsmen from German-speaking Switzerland founded the association in Geneva in 1838. It combined further education, social life and love of the fatherland.
33343.m: The Grütli Association was a patriotic educational association.

33344.q: What does the name “Grütli Association” recall?
a: The oath on the Rütli from the founding legend
33344.e: Grütli is an older form of Rütli. With the name, the association referred to the founding legend of the Confederacy.
33344.m: The Grütli Association named itself after the Rütli.

33345.q: What was the motto of the Grütli Association?
33345.e: Through further education, journeymen were to become independent masters and responsible citizens. Later the association also became politically active.
33345.m: The Grütli Association saw education as the path to freedom.

33346.q: Whom did the Grütli Association mainly appeal to?
33346.e: Its members were mainly travelling journeymen and later workers. The association combined education, social life and love of the fatherland.
33346.m: The Grütli Association was an association for journeymen and workers.

33347.q: What was the Grütli Association’s publication called from 1851?
33347.e: The newspaper appeared from 1851 and from 1906 to 1923 even daily. For a time it bore the subtitle “Social Democratic Daily”.
33347.m: Der Grütlianer was the newspaper of the Grütli Association.

33348.q: What happened in 1901 in the so-called “Solothurn wedding”?
a: The Grütli Association merged with the SP
The Grütli Association split into two parties
The Grütli Association merged with the Radicals
The Grütli Association founded the Trade Union Federation
33348.e: The Grütli Association and the Social Democratic Party united, but the association remained organisationally independent. The link did not last.
33348.m: In 1901 the Grütli Association and the SP joined together in Solothurn.

33349.q: Why did the Grütli Association leave the SP again in 1916?
a: It resisted complete integration into the SP and its left-wing course
It wanted to merge with the Catholic Conservative Party
It had been banned by the Federal Council
33349.e: The patriotic Grütli Association wanted to keep its independence and opposed the SP’s more radical course during the First World War. After that it lost many members and dissolved in 1925.
33349.m: The Grütli Association split from the SP during the First World War.

33351.q: Which SP politician led the national strike of 1918 as president of the Olten Action Committee?
33351.e: Robert Grimm was the leading figure of the national strike of November 1918. After the strike was called off he was sentenced to prison.
33351.m: Robert Grimm led the national strike of 1918.

33352.q: Whose interests did the SP mainly want to represent when it was founded in 1888?
33352.e: The SP grew out of the labour movement. It wanted to solve the social question, that is poverty and poor working conditions, through politics.
33352.m: The SP was founded as the party of the working class.

33353.q: Which position did the SP’s party programme of 1888 take?
a: It rejected revolution and relied on democratic reforms
It demanded that Switzerland leave Europe
It called for the guilds to be brought back
33353.e: The programme wanted to solve the social question using the tools of direct democracy. Only in 1904 did the party adopt a Marxist programme.
33353.m: The young SP relied on reform rather than revolution.

33354.q: In which year did the SP win its first seat on the Federal Council, with Ernst Nobs?
33354.e: In the middle of the Second World War, the Federal Assembly elected Ernst Nobs from Zurich to the Federal Council. This brought the SP into the national government for the first time.
33354.m: The SP has sat on the Federal Council since 1943, with a break from 1954 to 1959.

33355.q: Which electoral system prevented the SP from having greater success in the National Council before 1919?
33355.e: In the majority system the majority in a constituency wins all the seats, which puts minorities at a disadvantage. Only with proportional representation from 1919 did the SP group grow strongly.
33355.m: The majority system put the SP at a disadvantage until 1919.

33356.q: Which labour movement organisation was founded in 1880, before the SP?
33356.e: The Trade Union Federation united the trade unions at national level. It later worked closely with the SP.
33356.m: The Swiss Trade Union Federation is older than the SP.

33357.q: Which precious metal was the basis of the franc of 1850?
33357.e: Like its French model, the new franc was a silver franc with a fixed fineness. Gold only played a bigger role with the later monetary union.
33357.m: The franc of 1850 was based on silver.

33358.q: Which total revision initiative was submitted in 1934 and rejected in 1935?
a: The initiative of the Fronts and the Young Conservatives
The initiative to leave the League of Nations
33358.e: Since 1891 only one total revision initiative has been submitted, backed by the National Front, the Young Conservatives and other groups. The people rejected it on 8 September 1935 with about 72 per cent voting no.
33358.m: The only total revision initiative since 1891 failed in 1935.

33359.q: Which form of initiative was introduced in 2003 and abolished again in 2009 without ever being used?
33359.e: With the general popular initiative, the people could have proposed a change at constitutional or legislative level. The procedure was considered too complicated and was dropped again in 2009.
33359.m: The general popular initiative only existed from 2003 to 2009.

33360.q: From which Geneva association did the Committee of Five emerge in 1863?
a: The Geneva Society for Public Welfare
33360.e: The Society for Public Welfare set up a commission to examine Dunant’s proposals. This became the later International Committee.
33360.m: The ICRC grew out of a commission of the Geneva Society for Public Welfare.

33361.q: Why did Henry Dunant have to leave the Geneva Committee in 1867?
a: His business in Algeria had gone bankrupt
He was expelled from the country by the Federal Council
He wanted to found a rival organisation in Paris
He was unable to work because of illness
33361.e: Dunant’s business in Algeria failed, and he was involved in a bankruptcy. After that he was considered unacceptable in Geneva and lived in poverty for a long time.
33361.m: A bankruptcy forced Dunant to leave the committee in 1867.

33362.q: In which year was the Swiss Red Cross founded?
33362.e: On the model of the Geneva Committee, a national Red Cross society was founded in Bern in 1866. As early as 1871 it helped to care for interned soldiers.
33362.m: The Swiss Red Cross was founded in 1866.

33363.q: Which event in August 1914 particularly outraged French-speaking Switzerland and deepened the divide between the language regions?
a: The German invasion of neutral Belgium
The assassination of the Austrian heir to the throne
Italy entering the war on the side of the Entente
Great Britain’s naval blockade against Germany
33363.e: In 1914 Germany violated Belgium’s neutrality. Many French-speaking Swiss saw this as a warning sign for neutral Switzerland and felt confirmed in their sympathy for France.
33363.m: The attack on neutral Belgium in 1914 shocked French-speaking Switzerland above all.

33364.q: What was the speech called in which Carl Spitteler called for unity between the language regions in Zurich in December 1914?
a: A Word to the French Swiss
33364.e: Spitteler gave the speech on 14 December 1914 to the New Helvetic Society. He urged German-speaking Swiss to show restraint towards Germany and stressed that all Swiss belong together.
33364.m: In 1914 Carl Spitteler called for Swiss unity with “Our Swiss Standpoint”.

33365.q: Which body elected Ulrich Wille as general in August 1914, even though many French-speaking Swiss mistrusted him?
33365.e: In Switzerland the general is elected by the United Federal Assembly, that is the National Council and Council of States together. On 3 August 1914 the choice fell on Ulrich Wille, who had been proposed by the Federal Council.
33365.m: In 1914 the United Federal Assembly elected Ulrich Wille as general.

33366.q: What happened in the so-called flag affair in Lausanne in January 1916?
a: The flag of the German consulate was torn down
A Swiss flag was burned in front of the Federal Palace
German soldiers raised a flag on Swiss soil
The army banned all foreign flags in the canton
33366.e: On the German emperor’s birthday, the flag at the German consulate in Lausanne was torn down. The incident showed how great the tensions were between French-speaking Switzerland and the pro-German attitude in parts of German-speaking Switzerland.
33366.m: The Lausanne flag affair of 1916 showed French-speaking Switzerland’s anger at Germany.

33367.q: Why was General Ulrich Wille particularly mistrusted in French-speaking Switzerland during the First World War?
a: He was pro-German and married to a Bismarck
He had previously served in the French army
He came from Ticino and hardly spoke French
He had publicly supported a separate peace with Russia
33367.e: Wille admired the Prussian military system and was married to Clara von Bismarck. This fed suspicion in French-speaking Switzerland that the army leadership was too close to Germany.
33367.m: Because of his closeness to Germany, General Wille was viewed with suspicion in French-speaking Switzerland.

33368.q: Which association was founded in 1914 to strengthen unity between the language regions of Switzerland?
33368.e: The New Helvetic Society was founded in 1914 as a patriotic association across the language borders. Carl Spitteler gave his famous speech to its Zurich group.
33368.m: From 1914 the New Helvetic Society wanted to bring Switzerland’s language regions together.

33369.q: Which two officers were at the centre of the Colonels’ Affair of 1916?
a: Karl Egli and Moritz von Wattenwyl
33369.e: Colonels Karl Egli and Friedrich Moritz von Wattenwyl worked on the General Staff. They passed confidential information to the Central Powers.
33369.m: Colonels Egli and von Wattenwyl triggered the Colonels’ Affair in 1916.

33370.q: What did the two colonels pass on in the Colonels’ Affair?
a: The General Staff’s secret daily bulletins
The plans of the Gotthard fortress
The lists of Swiss spies in France
33370.e: They passed on the General Staff’s daily situation reports and decoded telegrams. In doing so they violated neutrality in favour of one side in the war.
33370.m: Through the colonels, secret daily bulletins of the General Staff reached the Central Powers.

33371.q: To whom did Colonels Egli and von Wattenwyl pass their information?
a: To the military attachés of Germany and Austria-Hungary
To the envoys of France and Great Britain
To the Russian embassy in Bern
33371.e: The information went to the military attachés of the Central Powers, Germany and Austria-Hungary. This particularly outraged pro-French French-speaking Switzerland.
33371.m: Through the Colonels’ Affair, the Central Powers received Swiss General Staff reports.

33372.q: How did the suspicion in the Colonels’ Affair come to light?
a: Through a confession by the two colonels
Through an article in a Berlin newspaper
Through a police search of a house
33372.e: A codebreaking expert from French-speaking Switzerland noticed that cracked telegrams contained content from Swiss General Staff reports. This put the General Staff under suspicion.
33372.m: Decoded telegrams set the Colonels’ Affair in motion.

33373.q: How did the trial before the divisional court in Zurich in February 1916 end for the two colonels?
a: They were acquitted of criminal charges
33373.e: The divisional court found the two officers not guilty under criminal law. The case went back to the military authorities for disciplinary judgement.
33373.m: In 1916 the military court acquitted the colonels of treason.

33374.q: Which punishment did General Wille impose on each of the two colonels after the verdict?
33374.e: Wille punished the two officers with twenty days’ detention each as a disciplinary measure. The Federal Council also removed them from their posts.
33374.m: In 1916 the colonels got away with twenty days’ detention each.

33375.q: Why did the Colonels’ Affair deepen the divide between German- and French-speaking Switzerland?
a: French-speaking Switzerland saw the mild verdict as proof of a pro-German army leadership
German-speaking Switzerland demanded the death penalty for the colonels
Both culprits came from French-speaking Switzerland
France threatened Switzerland with war because of it
33375.e: French-speaking newspapers sharply criticised the mild verdict, while in German-speaking Switzerland it tended to be played down. A crisis of confidence in the army and government arose.
33375.m: The mild verdict in the Colonels’ Affair fuelled mistrust of the army leadership in French-speaking Switzerland.

33376.q: Which international movement of opponents of the war had Robert Grimm founded in 1915 with a conference in the canton of Bern?
33376.e: In September 1915 Robert Grimm organised the Zimmerwald Conference, attended by socialist opponents of the war from various countries. The Zimmerwald movement grew out of it.
33376.m: In 1915 Robert Grimm organised the conference of opponents of the war in Zimmerwald.

33377.q: Which department did Federal Councillor Arthur Hoffmann head at the time of the Grimm-Hoffmann affair?
a: The Department of Justice and Police
33377.e: As head of the Political Department, Arthur Hoffmann was responsible for foreign policy. That is why his telegram to Grimm carried particular weight.
33377.m: In 1917, as head of the Political Department, Arthur Hoffmann was Switzerland’s foreign minister.

33378.q: What did Grimm and Hoffmann want to achieve with their action in 1917?
a: A separate peace between Germany and Russia
A ceasefire between France and Germany
33378.e: Hoffmann informed Grimm in Petrograd by telegram that Germany would not attack in the east as long as a separate peace was possible. Such a peace would mainly have benefited Germany.
33378.m: In 1917 Grimm and Hoffmann wanted to promote a separate peace between Germany and Russia.

33379.q: In which city was Robert Grimm staying in 1917 when the affair came to light?
33379.e: After the February Revolution of 1917, Grimm travelled to Petrograd, today’s St Petersburg. After the telegram was published he had to leave Russia.
33379.m: Robert Grimm was in Petrograd in 1917 and had to leave Russia after the affair.

33380.q: What consequence did the Grimm-Hoffmann affair have for Federal Councillor Arthur Hoffmann?
a: He became President of the Confederation
33380.e: After the telegram was published, the Allies accused Switzerland of violating its neutrality. Hoffmann resigned in June 1917.
33380.m: The affair cost Federal Councillor Hoffmann his office in 1917.

33381.q: Who was elected to the Federal Council in June 1917 as Arthur Hoffmann’s successor?
33381.e: The Federal Assembly elected the Geneva Liberal Gustave Ador. Electing a French-speaking Swiss and friend of the Entente was meant to reassure French-speaking Switzerland and the Allies.
33381.m: In 1917 Gustave Ador, a Genevan friend of the Entente, joined the Federal Council.

33382.q: Which organisation was Gustave Ador president of when he was elected to the Federal Council in 1917?
a: The International Committee of the Red Cross
33382.e: Gustave Ador was President of the ICRC from 1910 to 1928. His election to the Federal Council strengthened the image of a humanitarian, impartial Switzerland.
33382.m: Gustave Ador was President of the ICRC when he became a Federal Councillor in 1917.

33383.q: With what share of the vote did the people accept the proportional representation initiative on 13 October 1918?
33383.e: The initiative received about 300,000 yes votes against 149,000 no votes, that is about 66.8 per cent yes. The majority of cantons was also clearly reached.
33383.m: The proportional representation initiative was accepted in 1918 with about two thirds yes.

33384.q: Which attempt was the successful proportional representation initiative of 1918?
33384.e: Proportional representation initiatives had failed in 1900 and 1910. Only the third attempt in 1918 brought the breakthrough.
33384.m: Only at the third attempt did proportional representation for the National Council succeed in 1918.

33385.q: Why did the proportional representation initiative of 1910 fail even though it won a majority of the cantons?
a: It narrowly missed a majority of the people
The Federal Council declared it invalid
33385.e: In 1910 most cantons agreed, but overall there were about 265,000 no votes against 240,000 yes votes. A constitutional amendment needs a majority of both the people and the cantons.
33385.m: The proportional representation initiative of 1910 failed for lack of a popular majority.

33386.q: Which demand about the electoral system did the Olten Action Committee put first in the national strike of November 1918?
a: Immediate new election of the National Council by proportional representation
Abolition of the Council of States
Election of the Federal Council by the people
Votes for women only in the cantons
33386.e: In the ultimatum of 11 November 1918, the immediate new election of the National Council by the new proportional system was the most important of nine demands. The regular election would not have been due until 1920.
33386.m: In 1918 the national strike first demanded an immediate proportional election of the National Council.

33387.q: Roughly how did the number of Radical seats in the National Council fall with the first proportional election in 1919?
33387.e: The Radicals lost 43 seats and fell to about 60 seats. They thus lost the absolute majority they had held in the National Council since 1848.
33387.m: In 1919 the Radicals lost almost forty National Council seats.

33388.q: How are the seats in the National Council distributed in a proportional election?
a: According to the parties’ share of the vote
The strongest party in the canton gets all the seats
Each party gets the same number of seats
According to the number of party members
33388.e: With proportional representation, a party receives roughly as many seats as its share of the vote. Under the earlier majority system, the strongest party often won almost all the seats in a constituency.
33388.m: With proportional representation, the parties’ share of the vote counts.

33389.q: When did the Social Democratic Party, which had benefited greatly from proportional representation in 1919, get its first Federal Councillor?
33389.e: Although the SP already had about 41 seats in 1919, it remained without a seat in government for a long time. Only in 1943 was Ernst Nobs elected as the first Social Democrat on the Federal Council.
33389.m: In 1943 Ernst Nobs became the first Social Democratic Federal Councillor.

33390.q: By what popular majority did Switzerland vote to join the League of Nations on 16 May 1920?
33390.e: Joining was accepted with 56.3 per cent yes. Turnout was over 77 per cent.
33390.m: In 1920 Switzerland joined the League of Nations with about 56 per cent yes.

33391.q: How narrow was the majority of cantons in the League of Nations vote of 1920?
33391.e: Only half a canton more made the majority. If a single half-canton had voted differently, joining would have failed for lack of a majority of the cantons.
33391.m: In 1920 the cantonal majority for joining the League of Nations was extremely narrow, 11½ to 10½.

33392.q: Which canton voted most clearly for joining the League of Nations in 1920, with over 90 per cent yes?
33392.e: Vaud said yes with 93.2 per cent. The Latin cantons all agreed clearly, while Uri and Schwyz, for example, rejected it by more than three quarters.
33392.m: In 1920 Vaud voted over 93 per cent in favour of the League of Nations.

33393.q: In which 1920 document did the Council of the League of Nations recognise Switzerland’s neutrality as a special case?
33393.e: The London Declaration of February 1920 exempted Switzerland from military sanctions but obliged it to take part in economic sanctions. This is known as differential neutrality.
33393.m: The London Declaration of 1920 allowed Switzerland differential neutrality.

33394.q: In which building on Lake Geneva did the League of Nations have its first seat before the Palais des Nations was finished?
33394.e: In 1920 the League of Nations moved into the former Hotel National, which was named Palais Wilson in honour of Woodrow Wilson. Today it is used by the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights.
33394.m: The League of Nations began its work in Geneva in the Palais Wilson.

33395.q: How did Switzerland vote in 1934 on admitting the Soviet Union to the League of Nations?
a: It was not entitled to vote
33395.e: Federal Councillor Giuseppe Motta rejected the admission of the communist Soviet Union in a sharp speech. Switzerland was one of the few states that voted no.
33395.m: In 1934, under Motta, Switzerland rejected the Soviet Union’s admission to the League of Nations.

33396.q: Against which state did the League of Nations impose sanctions in 1935, which Switzerland only partly took part in?
33396.e: Italy had attacked Abyssinia. Switzerland only partly supported the economic sanctions, which prepared its later return to integral neutrality.
33396.m: In the Abyssinian War of 1935, Switzerland only partly joined the sanctions against Italy.

33397.q: Which event triggered the so-called Frontenfrühling (Spring of the Fronts) in Switzerland in 1933?
a: The Wall Street Crash in New York
33397.e: After Hitler took power in January 1933, far-right “Fronts” in Switzerland enjoyed a brief upswing. This phase is called the Frontenfrühling.
33397.m: Hitler’s seizure of power in 1933 triggered the Frontenfrühling in Switzerland.

33398.q: What was the most influential group of the Frontenfrühling called?
33398.e: The National Front was formed in 1933 from a merger with the New Front. It published the newspaper “Die Front”.
33398.m: The National Front was the most important Front group of the 1930s.

33399.q: In which city did the National Front celebrate one of its greatest successes in the municipal elections of 1933?
33399.e: In 1933 the National Front won ten of 125 seats in the Zurich city parliament. That was one of its biggest election successes.
33399.m: The National Front had its greatest success in Zurich in 1933.

33400.q: Why did the Fronts remain on the political fringe in Switzerland despite the Frontenfrühling?
a: The major parties and most of the population rejected them
The Federal Council banned them as early as 1933
33400.e: In 1935 the Fronts won only two National Council seats, including that of Robert Tobler in Zurich. The democratic parties clearly distanced themselves from them.
33400.m: Most Swiss people rejected the Fronts.

33401.q: How many seats did the Fronts win altogether in the National Council elections of 1935?
33401.e: Out of 187 seats, the Front movement won only two and came away empty-handed in four other cantons. Politically, the Fronts thus remained on the fringe.
33401.m: With two National Council seats in 1935, the Fronts remained a small minority.

33402.q: What was the aim of the Fonjallaz initiative, which the people rejected in 1937?
a: A ban on the Social Democratic Party
The reintroduction of the death penalty
A restriction of women’s voting rights in municipalities
33402.e: The initiative, backed by Arthur Fonjallaz and circles of the Fronts, wanted to ban Masonic lodges and similar associations. The people and the cantons clearly rejected it in November 1937.
33402.m: The Fronts’ initiative against the Freemasons clearly failed in 1937.

33403.q: Which umbrella movement of the Fronts did the Federal Council dissolve in November 1940?
33403.e: The National Movement of Switzerland (NBS) was formed in 1940 from a merger of Front groups and was controlled from Germany. The Federal Council dissolved it in November 1940.
33403.m: In 1940 the Federal Council banned the National Movement of Switzerland, a Front group.

33404.q: In which document did the Federal Council set out the programme of Spiritual National Defence in December 1938?
a: In the decree on emergency powers
33404.e: The Culture Message of 9 December 1938, under Federal Councillor Philipp Etter, described how Switzerland should cultivate and defend its cultural character. It also led to the founding of Pro Helvetia.
33404.m: The Culture Message of 1938 was the basic programme of Spiritual National Defence.

33405.q: Which army organisation informed the troops and the population in the spirit of Spiritual National Defence from 1939?
33405.e: The Army and Home section gave talks and spread information to strengthen the will to resist. It was part of the army staff.
33405.m: During the Second World War, Army and Home strengthened the will to resist of the troops and the people.

33406.q: Which medium started in 1940 as a tool of Spiritual National Defence and was shown in cinemas before the feature films?
33406.e: From 1940 the Swiss Film Weekly showed Swiss news in cinemas. It was meant to counterbalance the foreign newsreels.
33406.m: From 1940 the Swiss Film Weekly showed Swiss news in cinemas.

33407.q: What task did Swiss feature films such as “Gilberte de Courgenay” (1941) have during the Second World War?
a: They strengthened the sense of community in the spirit of Spiritual National Defence
They were used to train recruits
They only showed foreign war news
33407.e: The film tells of an innkeeper’s daughter who looks after the soldiers in the Jura during the First World War. Such films were meant to promote unity and the will to resist.
33407.m: During the war, Swiss films strengthened unity in the country.

33408.q: Which association for the cultivation of Swiss German dialect was founded in 1938 as part of Spiritual National Defence?
33408.e: Dialect was meant to set German-speaking Switzerland apart linguistically from National Socialist Germany. The Bund Schwyzertütsch therefore promoted the use of dialect.
33408.m: From 1938 the Bund Schwyzertütsch promoted dialect as a sign of independence.

33409.q: Which values did Spiritual National Defence present as typically Swiss?
a: Centralism, one national language and the leader principle
Industry, export strength and free trade
Monarchy, nobility and a state church
33409.e: Switzerland was presented as a nation of will that democratically unites different languages and cultures. This set it apart from the ethnic nationalism of the dictatorships.
33409.m: Spiritual National Defence stressed Switzerland as a democratic, multilingual nation of will.

33410.q: What do historians criticise about Spiritual National Defence today?
a: It promoted a conservative, inward-looking self-image
It was completely rejected by the Social Democrats
33410.e: As well as protecting against the dictatorships, it promoted a backward-looking, rural Alpine image of Switzerland. This defensive attitude lasted into the Cold War.
33410.m: Spiritual National Defence also left behind a conservative and inward-looking self-image.

33411.q: Who designed the famous Landi chair made of aluminium?
33411.e: Hans Coray designed the chair of hardened aluminium for the National Exhibition of 1939. Today it is regarded as a design classic.
33411.m: For the Landi of 1939, Hans Coray created the aluminium chair that is still well known today.

33412.q: What record did the cable car over Lake Zurich set at the Landi of 1939?
a: At 900 m it had the longest span in the world
It was the first electric railway in Switzerland
It was faster than any train
It had the tallest wooden towers in Europe
33412.e: The cable car linked the Landiwiese with the Zürichhorn over a span of 900 metres. Its two towers were 75 metres high.
33412.m: In 1939 the Landi cable car spanned Lake Zurich with 900 metres, the longest in the world.

33413.q: Which political idea particularly shaped the 1939 National Exhibition in Zurich?
33413.e: In the face of the threat from National Socialism and Fascism, the Landi was meant to show the unity and character of Switzerland. This attitude is called Spiritual National Defence.
33413.m: The Landi of 1939 was shaped by Spiritual National Defence.

33414.q: Where was the site of the 1939 Landi in Zurich?
a: On both shores of Lake Zurich
33414.e: The exhibition occupied the Landiwiese in Wollishofen on the left shore and the Zürichhorn on the right shore. A cable car and boats linked the two parts.
33414.m: The Landi of 1939 lay on both sides of Lake Zurich.

33415.q: Which President of the Confederation gave the opening speech of the Landi in May 1939?
33415.e: Philipp Etter was President of the Confederation in 1939 and at the same time the most important promoter of Spiritual National Defence. About 49,500 people came to the opening ceremony.
33415.m: President of the Confederation Philipp Etter opened the National Exhibition in Zurich in 1939.

33416.q: How did the Landi of 1939 end financially?
a: With a net profit of about 6 million francs
With a deficit of about 6 million francs
With a loss covered by the city of Zurich
33416.e: Ticket sales clearly exceeded the budget of 5.5 million. With the net profit of 6.4 million francs, the subsidies could be repaid.
33416.m: The Landi of 1939 ended with a profit of over six million francs.

33417.q: Roughly how many admissions did the 1939 National Exhibition record?
33417.e: The Landi recorded over 10 million admissions, at a time when Switzerland had just over 4 million inhabitants. Many people visited it several times.
33417.m: The Landi of 1939 recorded over 10 million admissions.

33418.q: In which sector was the 1937 Peace Agreement between employers and union concluded?
a: In the engineering and metal industry
33418.e: The agreement was concluded in July 1937 for the engineering and metal industry. It is regarded as the cornerstone of industrial peace in Switzerland.
33418.m: The Peace Agreement of 1937 applied to the engineering and metal industry.

33419.q: Which trade union leader took the initiative for the Peace Agreement of 1937?
33419.e: Konrad Ilg, president of the Swiss Metal and Watch Workers’ Union, pushed the agreement through even against resistance within his own union.
33419.m: Konrad Ilg was the trade unionist behind the Peace Agreement of 1937.

33420.q: Who concluded the Peace Agreement of 1937 with each other?
a: The employers’ association and the union of the metal sector
The Federal Council and the Trade Union Federation
The employers and the Federal Council
33420.e: The agreement was a contract between the social partners, without the state. Ernst Dübi signed for the employers and Konrad Ilg for the union.
33420.m: Employers and union concluded the Peace Agreement directly with each other.

33421.q: What did the parties commit themselves to in the Peace Agreement of 1937?
a: An absolute obligation to keep the peace
An annual pay rise of 10 per cent
A ban on all trade unions
33421.e: Both sides gave up industrial action such as strikes and lockouts. Conflicts were to be resolved through negotiation in good faith.
33421.m: In the Peace Agreement, employers and unions gave up strikes and lockouts.

33422.q: How were disputes to be resolved under the Peace Agreement of 1937 if negotiations failed?
a: By the Federal Supreme Court in Lausanne
By a decision of the army
33422.e: The agreement provided a procedure in several stages, up to an arbitration court. In this way conflicts could be settled without industrial action.
33422.m: The Peace Agreement resolved conflicts with a multi-stage arbitration procedure.

33423.q: Which term describes the cooperation between employers and unions that began with the Peace Agreement?
33423.e: The Peace Agreement replaced industrial action with negotiation. This social partnership still shapes the Swiss world of work today and explains why strikes are rare.
33423.m: The Peace Agreement of 1937 laid the foundation of Swiss social partnership.

33424.q: What did the Peace Agreement of the metal and engineering industry become in 1974?
a: An article of the Federal Constitution
33424.e: The originally short agreement was renewed several times and in 1974 was expanded into a comprehensive collective labour agreement.
33424.m: In 1974 the Peace Agreement became a full collective labour agreement.

33425.q: Which political office did Friedrich Traugott Wahlen later take on?
a: He became General of the Army
He became President of the ICRC
He became Secretary-General of the UN
33425.e: Wahlen was elected to the Federal Council in 1958 and was President of the Confederation in 1961. Before that he also worked for the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO).
33425.m: The planner of the Cultivation Battle later became a Federal Councillor.

33426.q: What was the aim of the Wahlen Plan?
a: Switzerland was to feed itself as far as possible
Switzerland was to export more cheese
Farmers were to do military service
The towns were to buy food from Germany
33426.e: In the war, imports were uncertain. With more arable farming, Switzerland was to produce as much food as possible itself.
33426.m: The Wahlen Plan was meant to increase Switzerland’s self-sufficiency.

33427.q: Did Switzerland achieve full self-sufficiency through the Cultivation Battle?
a: No, but the degree of self-sufficiency rose markedly
Yes, from 1941 no more rationing was needed
33427.e: The arable area almost doubled, from 183,000 to 352,000 hectares. But Switzerland never became fully independent of imports, and rationing remained.
33427.m: The Cultivation Battle increased self-sufficiency but did not fully achieve it.

33428.q: Besides the Cultivation Battle, which measure ensured that scarce food was distributed fairly during the war?
a: A ban on all meat products
33428.e: From 1939 there were ration cards. Each person could only buy a certain amount of sugar, bread, fat or meat.
33428.m: During the Second World War, food in Switzerland was rationed.

33429.q: How was extra arable land obtained during the Cultivation Battle?
a: By clearing land and land improvement
By cutting down all fruit trees
33429.e: Forests were cleared, marshes drained, and fallow land and parks ploughed up. Industrial firms also had to cultivate land.
33429.m: Land clearance and improvement created new arable land in the Cultivation Battle.

33430.q: Which film, based on a story by Meinrad Inglin, shows a farmer resisting the rules of the war economy?
a: Die Käserei in der Vehfreude (The Cheese Dairy in Vehfreude)
33430.e: “Der schwarze Tanner” tells of a mountain farmer who defies the obligation to grow crops. It shows that not everyone was happy to follow the state’s rules.
33430.m: “Der schwarze Tanner” shows a farmer’s resistance to the obligation to grow crops.

33431.q: Besides farmers, who also had to cultivate land during the Cultivation Battle?
33431.e: Larger firms had to farm their own plots, and municipalities used parks and sports grounds. Many families also grew vegetables in their gardens.
33431.m: In the Cultivation Battle, firms and municipalities also had to cultivate land.

33432.q: In which year did Switzerland and Germany agree to mark the passports of German Jews with a “J”?
33432.e: The agreement was made in September 1938, shortly after the wave of refugees from Austria. From October 1938 passports were stamped accordingly.
33432.m: The J stamp was agreed between Germany and Switzerland in 1938.

33433.q: Which senior Swiss official played a major part in introducing the J stamp?
33433.e: Heinrich Rothmund headed the police division of the Department of Justice and Police and thus the aliens police. He wanted to limit the entry of Jewish refugees.
33433.m: As head of the aliens police, Heinrich Rothmund shaped the harsh refugee policy.

33434.q: Which event in March 1938 triggered a wave of Jews fleeing to Switzerland?
a: The start of the Second World War
33434.e: After Austria was annexed to the German Reich, many Austrian Jews fled. Switzerland then introduced a visa requirement for holders of Austrian passports.
33434.m: The Anschluss of Austria in 1938 drove many Jews to flee to Switzerland.

33435.q: What did Switzerland threaten Germany with in 1938 before the J stamp was agreed?
a: A visa requirement for all German citizens
33435.e: A general visa requirement would also have affected non-Jewish Germans, which Germany wanted to avoid. With the J stamp, Switzerland could identify Jewish travellers specifically.
33435.m: The threat of a visa requirement for all Germans led to the J stamp in 1938.

33436.q: From autumn 1938, what did holders of a German passport with a J stamp need to enter Switzerland?
a: A guarantee from their canton of residence
33436.e: The J stamp allowed border officials to recognise Jewish travellers immediately. A visa requirement applied to them, while other Germans could still enter without a visa.
33436.m: From 1938 anyone with a J in their passport could only enter Switzerland with a visa.

33437.q: Under the Washington Agreement, what did Switzerland have to do with assets in Switzerland belonging to Germans living in Germany?
a: Give them to the National Bank
33437.e: The German assets, frozen since February 1945, were to be registered and sold. Half the proceeds were meant for Switzerland and half for the reconstruction of Europe.
33437.m: The Washington Agreement required the liquidation of German assets in Switzerland.

33438.q: How did the Federal Council react when Switzerland’s share of responsibility for the J stamp became public in 1954?
a: It commissioned an investigation into refugee policy
It had all the files destroyed
33438.e: In 1954 the magazine Beobachter published documents on the origins of the J stamp. This led to the report by Carl Ludwig, which appeared in 1957.
33438.m: The revelation of 1954 led to the first official investigation.

33439.q: How many refugees turned back at the border during the Second World War did the Bergier Commission document?
33439.e: The commission found evidence of over 20,000 refusals, including many Jews. The real number was probably higher.
33439.m: During the Second World War Switzerland turned back over 20,000 refugees at the border.

33440.q: With which trick did Paul Grüninger help Jewish refugees, even though the border was closed in 1938?
a: He backdated their dates of entry
He hid them in military camps
He smuggled them to Italy by boat
33440.e: Grüninger entered dates of entry before the border closure of August 1938. In this way the refugees counted as having entered legally and could stay.
33440.m: Paul Grüninger saved refugees with backdated entry dates.

33441.q: Near which place in the St Gallen Rhine Valley did many of the refugees Grüninger helped cross the border in 1938?
33441.e: Many Jews from Austria crossed the Old Rhine near Diepoldsau. A refugee camp was also set up there.
33441.m: Many Jewish refugees came into Switzerland near Diepoldsau in 1938.

33442.q: What was Paul Grüninger convicted of in 1940?
a: Breach of official duty and forging documents
33442.e: The St Gallen district court sentenced him to a fine. He lost his job and his pension rights and afterwards lived in poverty.
33442.m: In 1940 Grüninger was convicted of breach of official duty and forging documents.

33443.q: Who politically rehabilitated Paul Grüninger in 1993?
33443.e: The government of the canton of St Gallen rehabilitated Grüninger in 1993. Legal rehabilitation followed later.
33443.m: The St Gallen government politically rehabilitated Paul Grüninger in 1993.

33444.q: Which office did Paul Grüninger hold in 1938 when he helped refugees?
a: Police commander of the canton of St Gallen
33444.e: As commander of the cantonal police, Grüninger was responsible for border control in the Rhine Valley. He used his office to let hundreds of refugees into the country.
33444.m: Paul Grüninger was police commander in St Gallen.

33445.q: What is the 2014 feature film about Paul Grüninger called?
a: Das Boot ist voll (The Boat Is Full)
33445.e: “Akte Grüninger” by Alain Gsponer tells the events of 1938 and 1939. The film made the story known to a wide audience.
33445.m: The film “Akte Grüninger” tells of the rescue operation of the St Gallen police commander.

33446.q: With which football club did Paul Grüninger become Swiss champion as a young man?
33446.e: As a young man Grüninger played for SC Brühl, which became Swiss champion in 1915. The club’s stadium today bears his name.
33446.m: Paul Grüninger became Swiss champion with SC Brühl in 1915.

33447.q: Why was Carl Lutz able to place Jews under Swiss protection in Budapest?
a: Switzerland represented foreign states in Hungary as protecting power
The ICRC had appointed him consul
33447.e: Lutz headed the department for foreign interests because Switzerland represented the USA and Great Britain, among others, in Hungary. He used this position for his rescue operation.
33447.m: Carl Lutz used Switzerland’s role as protecting power to save Jews.

33448.q: When did Carl Lutz’s large rescue operations in Budapest take place?
a: In 1944, after the German occupation of Hungary
In 1939, at the outbreak of war
In 1946, after the end of the war
33448.e: Lutz had been in Budapest since 1942. When Germany occupied Hungary in March 1944, the deportations began, and Lutz then placed tens of thousands under Swiss protection.
33448.m: In 1944 Carl Lutz saved tens of thousands of Jews in Budapest.

33449.q: How did Carl Lutz stretch the permission to allow 8,000 Jews to emigrate to Palestine?
a: He interpreted the 8,000 as families instead of individuals
He forged the Federal Council’s signature
33449.e: Lutz interpreted the number 8,000 as families and numbered protective letters several times over. In this way he could protect many more people than intended.
33449.m: Carl Lutz multiplied the number of people protected by counting 8,000 families instead of people.

33450.q: Which honour did Yad Vashem award Carl Lutz in 1964?
33450.e: Carl Lutz was the first Swiss person to be honoured as Righteous Among the Nations. This award is given to non-Jews who saved Jews at the risk of their own lives.
33450.m: In 1964 Carl Lutz became the first Swiss person to be named Righteous Among the Nations.

33451.q: Who actively helped Carl Lutz to save persecuted Jews in Budapest?
33451.e: Gertrud Lutz-Fankhauser looked after protected houses and persecuted people. Later she worked for UNICEF.
33451.m: Gertrud Lutz-Fankhauser was an important helper of her husband in Budapest.

33452.q: In which country did Carl Lutz live and work from 1913 to 1934?
33452.e: Lutz emigrated to the USA as a young man, studied there and later worked at the Swiss legation in Washington. After that his career as a consular official abroad began.
33452.m: Carl Lutz spent over twenty years in the USA.

33453.q: With which documents did Carl Lutz place persecuted people under Swiss protection?
33453.e: The protective letters confirmed that their holder was under the protection of the Swiss legation. Lutz issued many more of them than was allowed.
33453.m: Carl Lutz saved people with Swiss protective letters.

33454.q: How much did Switzerland pay the Allies under the Washington Agreement of 1946?
33454.e: Switzerland contributed 250 million francs to the reconstruction of Europe without recognising any legal obligation. In return, the Allies gave up further claims relating to the gold purchases.
33454.m: Under the Washington Agreement of 1946, Switzerland paid 250 million francs.

33455.q: With which states did Switzerland conclude the Washington Agreement in 1946?
a: The USA, Great Britain and France
The USA, the Soviet Union and China
33455.e: The three Western Allies negotiated with Switzerland in Washington over German assets and looted gold. The agreement was signed on 25 May 1946.
33455.m: Switzerland concluded the Washington Agreement with the Western Allies in 1946.

33456.q: Why was the German Reichsbank so interested in Swiss francs during the Second World War?
a: The franc was freely convertible and accepted worldwide
The franc was backed by silver
Germany had to pay war debts to Switzerland
Swiss weapons could only be bought with francs
33456.e: With francs, Germany could buy important raw materials in neutral countries such as Portugal or Spain. That is why gold was exchanged for foreign currency in Switzerland.
33456.m: The freely convertible franc made Switzerland the hub for German gold.

33457.q: What happened to the Belgian gold that the Reichsbank had seized?
a: It was melted down and backdated to pre-war years
It was returned to Belgium during the war
It was sunk in the Rhine
It was minted into coins for the Wehrmacht
33457.e: The Reichsbank melted down the gold of the Belgian central bank and stamped it with false years such as 1938. This was meant to hide where it came from.
33457.m: The Reichsbank disguised looted Belgian gold by melting it down and backdating it.

33458.q: In connection with the Second World War, what is meant by looted gold?
a: Gold that the Nazi regime stole from occupied states and persecuted people
Gold that smugglers brought across the Alps
Gold that Switzerland hid during the war
33458.e: Nazi Germany stole gold from the central banks of occupied countries and from persecuted people, including victims of the concentration camps. The Reichsbank sold a large part of it to Switzerland.
33458.m: Looted gold came from plunder by the Nazi regime.

33459.q: What argument did the Swiss National Bank put forward after the war to justify its gold purchases?
a: It had acquired the gold in good faith
It had only bought gold from Belgium
It had not needed permission from the Federal Council
It had returned the gold immediately
33459.e: The National Bank pointed to acquisition in good faith and to neutrality. The Bergier Commission stated that those responsible could have known early on where the looted gold came from.
33459.m: The National Bank justified its gold purchases by claiming good faith.

33460.q: According to the Bergier Commission, what share of the Reichsbank's gold deliveries abroad went through Switzerland?
a: Almost all of it, namely 99 per cent
33460.e: According to the commission, around 77 per cent of the Reichsbank's gold transactions with other countries were handled through Switzerland. The National Bank played the main role.
33460.m: Around three quarters of German gold exports went through Switzerland.

33461.q: Which fund was created in 1997, partly with money from the National Bank, for needy Holocaust survivors?
a: The Special Fund for Needy Victims of the Holocaust/Shoah
33461.e: The Special Fund was set up in 1997, when Switzerland's role in the Second World War was being strongly criticised internationally. Banks, businesses and the National Bank paid into it.
33461.m: The Special Fund of 1997 supported needy survivors of the Holocaust.

33462.q: In which year was the party make-up of the Federal Council known as the “magic formula” introduced?
33462.e: In the Federal Council elections of December 1959, the SP received two seats, which created the 2:2:2:1 distribution. It lasted until 2003.
33462.m: The magic formula came about in the Federal Council elections of 1959.

33463.q: Which distribution of seats (FDP, CVP, SP, SVP or BGB) does the magic formula describe?
33463.e: The FDP, the Catholic Conservatives (later the CVP) and the SP each had two federal councillors, the BGB (later the SVP) had one. In this way the four largest parties were represented according to their strength.
33463.m: The magic formula shared out the seven seats in the ratio two, two, two and one.

33464.q: Which two Social Democrats were elected to the Federal Council in 1959?
33464.e: With Tschudi from Basel-Stadt and Spühler from Zurich, the SP entered the national government with two members in 1959. As interior minister, Tschudi later shaped the expansion of the AHV.
33464.m: Tschudi and Spühler were the first SP federal councillors of the magic formula.

33465.q: Which political principle does the magic formula embody in the Swiss system of government?
33465.e: Concordance means that the main parties form the government together, instead of a majority governing against an opposition. The magic formula put this principle into numbers.
33465.m: The magic formula stands for concordance, in which all the large parties share in government.

33466.q: Which event ended the classic magic formula in 2003?
a: The election of Christoph Blocher in place of Ruth Metzler
The SP leaving the Federal Council
The election of the first Green to the Federal Council
The BDP splitting off from the SVP
33466.e: In December 2003, the Federal Assembly elected Christoph Blocher (SVP) and voted out the CVP federal councillor Ruth Metzler. The SVP now had two seats and the CVP only one.
33466.m: With Blocher's election in 2003, the SVP gained a second Federal Council seat at the CVP's expense.

33467.q: Which party gained a second seat on the Federal Council with the magic formula in 1959?
33467.e: From 1954 to 1959 there was no Social Democrat on the Federal Council. In 1959 the SP received two seats, and the FDP and Catholic Conservatives each gave up one in return.
33467.m: With the magic formula, the SP got two Federal Council seats in 1959.

33468.q: How long did the magic formula remain unchanged?
33468.e: The distribution only changed with the election of Christoph Blocher in 2003. The SVP gained a second seat and the CVP lost one.
33468.m: The magic formula lasted from 1959 to 2003.

33469.q: Roughly how many “Fichen” (index cards) did state security in Switzerland create between 1900 and 1990?
33469.e: The Federal Police and cantonal offices collected around 900,000 index cards on people and organisations. Their discovery in 1989 triggered a national crisis.
33469.m: State security had created around 900,000 index cards.

33470.q: Which body uncovered the systematic surveillance by state security in 1989?
a: The Control Committee of the Council of States
33470.e: A parliamentary commission of inquiry (PUK) examined what had happened in the Federal Department of Justice and Police and presented its report in November 1989. In doing so it came across the huge card index of the Federal Police.
33470.m: A parliamentary commission of inquiry brought the secret files scandal to light.

33471.q: Which federal office kept the central card index of files?
a: The Federal Police of the Office of the Attorney General
33471.e: The political police was part of the Office of the Attorney General and collected information about suspected people. Cantonal police offices sent it many reports.
33471.m: The Federal Police kept the federal card index of files.

33472.q: Who had state security mainly kept under surveillance?
33472.e: In the climate of the Cold War, left-wingers, peace activists, trade unionists and many foreigners were regarded as suspicious. Often harmless activities such as attending demonstrations were noted down.
33472.m: During the Cold War, state security mainly watched people on the political left.

33473.q: How many people demonstrated in Bern on 3 March 1990 against the “snooping state”?
33473.e: About 30,000 people protested on the Bundesplatz against the surveillance. It was one of the largest demonstrations of that time.
33473.m: Around 30,000 people protested in Bern in 1990 against the snooping state.

33474.q: What could citizens request after the secret files scandal?
a: The abolition of the Federal Police by signature
33474.e: Hundreds of thousands asked to see their file. They received copies in which the names of third parties had been blacked out.
33474.m: After the scandal, people were allowed to see their own file.

33475.q: Which secret organisation was revealed in 1990 during the investigations after the secret files scandal?
33475.e: A second parliamentary commission of inquiry, which examined the Military Department, came across the secret cadre organisation P-26. It was meant to put up resistance in the event of an occupation.
33475.m: The inquiry into the Military Department uncovered the secret organisation P-26 in 1990.

33476.q: How did the National Action's initiative against “foreign infiltration” fare in 1974?
a: Rejected with about 66 per cent voting no
Accepted with about 52 per cent voting yes
Rejected with about 51 per cent voting no
33476.e: The 1974 initiative demanded even greater cuts than the one of 1970. It was clearly rejected, with about two thirds voting no.
33476.m: The second initiative against “foreign infiltration” failed clearly in 1974.

33477.q: To what share did the Schwarzenbach initiative want to limit the foreign population in each canton?
33477.e: The initiative demanded an upper limit of 10 per cent per canton. An exception of 25 per cent was planned for Geneva.
33477.m: The Schwarzenbach initiative wanted to reduce the share of foreigners to 10 per cent.

33478.q: For which canton did the Schwarzenbach initiative provide an exception?
33478.e: Because of the international organisations, Geneva was to be allowed a higher share of foreigners of 25 per cent. All the other cantons would have had to keep to the 10 per cent limit.
33478.m: Geneva would have been the only canton allowed to keep more foreigners.

33479.q: Which movement did James Schwarzenbach belong to as a member of the National Council in 1970?
a: National Action against the Foreign Infiltration of People and Homeland
33479.e: Schwarzenbach had been elected to the National Council for the National Action in 1967. The movement campaigned against so-called foreign infiltration.
33479.m: James Schwarzenbach sat in the National Council for the National Action.

33480.q: How narrowly was the Schwarzenbach initiative rejected on 7 June 1970?
a: With about 54 per cent voting no
With about 90 per cent voting no
With about 75 per cent voting no
With about 66 per cent voting no
33480.e: The initiative was rejected with 54 per cent voting no, on a very high turnout of about 75 per cent. The narrow result showed how controversial policy on foreigners was.
33480.m: The Schwarzenbach initiative failed only narrowly in 1970.

33481.q: Roughly how many foreigners would have had to leave Switzerland if the Schwarzenbach initiative had been accepted?
33481.e: To reach the 10 per cent limit, an estimated 300,000 people would have had to leave. Italian workers would have been affected most.
33481.m: The initiative would have forced around 300,000 people to leave.

33482.q: Why were women not allowed to vote on the Schwarzenbach initiative in 1970?
a: Women only got the vote at federal level from 1971
Women were excluded from questions about foreigners
The vote only took place in parliament
It was purely a cantonal vote
33482.e: Women's suffrage at federal level was only accepted on 7 February 1971. That is why only men voted in 1970.
33482.m: Only men decided on the Schwarzenbach initiative in 1970.

33483.q: What did the seasonal worker statute regulate?
a: Temporary work permits for foreign workers for a few months
The opening hours of hotels in the winter season
The naturalisation of children of foreign parents
33483.e: Seasonal workers were allowed to work in Switzerland for a maximum of nine months a year, for example in construction or in hotels and restaurants. After that they had to return to their home country.
33483.m: Seasonal workers were only allowed to work in Switzerland for a few months a year.

33484.q: What were seasonal workers in Switzerland generally not allowed to do?
a: Bring their family to join them
Be a member of a trade union
33484.e: At first, seasonal workers were not allowed to bring their family to Switzerland. This only became possible under strict conditions after several full seasons.
33484.m: For a long time, seasonal workers were not allowed to bring their families.

33485.q: What abolished the seasonal worker statute in 2002?
a: The free movement of persons with the EU
33485.e: With the Bilateral Agreements I, the free movement of persons came into force in 2002. This ended the controversial seasonal worker statute. Switzerland has never joined the EEA.
33485.m: The free movement of persons ended the seasonal worker statute in 2002.

33486.q: After how many consecutive full seasons could a seasonal worker receive an annual residence permit?
33486.e: Anyone who had worked the full season four years in a row could apply to convert it into an annual permit. Only then was bringing the family also possible.
33486.m: After four full seasons, a seasonal worker could apply for an annual permit.

33487.q: Why did many children of seasonal workers live secretly in Switzerland?
a: Seasonal workers were not allowed to bring their families
They had to hide from military service
Foreign children were not allowed to go to school
Their parents had no work permit
33487.e: Because family reunification was forbidden, an estimated tens of thousands of children lived hidden with their parents. Many were not allowed to go to school for years and hardly ever went outside.
33487.m: Because of the seasonal worker statute, many children had to live in hiding.

33488.q: Which model of policy on foreigners increasingly excluded seasonal workers from states such as Yugoslavia from 1991?
33488.e: The three-circle model favoured workers from EC and EFTA states. People from the third circle, for example from Yugoslavia, were hardly admitted any more.
33488.m: From 1991, the three-circle model divided countries of origin into groups.

33489.q: In which disaster in Valais in 1965 did 88 workers die, many of them Italian seasonal workers?
33489.e: During the construction of the Mattmark dam, a piece of glacier broke off and buried the workers' huts. 56 of the 88 dead were Italians.
33489.m: The Mattmark disaster of 1965 mainly struck Italian guest workers.

33490.q: In which canton is Kaiseraugst, where the building site of a nuclear power station was occupied in 1975?
33490.e: Kaiseraugst is in the Fricktal in the canton of Aargau, near the border with Basel-Landschaft. The resistance came strongly from the whole of north-western Switzerland.
33490.m: Kaiseraugst lies on the Rhine in the canton of Aargau.

33491.q: In which month of 1975 did the large occupation of the building site in Kaiseraugst begin?
33491.e: On 1 April 1975, opponents of nuclear power occupied the building site. Many people first thought the news was an April Fool's joke.
33491.m: The occupation of Kaiseraugst began in April 1975.

33492.q: Roughly how many people took part in the occupation in Kaiseraugst in 1975?
33492.e: In total, about 15,000 people occupied the site and held up the excavation work. They came from very different political camps.
33492.m: Around 15,000 people took part in the occupation of Kaiseraugst.

33493.q: How long did the occupation of the Kaiseraugst building site last in 1975?
33493.e: The occupiers held out for eleven weeks. After that, the authorities postponed the start of construction and negotiated with the opponents.
33493.m: The occupation of Kaiseraugst lasted eleven weeks.

33494.q: How did the Kaiseraugst nuclear power station project end?
a: It was abandoned for political reasons in 1988
It was demolished in 2011 after Fukushima
It was converted into a gas power station
33494.e: At the end of the 1980s, the project was dropped for political reasons; 1988 is regarded as the year it was abandoned. The power station was never built.
33494.m: The Kaiseraugst nuclear power station was never built.

33495.q: Which reactor accident in 1986 strengthened resistance to building the Kaiseraugst nuclear power station?
33495.e: After the Chernobyl disaster in the Soviet Union, fear of nuclear accidents grew strongly. Shortly afterwards, the Kaiseraugst project was abandoned.
33495.m: After Chernobyl in 1986, Kaiseraugst could no longer be pushed through politically.

33496.q: Which form of protest mainly characterised the occupation of Kaiseraugst?
a: A hunger strike in the Federal Palace
33496.e: The occupiers followed a non-violent approach and stayed peacefully on the site. Kaiseraugst thus became a symbol of the Swiss anti-nuclear movement.
33496.m: Kaiseraugst is seen as an example of non-violent civil disobedience.

33497.q: Which decision triggered the youth riots in Zurich in 1980?
a: A loan of 60 million francs for the opera house
33497.e: The city approved 60 million francs for renovating the opera house. Young people felt that, in contrast, nothing was being done for their culture.
33497.m: The opera house loan triggered the Zurich youth riots of 1980.

33498.q: What did the young people of the “Movement” in Zurich mainly demand in 1980?
33498.e: The Movement demanded space for a self-managed, alternative youth culture. The AJZ (autonomous youth centre) was the central demand.
33498.m: The Zurich youth movement fought for an autonomous youth centre.

33499.q: By what name is the youth movement that began with the opera house riot known?
33499.e: The riots began in Zurich on the night of 30 to 31 May 1980. The Eighties Movement then also spread to Basel, Bern and Lausanne.
33499.m: The Eighties Movement began with the opera house riot of 1980.

33500.q: Which concert brought extra demonstrators on the evening of the opera house riot?
33500.e: People who had been to a Bob Marley concert in the Hallenstadion joined the demonstration. As a result, the crowd grew a lot.
33500.m: On the evening of the opera house riot, Bob Marley was playing in Zurich.

33501.q: Which slogan became the trademark of the Zurich youth movement?
a: “We want everything, and we want it subito!”
33501.e: The slogan expressed the young people's impatience with the authorities and society. It became one of the best-known slogans of the 1980s.
33501.m: The Eighties Movement wanted “everything, and subito”.

33502.q: What is the name of the Videoladen Zurich documentary about the riots of 1980?
33502.e: “Züri brännt” (“Zurich is burning”) shows the events from the Movement's point of view. The film came out in 1981.
33502.m: The film “Züri brännt” documents the Zurich youth riots.

33503.q: Where was the first autonomous youth centre (AJZ) in Zurich?
33503.e: The AJZ opened in 1980 in a building by the coach park near the main railway station. It was closed several times and demolished in 1982.
33503.m: The first AJZ was next to Zurich main railway station.

33504.q: In which decade did “forest dieback” dominate the environmental debate in Switzerland most?
33504.e: At the beginning of the 1980s, studies showed damaged treetops. Fear of losing the forests became a major political issue.
33504.m: Forest dieback was the big environmental issue of the 1980s.

33505.q: What was mainly blamed for forest dieback?
33505.e: Sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides from traffic, industry and heating were seen as the main cause. They cause acid rain and damage leaves and soils.
33505.m: Air pollution was mainly blamed for forest dieback.

33506.q: Which technical measure against car exhaust became compulsory for new petrol cars in Switzerland from 1987?
33506.e: Strict exhaust rules made the three-way catalytic converter effectively compulsory for new petrol cars. It greatly reduces nitrogen oxide emissions.
33506.m: From 1987, new petrol cars in Switzerland needed a catalytic converter.

33507.q: Which ordinance did the Federal Council issue in 1985 in response to air pollution?
a: The Ordinance on Air Pollution Control
33507.e: The Ordinance on Air Pollution Control (LRV) set limits for pollutants and came into force in 1986. It is based on the Environmental Protection Act of 1983.
33507.m: The Ordinance on Air Pollution Control set limits for air quality.

33508.q: Which chemical accident near Basel turned the Rhine red for many kilometres in 1986?
33508.e: On 1 November 1986, a Sandoz warehouse burned at Schweizerhalle. Poisons got into the Rhine with the water used to put out the fire, and many fish died.
33508.m: The Schweizerhalle fire of 1986 poisoned the Rhine.

33509.q: How does research mostly judge the forest dieback of the 1980s today?
a: The feared large-scale destruction of the forests did not happen
Swiss forests have almost completely died
33509.e: Thanks to measures against air pollution, and because the forecasts were too pessimistic, the great dieback did not happen. But many experts stress that the warnings led to important environmental laws.
33509.m: The feared great forest dieback did not happen in Switzerland.

33510.q: Which federal programme has recorded the health of Swiss forests since the mid-1980s?
33510.e: The Sanasilva inventory has regularly recorded the condition of treetops since 1985. It was created in response to the forest dieback debate.
33510.m: With the Sanasilva programme, the federal government monitored the health of the forest.

33511.q: What did Elisabeth Kopp become in 1984 as the first woman in Swiss history?
33511.e: The Federal Assembly elected Elisabeth Kopp to the Federal Council on 2 October 1984 as the first woman. Until then, only men had formed the national government.
33511.m: In 1984, Elisabeth Kopp was the first woman on the Federal Council.

33512.q: Which party did Elisabeth Kopp belong to?
33512.e: Kopp belonged to the Free Democrats. From 1979 she sat in the National Council for this party.
33512.m: Elisabeth Kopp was a member of the FDP.

33513.q: Which department did Elisabeth Kopp lead as a federal councillor?
33513.e: Kopp headed the Federal Department of Justice and Police (EJPD). There she was responsible for asylum matters, among other things.
33513.m: Elisabeth Kopp led the Federal Department of Justice and Police.

33514.q: Why did Elisabeth Kopp resign on 12 January 1989?
a: Because of a phone call in which she warned her husband
Because she moved to the UN
Because of a lost popular vote
33514.e: Kopp had advised her husband to step down from the board of a company that was being investigated. Because she kept this quiet, she came under pressure.
33514.m: A phone call with her husband led to Kopp's resignation.

33515.q: Which office would Elisabeth Kopp probably have taken on in 1990 if she had not resigned?
33515.e: In December 1988, Kopp had been elected Vice-President of the Federal Council for 1989. Following the usual order, she would have become President of the Confederation in 1990.
33515.m: Without her resignation, Kopp would have become the first female President of the Confederation in 1990.

33516.q: Who succeeded Elisabeth Kopp on the Federal Council in 1989?
33516.e: The Federal Assembly elected the Lucerne Free Democrat Kaspar Villiger. He first took over the Military Department.
33516.m: Kaspar Villiger succeeded Elisabeth Kopp in 1989.

33517.q: How did the criminal proceedings against Elisabeth Kopp for breach of official secrecy end?
a: With an acquittal by the Federal Supreme Court
33517.e: The Federal Supreme Court acquitted Kopp in 1990. Politically, however, her resignation remained a major turning point.
33517.m: Elisabeth Kopp was acquitted by the Federal Supreme Court.

33518.q: Which organisation launched the popular initiative “For a Switzerland without an army”?
a: The Group for a Switzerland without an Army (GSoA)
33518.e: The GSoA was founded in 1982 and submitted the initiative in 1986. It demanded the abolition of the army and a comprehensive peace policy.
33518.m: The GSoA launched the initiative to abolish the army.

33519.q: Which duty for Swiss men would the initiative “For a Switzerland without an army” have abolished in 1989?
33519.e: Without an army, general conscription would also have disappeared. The initiative was rejected on 26 November 1989, and compulsory service still applies today.
33519.m: In 1989, Switzerland voted on abolishing the army and thus compulsory service.

33520.q: What percentage of yes votes did the initiative to abolish the army receive in 1989?
33520.e: The initiative was rejected but reached 35.6 per cent yes. Many observers were surprised by this high share.
33520.m: More than a third voted to abolish the army in 1989.

33521.q: Which two cantons accepted the initiative to abolish the army in 1989?
33521.e: Only in the cantons of Jura and Geneva was there a yes majority. Overall, the people and the cantons rejected the initiative.
33521.m: Jura and Geneva were the only cantons to vote for abolishing the army.

33522.q: Which reform followed the initiative to abolish the army in the 1990s, among other things?
a: The introduction of a professional army
33522.e: In 1992, the people accepted a constitutional article for an alternative civilian service, which started in 1996. Before that, conscientious objectors were punished.
33522.m: Since 1996, Switzerland has had a civilian service.

33523.q: How did the GSoA's second initiative to abolish the army fare in 2001?
a: It only received about 22 per cent yes
It received about 45 per cent yes
33523.e: The initiative “For a credible security policy and a Switzerland without an army” reached only 21.9 per cent yes on 2 December 2001. That was much less than in 1989.
33523.m: The second initiative to abolish the army failed clearly in 2001.

33524.q: Which world event took place only a few weeks before the vote on abolishing the army?
a: The fall of the Berlin Wall
33524.e: The Berlin Wall fell on 9 November 1989. The end of the Cold War influenced the debate about the army.
33524.m: The vote on abolishing the army took place shortly after the fall of the Wall.

a: Accounts whose owners have not been in touch for a long time
33525.e: These are balances whose holders the bank no longer has any contact with. In the 1990s, the issue was mainly the accounts of Holocaust victims.
33525.m: Dormant assets are accounts with no contact with the people entitled to them.

33526.q: Which security guard rescued files from the shredding room of a major bank in 1997?
33526.e: At the Union Bank of Switzerland, Christoph Meili found documents from the time of the Second World War that were due to be destroyed. He handed them over to a Jewish organisation.
33526.m: In 1997, Christoph Meili saved bank files from the shredder.

33527.q: Which commission investigated Switzerland's role in the Second World War on behalf of the federal government from 1996?
33527.e: The Independent Commission of Experts under the historian Jean-François Bergier examined refugee policy as well as gold and economic relations. Its final report came out in 2002.
33527.m: The Bergier Commission researched Switzerland in the Second World War.

33528.q: How large was the settlement that UBS and Credit Suisse reached with class action plaintiffs in the USA in 1998?
33528.e: In August 1998, the big banks agreed to pay 1.25 billion dollars. This settled the class actions.
33528.m: In 1998, the big Swiss banks paid a settlement of 1.25 billion dollars.

33529.q: Which international organisation pushed the debate about dormant assets forward most strongly in the 1990s?
33529.e: The World Jewish Congress under Edgar Bronfman demanded clarification and the return of the money. It was supported by US Senator Alfonse D'Amato.
33529.m: The World Jewish Congress pressed for the dormant assets to be cleared up.

33530.q: Which federal councillor caused outrage in 1996 by saying the demands were a kind of “blackmail”?
33530.e: At the end of 1996, President of the Confederation Delamuraz from Vaud spoke of blackmail and ransom. He later apologised for the remark.
33530.m: In 1996, Federal Councillor Delamuraz caused outrage with his accusation of blackmail.

33531.q: Which body, led by a former head of the US central bank, searched Swiss bank accounts from 1996?
33531.e: The ICEP under Paul Volcker had millions of accounts checked. It found around 54,000 accounts with a possible link to Holocaust victims.
33531.m: The Volcker Commission examined the accounts of Swiss banks.

33532.q: What was the name of the holding company that Swissair belonged to at the time of the grounding?
33532.e: Besides the airline, SAirGroup also included catering, ground handling and shareholdings. Its collapse dragged Swissair down with it.

33533.q: What was the name of the expansion strategy that led Swissair into crisis?
33533.e: With the Hunter strategy, Swissair bought stakes in many smaller airlines. These holdings caused enormous losses.

33534.q: In which Belgian airline did Swissair have a large stake?
33534.e: Swissair held 49.5 per cent of Sabena. The Belgian airline made heavy losses and also went bankrupt in November 2001.
33534.m: The stake in Sabena was a heavy burden on Swissair.

33535.q: Which airline was created in 2002 as the successor to Swissair?
33535.e: Swiss was formed in 2002 from the regional airline Crossair and parts of Swissair. Since 2005 it has belonged to the Lufthansa Group.
33535.m: Swiss is the successor to Swissair.

33536.q: Which world event in autumn 2001 made Swissair's financial difficulties even worse?
a: The outbreak of the Iraq War
33536.e: After the attacks in the USA, air traffic collapsed worldwide. For Swissair, which was already deep in debt, this came at the worst possible time.
33536.m: The attacks of 11 September 2001 made the Swissair crisis worse.

33537.q: Which regional airline formed the basis for the new Swiss in 2002?
33537.e: Crossair from Basel was a subsidiary of SAirGroup and survived the grounding. It was renamed and took over parts of the Swissair fleet.

33538.q: How did the criminal trial of the former Swissair managers end in 2007?
a: With acquittals for all the accused
With a conviction of the whole board of directors
It was never held because of the statute of limitations
33538.e: In 2007, the Bülach District Court acquitted all 19 accused. Many people found the verdict unsatisfactory.
33538.m: In the Swissair trial of 2007, all the accused were acquitted.

33539.q: Which vote in 1992 led Switzerland to take the bilateral path with the EU?
a: The no to joining the EEA
The no to joining the UN
The yes to the Alpine Initiative
33539.e: On 6 December 1992, the people and the cantons narrowly rejected joining the European Economic Area. After that, Switzerland negotiated individual treaties with the EU.
33539.m: After the EEA no in 1992, Switzerland chose the bilateral path.

33540.q: What did the people accept with about 56 per cent yes on 25 September 2005?
a: Extending the free movement of persons to ten new EU states
33540.e: After the EU's eastward enlargement in 2004, the free movement of persons had to be extended to the new member states. The people agreed with about 56 per cent.
33540.m: In 2005, Switzerland extended the free movement of persons to the new EU states.

33541.q: What are the measures called that, since 2004, are meant to protect Swiss wages from wage dumping under the free movement of persons?
33541.e: The flanking measures allow wages and working conditions to be checked, including for posted workers. They came into force on 1 June 2004.
33541.m: The flanking measures protect wages in Switzerland.

33542.q: With what share of yes votes did the people accept the Bilateral Agreements I on 21 May 2000?
33542.e: Voters said yes with 67.2 per cent. This cleared the way for the agreements.
33542.m: Two thirds voted for the Bilateral Agreements I in 2000.

33543.q: Which agreement of the Bilateral Agreements I regulates, among other things, heavy goods traffic across the Alps and the lorry charge?
33543.e: The Land Transport Agreement allows Switzerland to levy the performance-related heavy vehicle charge (LSVA). In return, the weight limit for lorries was raised to 40 tonnes.
33543.m: The Land Transport Agreement regulates lorry traffic through the Alps.

33544.q: Which older agreement from 1972 still regulates duty-free trade in industrial goods between Switzerland and the EU today?
33544.e: The Free Trade Agreement was accepted by the people in 1972 with about 72 per cent. It removed customs duties on industrial goods.
33544.m: The Free Trade Agreement of 1972 is the basis of trade with the EU.

33545.q: Which popular initiative to end the free movement of persons did the people reject in September 2020?
33545.e: The Limitation Initiative was rejected on 27 September 2020 with about 62 per cent voting no. If it had been accepted, the Bilateral Agreements I could have been terminated.
33545.m: In 2020, the people rejected the Limitation Initiative.

33546.q: What is the package of agreements with the EU called whose negotiations were concluded in substance in December 2024?
33546.e: The package updates existing agreements and adds new ones, for example on electricity and health. The negotiations were concluded on 20 December 2024.
33546.m: The new package with the EU is called Bilaterals III.

33547.q: In which package of agreements was Switzerland's association with Schengen included?
a: In the Free Trade Agreement of 1972
33547.e: Schengen and Dublin were part of the Bilateral Agreements II, signed in October 2004. They also included agreements on fighting fraud and on taxing savings.
33547.m: The association with Schengen was part of the Bilateral Agreements II.

33548.q: With what share of yes votes did the people approve Schengen and Dublin on 5 June 2005?
33548.e: The proposal was accepted with 54.6 per cent yes. Opponents of closer ties with the EU had called the referendum.
33548.m: Schengen and Dublin were accepted in 2005 with almost 55 per cent.
